#3371. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3370. 39 Years Later, Inigo Montoya's Princess Bride Line Is Still The Greatest Movie Quote Ever

Do you love big, sweeping, epic romances where the lovers are kept apart for years, only to reunite in a scene that takes your breath away? Do you love clever, quippy, dialogue? Do you love swashbuckling adventures with a touch of vengeance? Great news. "The Princess Bride" has literally all of those things.

In 1987, writer-director Rob Reiner released "The Princess Bride," an adaptation of William Goldman's novel of the same name — and with Goldman adapting his own work into the screenplay, every second isn't just true to the book, but elevates the material. Robin Wright made her feature film debut as Princess Buttercup, a lovelorn woman who mourns the apparent loss of her one true love, a stable boy named Westley (Cary Elwes), and, believing him dead, agrees to marry the horrible Prince Humperdinck (Chris Sarandon). Elsewhere, swordsman Inigo Montoya (Mandy Patinkin), who always travels with the friendly giant Fezzik (André the Giant), wants revenge on the man who killed his father, and when Westley reappears as the Dread Pirate Roberts, he ends up teaming up with Inigo and Fezzik to also rescue Buttercup. Wallace Shawn, Carol Kane, and Billy Crystal play pivotal supporting roles in this film. It's basically perfect.

If you've seen "The Princess Bride" — and the odds are that you have — you know it's chock-a-block full of quotable lines. Today, though, we're celebrating one of its most beloved and well-known quotes, 39 years after its release.

Throughout "The Princess Bride," Mandy Patinkin's dashing and skilled swordsman Inigo Montoya has one goal: to find the six-fingered man who killed his father when Inigo was just a boy. For years, Inigo has been searching for this specific killer to avenge his dear old dad — and he finds him in the film in the form of Count Tyrone Rugen (Christopher Guest). So why is this line so important to the film, and why is it so beloved after nearly four decades?

For one thing, Inigo says it, like, 80 times in the movie, so it's easy to remember. It's a testament to Rob Reiner's sharp, exacting sense of comedic timing that the line never loses any luster, but remains funny every single time Patinkin delivers it (which is also a credit to Patinkin, a truly formidable performer who's been excellent for generations at this point). It's also connected to the movie's enduring message of love, even though it definitely seems a little more murdery than the flowery declarations of passion exchanged between Westley and Buttercup. Inigo truly loved his father, and once he kills the genuinely evil Rugen, the character delivers a line that defined Patinkin's actual life.

Reiner, who was tragically killed alongside his wife Michele Singer Reiner in late 2025 at his home in Los Angeles, made movies with big jokes and even bigger hearts. This line perfectly exemplifies that, and across the board, "The Princess Bride" is one of his very best films. So what other "Princess Bride" quotes stand the test of time?

Hitmen are pretty common in the film landscape. They’re often the epitome of masculinity, secrecy, and, to some, sex appeal. We’re used to seeing hitmen depicted one way in movies, books, and TV shows. However, the idea of the typical hitman has evolved. Wild Horse Nine, which hits the 2026 movie schedule this weekend, may be one of the best representations of the evolution of the hitman.

John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell star as Chris and Lee, two hitmen on one final adventure. It’s one of Malkovich’s best works and a film sure to gain a lot of award season attention. It’s a good film that thrives on its performances. The film also highlights that hitmen can have feelings.

Warning: Wild Horse Nine spoilers are ahead. Proceed with caution.

Wild Horse Nine is an impeccable bromance movie. It could rank among the best of this genre. Unlike writer and director Martin McDonagh’s Oscar-nominated The Banshees of Inisherin, this is very much a film about two men who still love each other. They’re not choosing to end their friendship; life is choosing for them. Lee and Chris aren’t overly emotional in the way people often characterize that trait. They don’t cry a lot in Wild Horse Nine.

However, they show their emotions in other ways, like being impulsive, irrational, and guided by love more than duty. That’s not often how hitmen are portrayed. They’re dedicated to their jobs and more emotionless. They make calculated decisions and avoid risky actions. That’s not Lee or Chris in Wild Horse Nine. McDonagh is a master at showcasing men as emotional creatures who act and behave like that, but in a very realistic way.

Men are humans. Humans are often emotional, even if they pretend to be steadier and more stable than they actually are.

Many of the best action movies (even lesser-known ones) focus on assassins or hitmen who live by a strict set of rules. This often includes not getting too close to anyone, because they cannot tell them about their profession. It would put this person’s life in danger. This is a common storyline that usually works well on film.

However, Wild Horse Nine showcases two men who have allowed themselves vulnerability. Chris even says in his recordings that he never really had a friend until Lee. I like the idea that hitmen live a lonely life, but they can sometimes let people in. It’s a risk, but most things in life are.

Chris and Lee are technically good at their jobs, especially Chris. He allegedly committed one of the most well-known assassinations in history. However, one of the signs of his deteriorating health is how bad he is becoming at assassinating. This is the comedy in Wild Horse Nine. However, even before Chris starts to lose his suave criminal behavior, I am not convinced these are top-level hitmen.

They make so many easily avoidable mistakes. Nonetheless, the movie wouldn’t be as fun if they were these flawless murderers. Wild Horse Nine showcases the marvel of being a flawed human, even with such a highly skilled profession. Wild Horse Nine is a must-watch fall movie.

I was fortunate enough to see an early screening of Wild Horse Nine at the 62nd Chicago International Film Festival. Catch it everywhere on November 6.

#3368. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.

#3367. Set Phasers To Stun: Star Trek's Different Phaser Settings Explained

Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

When Gene Roddenberry was first assembling "Star Trek" in the mid-1960s, the term "laser guns" was common enough sci-fi parlance that he astutely wanted to avoid using it. To make "Star Trek" seem a little more futuristic, Roddenberry invented "phasers" instead of "lasers," and the weapon became a staple of the franchise. Starfleet vessels are equipped with powerful phaser weapons used for ship-to-ship combat, and Starfleet officers carry hand-held phasers into potentially dangerous situations.

In the pilot episode for "Star Trek: Enterprise," a series set a century prior to the events of the original "Star Trek," Captain Archer (Scott Bakula) was shown a hand-held phaser — then called a phase pistol — for the first time, so Starfleet has been using them since the very start. Phasers tend to fire single, confined beams, but would also eventually come to fire brief, bullet-like pulses.

"Star Trek," however, is also meant to take place in a peaceful utopia, so the phasers were said to have a "stun" setting that could render an attacker unconscious from a distance. Only in extreme scenarios would a phaser be adjusted to the "kill" setting, which could blast the life out of someone. Indeed, throughout "Star Trek," the powerful kill setting was seen to vaporize a person's body entirely.

On "Enterprise," phasers only had "stun" and "kill" settings, but later on, there were other, gentler settings. Throughout the franchise, characters have been explicit about the various settings a hand phaser was capable of using, sometimes referring to "light stun," "heavy stun," or a numerical system.

What do those numbers and settings mean? Let's take a look.

Eagle-eyed "Star Trek" viewers might notice that Starfleet officers typically use two different types of phasers. The Type-1 phasers are the smaller, thumb-activated, remote-control-looking widgets, while the larger, pistol-shaped phasers are Type-2. On "Next Generation," the Type-2 also became a thumb-operated device. Only very occasionally would one see a larger phaser rifle, like the one Captain Kirk (William Shatner) used in the episode "Where No Man Has Gone Before."

In the "Star Trek: Discovery" episode "Saints of Imperfection," Tilly (Mary Wiseman) also noted that the rifle is designated a Type-3 weapon by saying, "It is more powerful and generally larger than the Type-1 or Type-2, which I guess is why they call it a 3."

The original phaser sound effect, a high-pitched whine, was repurposed from the 1953 film "The War of the Worlds." The common "Star Trek" phaser sound has remained a variant of that whine ever since.

It was in the episode "The Enemy Within" that "setting one," a phaser's lowest setting, was first mentioned. This was enough to, well, stun the average humanoid. In the episode "The Return of the Archons," the Enterprise crew set their phasers to a wide-beam setting that could essentially spray across a crowd, stunning multiple people at once. (It's a good thing I don't have a phaser with a wide-beam setting; I would never wait in line for a ride at Disneyland ever again.)

On "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine," specifically in the episode "Homefront," there was some mention that setting 3.5 or 3.6 constituted a "heavy stun." It wouldn't be until a phaser was set to setting 10 that it would be capable of vaporizing someone. Starfleet seems more interested in gradations of stunning someone before it considers a kill setting ... but those puppies can do a lot of damage.

In the "Next Generation" episode "Frame of Mind," Riker (Jonathan Frakes) has a scene where he sets a Type-2 phaser to its maximum setting of 16. He states out loud that if a phaser were to fire at such a setting, it would destroy half the building. Phasers, if wielded irresponsibly, could apparently do a great deal of damage. Of course, these are hand-held devices and don't have an infinite power supply. I think it's safe to assume that a phaser, firing a level-16 blast, could only do it once. I'd hate to live in a world where someone could stroll through a city, blasting open multiple buildings willy-nilly with a single handgun-sized object.

A stun setting could knock someone out without leaving a mark, but, judging by various makeup jobs seen throughout "Star Trek," heavier settings left bruises or even burn marks on people. Before you think you could withstand a heavy stun, watch one of those foolish online videos where macho idiots — or perhaps just the cast members of the "Jackass" crew — test to see if they can withstand a taser or pepper spray. I imagine a phaser blast would be the sci-fi version of that.

Of course, throughout "Star Trek," officers also used phasers for things other than tactical confrontations. They could be used as cutting torches, or to heat up rocks in order to keep warm in frozen climates. In the "Next Generation" episode "Disaster," a phaser's power cell was used as a power source for a computer terminal. Phasers may have the ability to explode entire buildings, but they are more often used as tools in a Starfleet officer's toolbox.

#3366. How Elizabeth Taylor’s Childhood and Career Were Defined by Her Overbearing Mother

Elizabeth Taylor, like many other actors of her time, experienced the demands of Hollywood from a very young age. Her parents could never have imagined on February 27, 1932, just how much their newborn baby would achieve artistically. Sooner rather than later, however, they recognized her potential. Although she spent most of her life in Southern California in the heart of the movie industry, Taylor was born in Hampstead, England, to an American family consisting of her father, Francis Lenn Taylor, her mother, Sara Sothern, and their son, Howard, the movie star’s brother with whom she was close. They didn’t remain in Great Britain long, returning to the United States in 1939, shortly before World War II.

Sara Sothern with her children, Elizabeth and Howard Taylor.

The family sailed from London to New York and then settled in Los Angeles. By then, Taylor already had some experience in the performing arts, as she had been taking ballet lessons since she was just three years old. She made her debut in a recital that same year. Once in California, the father of the violet-eyed legend opened an art gallery featuring works imported from the UK. This would turn out to be an important step that brought the Taylors into the world of Hollywood. As biographer Alexander Walker would recount in Elizabeth: The Life of Elizabeth Taylor (Grove Press), the space “opened many doors for the Taylors, leading them directly into the society of money and prestige.”

Despite their differences, mother and daughter grew closer as they matured.

Sothern, the mother of this acting prodigy, saw her daughter as the perfect excuse to live the dream she didn’t fulfill because she was focused on caring for her family. If she couldn’t pursue an acting career, her daughter would. Seeing the effect that Taylor’s beauty had on others, Sothern set out to introduce her to people in the film industry. “Elizabeth Taylor probably wouldn’t have been an actress if it hadn’t been for her mother,” notes actor George Hamilton in the BBC documentary Elizabeth Taylor: Rebel Superstar. In this same documentary, Liz herself can be heard saying in an old recording: “My mother was an actress, but then she married my father, and he didn’t want her to be one, so she gave it up. I think she lived her life through me.”

Kate Andersen Brower, author of Elizabeth Taylor: The Grit and Glamour of an Icon (Harper Collins), explains that Sothern was behind the scenes trying to control every aspect of her daughter’s life in order to make her famous. This included sending Taylor to the same schools as the children of movie studio executives. Soon, thanks to a meeting with the fiancée of a high-ranking Universal Pictures exec who visited the gallery run by Taylor’s father, Elizabeth made her big-screen debut. Her early Hollywood years were propelled by connections her mother painstakingly built.

In 1949, Elizabeth Taylor and Sara Sothern pose at their home in Beverly Hills.

Taylor’s first movie was There’s One Born Every Minute, filmed when she was only 10 years old. Also starring Carl Switzer, who played Alfalfa in Our Gang, it was not a success, and Universal chose not to extend her option. Andersen Brower quotes the studio’s casting director: “The kid has nothing. Her eyes are too old; she doesn’t have the face of a kid.” Sara persisted, however, and through her husband, she met Sam Marx, a producer working on an MGM film, Lassie Come Home. Taylor would be cast in a small role.

Elizabeth Taylor and her mother in a 1948 photo taken in London.

Its success paved the way for another milestone in Taylor’s early career. At age 12, she landed the role of Velvet Brown in National Velvet, alongside Mickey Rooney and Angela Lansbury. Released in December 1944, it grossed almost $6 million worldwide, making it one of MGM’s top films of that period. Taylor signed a new contract with the studio, though she later complained about how she was treated by its head, Louis B. Mayer.

Elizabeth Taylor helps her mother prepare hot dogs and hamburgers at their home in Los Angeles in 1947.

At the same time, her father was both astonished by and jealous of his teenage daughter’s success. An alcoholic and physically abusive, on one occasion he punched her in the jaw, and for the rest of her life, she suffered from TMJ, or lockjaw. Andersen Brower writes, “She explained it away—as she always had—saying that her father was embarrassed that Taylor was the breadwinner of the family and that he felt emasculated.”

Sothern was a practicing Christian (though she was also interested in Judaism, which may have contributed to Taylor’s decision to convert to that religion so that she could marry Eddie Fisher, her fourth husband), and she taught her daughter from an early age that she could not sleep with any man until she was married to him. It’s a view that Taylor appears to have adopted: “Nothing comes off until the ring goes on,” she told gossip columnist Louella Parsons. Sothern, however, had her doubts. Before Taylor married Conrad “Nicky” Hilton in 1950, when she was just 18 years old, Sothern paid a doctor to confirm that her daughter was still a virgin and also to open her hymen to spare her pain during the first time she had sex.

Years later, Taylor would admit that her early years in the film industry were not easy. Her parents spent practically all the money she earned as a child actor. In a 1997 interview with Barbara Walters on 20/20, she described her childhood as “lonely.” She once confided to her close friend George Hamilton that she just wanted “to be a little girl again,” to relive those years that she never got to enjoy.

It won't be long before HBO's Harry Potter series hits the 2026 TV schedule and fans of various generations are introduced to a new take on the Wizarding World. So, this streaming schedule will see a whole new set of actors bringing their own doses of magic to the franchise's iconic characters. That includes Fred and George Weasley, and actors Oliver and James Phelps (who originated the roles in the films) have made a lovely gesture to their successors. And as a fan, I couldn't love this more!

For the highly anticipated Harry Potter TV show, Tristan and Gabriel Harland will be playing the troublesome but lovable Weasley Twins. James and Oliver Phelps recently spoke with TV Insider while promoting the latest season of their show, Wizards of Baking, and discussed the newcomers. Oliver revealed that after the Harlands were cast, he and James sent a personal message to Tristian and Gabriel:

We dropped them each an individual letter, just saying some experiences we’ve had over the years, and wishing them all the best with it. And it was a very, very, very private message or note, but it was more a case of wishing them all the best with what they’re doing, which I know that a few of the other cast members from the films have done as well.

I love that! When I hear that James and Oliver Phelps sent letters to the actors of the TV series, it reminds me of Harry getting his Hogwarts letter in the mail for the first time. As young Potter was given the opportunity of a lifetime through a letter, the Phelps' gesture somewhat mirrors that. On top of that, though, this is also just feels like a natural passing-of-the-torch moment.

Another reason I commend the Phelps Twins for reaching out to Tristan and Gabriel Harland is that instead of offering them advice, they simply chose to wish them the best in these iconic roles. Here's Oliver Phelps’ reasoning for that:

We just wish the best for those guys on their journey, because we were very lucky to have been able to play the characters for when we did.

Oliver and James Phelps truly are incredibly lucky to have had their Harry Potter experience, and they certainly seem to be cognizant of that. With all the new young actors taking over, I'm hopeful that their time playing these characters will be just as enjoyable as their predecessors'.

When the Phelps siblings previously weighed in on new actors portraying Fred and George, they said they wanted to give the new actors “their own space” to do their own interpretations. The British actors said, though, that they would always available for the new stars should they need help. It's great that the Phelps want the Harlands to have their own freedom to explore these roles, just like they themselves did in the movies.

So, wands up for Oliver and James Phelps for wishing the new Weasley Twins the best of luck. At this point, I'm all the more psyched to see how Tristan and Gabriel Harland will bring their own originality to the troublemaking twins we all love. (And I’m truly hoping the Phelps Twins’ TV series wish comes true, in that the Harland Brothers get to play out the Chamber of Secrets de-gnoming scene.)

Check out the new Harry Potter TV series when it premieres on HBO on Christmas Day and becomes available with an HBO Max subscription. The OG films are also available to stream on the same streamer. You can also find the Phelps Twins’ Wizards of Baking series streaming on that service, and new episodes air on Wednesday nights at 8/7c on Food Network.

#3363. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.

#3362. Disney Tried To Resurrect A Groundbreaking '60s Sitcom With A Movie That Bombed

In 1999, Disney decided it was time to bring back a 1960s sitcom about a lovable alien who shacks up with a newspaper reporter. It wasn't the most convincing reboot idea the studio ever had, but Disney pushed ahead with "My Favorite Martian" anyway. Unfortunately, the movie made just over half its budget back and has — like the sitcom on which it was based — been mostly forgotten.

"My Favorite Martian" became America's first fantasy sci-fi sitcom when it debuted in 1963, beating more well-known examples of the format such as "Bewitched" and "I Dream of Jeannie." "Mister Ed" had arrived two years prior and introduced the concept of a fantastical character being thrown into an otherwise standard sitcom setup (i.e. a talking horse living with an architect in his suburban home). But "My Favorite Martian" was the first sitcom to feature a human-looking being with fantastical powers. As such, it remains one of the most significant and quietly influential sitcoms in TV history.

The movie version, however, was neither significant nor influential. Disney brought in Christopher Lloyd and Jeff Daniels to lead this ill-advised reboot, which debuted in February 1999 and ended up making back just $36.8 million against a $65 million budget. What was the plan here? Well, "My Favorite Martian" was conceivably one of several '60s sci-fi shows that deserved a modern reboot. The problem was that the film wasn't any good.

The original version of "My Favorite Martian" is one of the best sci-fi sitcoms that takes place on Earth. It stars Bill Bixby as Los Angeles Sun reporter Tim O'Hara, who discovers the crashed spaceship of a 450-year-old Martian anthropologist (Ray Walston). With the alien's ship completely wrecked, Tim invites him to stay in his garage apartment, where the Martian quickly establishes himself as the wacky yet genial figure of "Uncle Martin." The pair agree to keep Uncle Martin's identity a secret while he tries to repair his ship, but they end up forming a bond that ultimately lasts for three seasons and 107 episodes.

"My Favorite Martian" episodes revolved around Uncle Martin's lack of familiarity with human customs, his incredible powers, and outlandish adventures that saw Tim and his alien pal using time machines and anti-gravity wristbands. The show also featured some esteemed guest stars, including a young Tom Skerritt who appeared in the 1963 episode "Mrs. Jekyll and Hyde." "My Favorite Martian" also welcomed "Gilligan's Island" star Alan Hale Jr., who appeared on an episode of the show the same year he set sail on his fateful voyage on the S.S. Minnow.

The sitcom came to an end in 1966, and 33 years later Disney decided it was time to give it another go. This time, however, the studio tried to reinvent the property as a family friendly big-screen adventure along the lines of "Flubber," which was itself based on a 1960s sci-fi comedy and had been distributed by Disney's Buena Vista Pictures in 1997. "My Favorite Martian," however, was nowhere near as successful as that Robin Williams-led comedy.

"My Favorite Martian" the movie is directed by Donald Petrie of "Mystic Pizza" and "Miss Congeniality" fame. It stars Jeff Daniels as Tim O'Hara, a news producer who, like in the original show, encounters a downed spacecraft while driving. In this version, however, the recently-fired O'Hara sees this discovery as a way to make it back into the news business. Christopher Lloyd plays The Martian, who follows Tim home and ends up staying. While Tim initially plans to expose his new friend and regain his job, he grows fond of Uncle Martin. When SETI starts hunting the pair, they have to work together to evade capture and get Uncle Martin back to his home planet.

Original Uncle Martin actor Ray Walston plays Armitan/Neenert in the film, a fellow Martian who became stranded on Earth years prior. This was a nice little full circle moment as it marked Walston's last theatrical film role prior to his death in 2001. Unfortunately, the film wasn't quite the tribute it could have been.

Aside from barely making half its budget back, "My Favorite Martian" earned a 14% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes. Kevin Thomas of the Los Angeles Times praised Walston for his "crisp wit and blithe sense of whimsy," which according to the critic was "otherwise lacking in this loser." Roger Ebert was slightly kinder, calling the movie "clever in its visuals," but "labored in its audios, and noisy enough to entertain kids up to a certain age." Otherwise the reviews were pretty damning, with Derek Adams of Time Out calling the film simply "Dire." Needless to say this was not one of the best sci-fi movies of 1999. You can see for yourself as the movie is available to watch on Disney+.

#3361. Kate Middleton Dresses Down for Appearance at Mental Health-Focused Charity

During a surprise engagement in West London, Kate Middleton reminded fans that she is the queen of country-set dressing. Prince William's wife joined the team at Dose of Nature, a charity that “prescribes” time spent outdoors to help improve mental health, telling staff members and volunteers that connecting with nature is a “healing” experience for her.

The future queen dressed down for the occasion, wrapping up warm in what looked to be a Barbour jacket and a pair of jeans. She left her hair to flow in waves and accessorized with her trademark “big blue” sapphire engagement ring.

At Pensford Field, where Dose of Nature has a site near Kew, the Princess of Wales met the charity's founder, Dr. Alison Greenwood, and clinical lead, Dr. Georgina Gould, as well as volunteer nature guide Tom, who told Catherine that support from Dose of Nature had made him more confident and resilient.

“Our journey has been very very different, but it’s so wonderful to hear how your nature connection and how it’s been so healing for you, and I felt the same,” Catherine said to him.

“The fact that you’re able to provide that to so many other people in this community; that sense of purpose and meaning, and belonging, through that experience, I think is something that has got the longevity and the sustainability of feeling like, almost without knowing what’s to come, without having the control in your life of knowing what the future might hold, the fact that you feel that you can cope with things, because you feel that interconnection, I think that makes it holistic in a very true essence,” she added.

The Princess of Wales visits Dose of Nature.

Kate Middleton has long been a champion of the importance of nature for mental and physical well-being. In a recent essay, she wrote: “By spending time in nature or being creative, we can nurture the very skills and emotions that cannot be digitised: awareness, empathy, humility, and above all, love.”

The future queen has been working with the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood on a project to “support the healthy development of babies and young children,” as she explained in a recent video, delivered from Cornwall while dressed in ME+EM.

“In this tech-driven, digital age, spending time outdoors has never been more important,” the Princess said.

“This project is about how nature, creativity, and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children,” she continued. “My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children, and their families across the UK.”

The Princess of Wales has spent many years dedicated to early childhood research, working hard advising the Foundation, even during her cancer treatment. This May, she visited the University of East London’s Institute for the Science of Early Years and Youth to see how the University’s researchers use state-of-the-art wearables and brain recording techniques to study how the diverse early living environments and relationships experienced by babies influence early stress—both in the child themselves and their parents and caregivers.

#3360. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

Another weekend means a new set of movies have hit theaters, and a particularly big title made its debut this week. The highly anticipated Godzilla Minus Zero hit cinemas, and it reigned supreme at the box office this weekend. Not only that, but the film set a major milestone in the process. I thought well-reviewed the glowing Minus Zero reviews might help the movie's chances, but I'd be lying if I said I thought it would earn a monster-sized achievement.

The sequel to 2023's Godzilla Minus One, this latest film from director Takashi Yamazaki earned $31,610,000 in its first three days. And, as a result of that, it now holds the all-time record for biggest opening weekend for a foreign live-action film. If anything, Minus Zero proved that shifting the Godzilla IP into weirder territory was the right move. It handily beat out The Cat In The Hat, despite the family-friendly movie's $20,500,000 being above what it was predicted to do by a few million. Check out the full rundown of the weekend below:

In man ways, it's not shocking to Godzilla Minus Zero do so well, given the acclaim the first movie received. However, I still wasn't expecting it to make box office history in such a way. Nevertheless, this weekend, it's the biggest IP out of the group above, and the biggest number-one take in a weekend since Street Fighter first hit the box office. I'm eager to see how it does next week and how it'll hang around the top ten list.

Godzilla Minus Zero Director’s Take On How He’s Adding ‘Terror’ To The Film Has Me Pumped

Wicker, meanwhile, continues to hold strong with a not-so-substantial decline from the previous week. Given there's a strong release lineup set for the rest of November amid the 2026 movie schedule, I wonder if this might be the last week we see the fantasy romance flick and Street Fighter on the Top 10 list.

Honestly, the same could be said about Godzilla Minus Zero as well. I Play Rocky, How To Rob A Bank, Ebenezer and the star-studded Paper Tiger are all just lurking around the corner, waiting for Thanksgiving weekend and people eager to step away from family events to sit in the comfort of their local theater. At the end of the day, I think the consumer is winning, because there will be plenty of great movies to watch in theaters at the end of this month.

For those wanting to see Godzilla Minus Zero but still have yet to see the original, know that Godzilla Minus One is available to stream with a Netflix subscription. I'm in that camp and need to catch up so I can see this acclaimed kaiju movie before it leaves theaters.

#3358. Before Ghost Rider, Nicolas Cage Nearly Played A Very Different Marvel Superhero

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Nicolas Cage is an absolute legend. Along with his Oscar-winning turn in "Leaving Las Vegas" and roles in hits like "National Treasure," he's also played some superheroes in his day. Perhaps most notably, he played Ghost Rider in a pair of films released in 2007 and 2012. This came about years after Cage's "Superman Lives" was canceled. But before he suited up as Johnny Blaze, he almost portrayed another, very different hero from the pages of Marvel Comics.

In a 1997 report from Variety going over the "mania" surrounding Marvel movies in development at that time, it was revealed that Cage was still "firmly" attached to star as "his favorite "Marvel hero," Iron Man. Indeed, more than a decade before Robert Downey Jr. would take on the role as Tony Stark, it was Cage who was being eyed to bring the Marvel Comics hero to life. "Iron Man" became the unlikely superhero that changed Hollywood forever, so Cage taking on the role could have literally rewritten this chapter in cinema history.

At the time, the "Iron man" script was being written by Jeff Vintar ("Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within"), with "Cops" creator John Langley on board to produce alongside Elie Cohn and Stephen Chao. It's unclear who was being eyed to direct or where the project was being set up, but this was just one of many, many Marvel movies in development at the time that never saw the light of day.

As just one example, "Black Panther" was almost made in the '90s with Wesley Snipes, even though he also starred in 1998's "Blade." Mind you, this was ages before the idea of a cinematic universe even existed. That '97 article even mentions a "Hulk" film directed by Joe Johnston ("The Rocketeer") and a "Sliver Surfer" movie, among others.

This was also around the time that director James Cameron was trying to get his "Spider-Man" movie adaptation off the ground. Cameron later called his unmade "Spider-Man" film "the greatest movie I never made."

The point is, there were a lot of superhero films swirling back then that would ultimately never be made. Nicolas Cage was part of that, as his and Tim Burton's "Superman Lives" remains one of the most curious, unrealized pieces of comic book cinema ever conceived. But Cage has been a vocal comic book fan for a very long time and, at least according to Variety at the time, Iron Man was his favorite hero.

It's worth remembering that, back then, Iron Man was far from an A-lister. It wasn't until "Iron Man" director Jon Favreau used a sneaky trick to cast Robert Downey Jr. as Tony Stark, and their ensuing movie became a surprise hit, that he ascended to the A-list. When Cage was eyeing the role, it was for the love of the game, in the hopes of perhaps elevating a character he adored. It didn't pan out. Had it panned out? It could have reshaped Marvel's entire future cinematically.

Instead, Cage's "Ghost Rider" flopped its way to a franchise, with the first movie performing well enough on home media to justify a lower-rent, badly-regarded sequel several years later. It's a shame that Cage didn't get to try his hand at something more befitting his talents in the 2010s, but his unrealized turn as Tony Stark is always going to exist as a curious bit of "What if?" alternate cinema history.

You can grab "Ghost Rider" and "Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance" on DVD from Amazon.

#3357. Will Josh O’Connor Be The Next James Bond?

Let’s clear up any potential misunderstandings: there are no official announcements on who will play James Bond at this time. But a British tabloid says that a conversation at a pub has revealed the top-secret casting—if an anonymously sourced rumor is to be believed.

A long list of stars are reportedly auditioning for the 007 role, but even former James Bond Pierce Brosnan says the casting process is a mystery. “I’m just the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history,” Brosnan tells Vanity Fair. “All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire.”

According to UK publication The Sun, the decision is rumored to have been made: a recent colleague of Josh O’Connor, a 36-year-old actor from Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, says Disclosure Day star has been cast in the role. If true, Turner beat out likely contenders including Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson.

Josh O'Connor at UK premiere for Disclosure Day on June 04, 2026.

The news comes as a bit of a game of telephone. Until last week, O'Connor was in the case of Golden Boy, Clifford Odets' 1937 drama about a violin player turned boxer in Depression-era New York City. Citing the claims of one of O'Connor's cast mates, an unnamed source tells The Sun “I bumped into one of Josh’s Golden Boy cast mates at The French House."

“Out of nowhere, and oiled by a few glasses of lager, they blurted out that Josh was the next James Bond."

When the source pushed back, the thespian grew more insistent. “They said that he had confided in them about getting the role when the cast of Golden Boy had celebratory drinks after the play finished its run on Halloween," a claim that implies the decision has been made for over a week.

Josh O'Connor, winner of the Outstanding Lead Actor In A Drama Series award for The Crown, at the 73rd Primetime Emmy Awards on September 19, 2021.

If this rumor comes to fruition, it would not be the first time O'Connor took on an iconic UK role. In 2021, he took home the outstanding lead actor Emmy for his role as then-Prince, now-King Charles III, in Netflix series The Crown. While in his role as the future king, he was encouraged to tap into a side that one might not expect.

“It’s Prince Charles as Walter White," he told The Guardian in 2020, making a reference to crime series Breaking Bad. "Our job was to make people feel sorry for [Charles], so that in season four, when he turns into this at times monstrous character, we understand how he got there.” A heel turn that isn't unBond, especially the darker Bond we grew used to with Daniel Craig. (Craig, in fact, has a direct connection to O’Connor, as the pair co-starred in Knives Out: Wake Up Dead Man.)

Speaking with the BBC, O'Connor did not confirm the casting rumor—but he didn't deny it either. (Vanity Fair has reached out to O'Connor's representatives for comment, but has not yet received a response.)

"To be considered in that same sort of bracket is extraordinary," O'Connor said this week.

"It's an incredibly bizarre pinch me moment...even being uttered in that same sentence and being considered for something like that. But I am afraid, there is nothing to say beyond that."

#3356. 25 Years Later, ‘Buffy the Vampire Slayer’s Best Quote Is Still the Most Inspiring Line in TV History

Buffy’s story has always revolved around death. Throughout its seven-season run, Buffy Summers (Sarah Michelle Gellar) has wanted to escape from it or, boldly, return to it. Upon a rewatch, death is one of the clearest themes of the series — this wasn’t the case on my first time watching, when I reacted in disbelief every time the series brought up the possibility of Buffy dying. Surely, they wouldn’t go there. But they did.

In the Buffy the Vampire Slayer season 5 finale, Sunnydale is collapsing, and Buffy’s allies have nowhere to go. Her little sister, Dawn (Michelle Trachtenberg), is the reason why a dangerous portal has opened, and she tries to jump in to close it. But Buffy stops her. “The hardest thing in this world is to live in it,” she tells her. “Be brave. Live. For me.”

The hardest thing in this world is to live in it.

The two share the same blood, so Buffy is capable of closing the portal on her own. She jumps in and dies. It’s a moment that closes out an arc that had been teased since season 1.

Season 5 is one of Buffy’s most emotional seasons. It’s also one of its boldest, committing to a new central dynamic: Buffy and Dawn. Maligned series creator Joss Whedon shared that he introduced Dawn as a way of giving Buffy an intense dynamic that wasn’t based in romance. After seasons of Angel, Riley, and hints of Spike, it feels like a breath of fresh air to see Buffy get mad, angry, happy, and distraught over a different type of relationship.

One of the show’s biggest twists was the introduction of Dawn. Buffy, a notorious single child for most of the show, suddenly has a sister, introduced in a throwaway moment that made me think I had skipped a few episodes. But Dawn’s introduction is not a plot hole. The season spends the rest of its runtime deconstructing this, revealing that Dawn is a Key made up of ancient energy that was put into the body of a girl, with monks giving Buffy and her friends memories of her.

With Dawn’s arrival, Buffy’s era as a teenager is officially over. The season is all about making her grow up fast, stripping her of almost everything that gave her a sense of safety, including her human boyfriend Riley and her mother Joyce. It’s the end of Buffy the Vampire Slayer’s lighter era. From then on, you can’t say that the series is about a scrappy group of teens trying to save the world.

“The Gift,” written by and directed by Whedon, neatly closes all of the storylines that it introduced in its first episode. Throughout the season Buffy and Dawn’s dynamic morphs, from annoying siblings to Buffy becoming Dawn’s caregiver. Buffy learns that Dawn isn’t real early on, but the discovery changes nothing. To Buffy, Dawn is the most important person in her life and only family left. In the finale, when Giles brings up the possibility of sacrificing Dawn to stop a ritual, Buffy immediately shuts him down.

“The Gift” takes its title from a line in “Intervention,” where Buffy goes on a vision quest to meet the First Slayer, a prehistoric girl who tells her: “Death is your gift.” The line reinforces one of Buffy’s biggest fears: that she’s a killing machine, closer to the vampires and demons she hunts than to the human world she’s so desperate to belong to. But Buffy’s words to Dawn show what her gift really means. For Buffy, being the Slayer has never been about strength or power; it’s about sacrifice. With her death, Buffy tasks her sister with living, no matter how difficult and lonely it gets. Those words will haunt her in season 6, finding Buffy at her most anguished and destructive after being ripped out of heaven and coming back to life.

While we now know that Buffy the Vampire Slayer continued for two more seasons and that it ended on a relatively happy note (at least she’s alive), the writers didn’t know that. Season 5 was the last to air on The WB, before the series found its final home on UPN. That uncertainty is why Whedon and company treated “The Gift” as a series finale, wrapping up Buffy’s story while engaging in a conversation with “Prophecy Girl,” the season 1 finale. That episode shows a younger Buffy, one who’s so afraid of dying that she can barely face the Master. This time around, Buffy chooses death calmly, because it means saving her sister.

“The Gift” ends with an indelible image. As Buffy’s friends mourn her and Dawn remembers her sister’s final words, we pan over Buffy’s body over a pile of rubble. We cut to her tombstone: “Buffy Anne Summers. Beloved sister. Devoted friend. She saved the world a lot.”

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

This season was when I started watching Buffy and remains a part of my teenage years... It was special. Thanks for reminding me of it all.

#3355. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Wordle.

Rejoice, as the holiday season is officially in full swing, and there are a plethora of upcoming Christmas movies that are flooding the 2026 TV schedule. While Hallmark’s Countdown to Christmas lineup is my usual go-to when I’m looking for a holiday rom-com, Hulu released The 12 Dates of Christmas, which has the potential to beat out the best Hallmark and Netflix movies this year.

The 12 Dates of Christmas follows Christina, a workaholic shop owner who has spent most of her life prioritizing her professional life over her personal life. Determined not to show up to her family’s holiday dinner single, Christina lets her best friend organize twelve dates leading up to Christmas to hopefully find her “Mr. Right.” While I don’t want to give away any major spoilers, this is a holiday romance movie, so Christina does eventually find her Mr. Right; it just takes a bit of time.

Directed and co-written by David Lipper, this holiday movie debuted on November 6th and has already climbed the ranks of Hulu’s Top 15 Movies list, sitting in the number two spot. As of this writing, it’s being beaten by Super Troopers 3, which fell short at the box office, but is now finding its audience on the streamer like other recent box office flops.

While The 12 Dates of Christmas didn’t have much competition in the new holiday movie genre on Hulu, it was up against some heavy hitters on the other platforms. Over on Netflix, the book-to-screen adaptation of A Dog’s Perfect Christmas starring the likes of Dennis Quaid and Milo Ventimiglia, dropped on November 4th, and it's currently sitting at number two in the platform's most-watched movies list. Meanwhile, Hallmark released two new original movies, Merry Memories and Holiday Unplugged.

It’s Still October, But I Think I Found My Favorite Hallmark Christmas Movie Of 2026

Unfortunately, there’s no definitive way to tell how well The 12 Dates of Christmas fared against the other new releases. However, given that it’s sitting in the number two spot on Hulu, there’s a reasonable chance it would have beaten or tied for viewership with the other new releases.

After all, one of the major selling points of the holiday flick is that it serves as a mini reunion for Pretty Little Liars stars Lucy Hale and Ian Harding. They famously played the romantic duo Aria Montgomery and Ezra Fitz on that series and at the teen drama show’s peak, the two were a fan-favorite pairing. However, fan opinion has soured over the years, as Ezra was Aria’s high school teacher when they started dating. Still, Harding and Hale always had amazing chemistry, so it’s no surprise they’ve gone on to star as romantic leads once again.

It also helps that Hale has a successful history of playing the lead in mid-budget rom-coms like Prime Video’s Puppy Love or the film adaptation of The Hating Game. Harding is also no stranger to the rom-com world, having starred opposite the Queen of Hallmark, Lacey Chabert, earlier this year in Lost in Paradise. He also starred in what I considered to be Netflix’s best holiday movie of 2024, Our Little Secret, with Lindsey Lohan.

So, if you’re in the mood for a Christmas flick, are tired of all the usual best Christmas movies and have access to a Hulu subscription, definitely give The 12 Dates of Christmas a try. It'll make for a nice watch as you prepare for your own holiday festivities.

#3353. Steven Spielberg Made Changes To One Of His Sci-Fi Movies Decades After Its Release

Movies are an artform with a uniquely long lifespan. A film can connect with viewers decades later just as much as it did when it was new, perhaps even more so. Cinema is a great cultural time capsule, but it's also evergreen with its heady mixture of thoughts and emotions. The danger, however, lies in feeling that the power of cinema's reach should exceed its grasp.

That's precisely what legendary filmmaker Steven Spielberg learned when revisiting his 1982 smash "E.T. The Extra Terrestrial" for its 20th anniversary in 2002. The opportunity arose at a perfect nexus point between movie culture and visual effects capabilities. By the early '00s, it was clear that home video (or at least home viewing) was here to stay, and many ordinary families as well as cinephiles were building personal film libraries thanks to the popularity of VHS and the then-new DVD format.

Part of the attraction of a new release of a classic film was getting bonus material or even a new cut, something that auteurs like James Cameron indulged in. Spielberg's colleague George Lucas went one further with his theatrical release of the "Star Wars" trilogy special editions in 1997, debuting versions which were intended to fully replace the original releases (which they still have done ... for now). Spielberg then seized upon the chance to make some changes to "E.T." to try and update its sensibilities to the modern era. While these alterations seemed prudent in an immediate post-9/11 world, a more sober Spielberg later admitted his error in trying to mess with cultural history too much.

After George Lucas' "Star Wars" trilogy special editions were released and Lucas made a point of taking the original cuts out of circulation, many fans and cinema preservationists alike cried foul. In addition to the blow against preservation, folks were less than pleased with some of the egregious and very obvious changes Lucas decided to make. When the news broke that Steven Spielberg would essentially be making an "E.T" special edition, producer Kathleen Kennedy told the Los Angeles Times that "there's no comparison" between the two, given that the changes to "Star Wars" were extensive while "E.T." would only be getting "a wide variety of subtle changes."

Those changes may have been subtle, but they were impactful all the same. In addition to cosmetic alterations like making digital adjustments to the 1982 E.T. animatronic, Spielberg elected to change the guns brandished by government officials in the film to walkie-talkies. In fairness to the filmmaker, he'd been vocalizing his wish to do so since at least 1995, where he explained his reasoning:

"I regret that a gun was used as a threat to stop children on bicycles [...] And if I ever reissue the picture, I'll use the digital miracle of, you know, CGI to take the guns out of the cops' hands. [...] I think those were, you know, distasteful moments to me."

While that change was already in the works before 9/11, the choice to delete a flippant off-screen line of dialogue involving a character trying to dress as a terrorist for Halloween was made as a response to the then very recent tragedy. Though understandable, these changes had a cumulative effect of making "E.T." feel significantly different altogether.

Despite making these changes to "E.T.," Steven Spielberg deserves a lot of credit for not making the same mistakes that George Lucas or some other filmmakers have made when tinkering with their work long after the fact. For one thing, Spielberg did have the original 1982 cut of "E.T." included on the film's DVD release in 2002. More than that, however, is Spielberg's retraction of the 2002 edition years later. Around the time of the release of "The Fablemans" in 2023, Spielberg gave a masterclass at the Time 100 summit, and expressed his regrets at ever having made the alterations to "E.T." in the first place:

"That was a mistake. I never should have done that. 'E.T.' is a product of its era. No film should be revised based on the lenses we now are, either voluntarily, or being forced to peer through. [...] Years went by and I changed my own views. I should have never messed with the archives of my own work, and I don't recommend anyone do that. All our movies are a kind of a signpost of where we were when we made them, what the world was like and what the world was receiving when we got those stories out there. So I really regret having that out there."

Spielberg, being the wise and observant person he is, came to the Ian Malcolm-esque realization that just because he could change things doesn't mean he should. While the temptation to alter or "fix" a movie is natural, a revision can only work in addition to the original, and cannot replace it. Only by observing our past can we understand our present and, hopefully, build a better future. Film is forever.

#3352. Kate Middleton, Prince William, King Charles, and Queen Camilla Gather For Remembrance Day

This Sunday, November 8, King Charles III, Queen Camilla, Kate Middleton, Prince William, Princess Anne and other members of the royal family came together to observe Remembrance Sunday, one of the most solemn events on the United Kingdom's calendar. The day marks the anniversary of the armistice that ended World War I, signed on “the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month” in 1918.

The focal point of every Remembrance Day is the Cenotaph in Whitehall, the Portland stone monument where tribute is paid to those who fell in the wars and conflicts in which the country has participated. Every year, representatives of the royal family, political leaders, the Armed Forces, and veterans gather there: This year, more than 10,000 marched alongside the king and the prime minister.

True to tradition, Charles III laid a wreath at the memorial on behalf of the nation and led the royal family. At his side was Prince William, Princess Anne, and the Duke of Edinburgh, who also paid their respects with a floral tribute. Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales, Kate Middleton, watched the ceremony from the balcony of the Foreign Office, as is customary. On the political front, Prime Minister Andy Burnham laid a wreath on his first Remembrance Sunday as head of the government, accompanied by Opposition Leader Kemi Badenoch and other political leaders.

The day before had already been a day of remembrance: the King, the Queen, and the Princes of Wales attended the Festival of Remembrance at the Royal Albert Hall, the major tribute to the armed forces that precedes Remembrance Sunday.

#3351. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input
