When I was watching Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, a project on the 2026 movie schedule that features a lot of talk about death, I couldn’t help but think about how often some of its stars have died on screen. Specifically, Steve Buscemi has famously kicked the bucket in a ton of projects, and Sam Rockwell has had his fair share of deaths (and kills) too. So, I asked them about all this, and I was shocked that they had very different takes on the matter.

While Steve Buscemi is on the record saying that the on-screen death that amused him most was his death in The Big Lebowski, I asked him who he was most excited to be killed by. He had a pretty great answer too, as he said:

I mean, Tony Soprano. That was a good one. Coen Brothers have done their best, too.

Listen, to die in such a classic TV show like The Sopranos (which you can watch with an HBO Max subscription), and at the hands of Tony Soprano himself, is pretty epic. Plus, as Buscemi mentioned, the Coen Brothers sure have done their best to creatively kill him too. Honestly, it’d be an honor to die on screen at the hands of any of these guys.

However, despite all this, and the fact that Buscemi has died in movies and TV shows what feels like countless times, he’s actually not a huge fan of watching that kind of thing. He brought that up in our conversation when I asked him to reveal something surprising about himself:

I'm pretty squeamish. I don't like watching violence, including my own death scenes. But you know, it's an occupational hazard for me.

Well, while it’s an occupational hazard for him, his Wild Horse Nine co-star, Sam Rockwell, has a totally different take on what it’s like to die on screen.

**Now, beyond this point there are major, and I mean MAJOR, spoilers for Wild Horse Nine. Please continue reading with caution, and go see the movie in theaters. **

Now, ironically, in the critically acclaimed Wild Horse Nine, Sam Rockwell’s character, Lee, is responsible for multiple deaths, including MJ’s, who Steve Buscemi plays, and Chris’ (John Malkovich). However, while the Oscar winner survived this film, he’s died in plenty of other projects, so I asked him about his favorite way he’s died and his favorite person he’s killed. Here’s what he had to say:

Whoa, favorite person I've killed, and favorite movie I've died? I died in Seven Psychopaths. That was pretty fun. Favorite person I've killed is probably John.

Well, notably, while Buscemi called dying on screen an “occupational hazard,” Rockwell was throwing around “fun” as his primary adjective. However, his death in Martin McDonagh’s Seven Psychopaths is objectively “pretty fun”. I mean, it involves a standoff, Rockwell’s Billy getting shot by Woody Harrelson’s Charlie, and one very memorable moment with a Shih Tzu.

Moving on from that, though, he said his favorite person to kill on screen was John Malkovich, which happens in Wild Horse Nine at the very end of the movie. While it’s by no means a fun scene, it is a very meaningful one, and when I asked Malkovich what it was like to be killed by Rockwell, he said:

Well, there you have it, sometimes dying on screen is fun, sometimes it’s great, and other times it's hard to watch. However, no matter how they react to it, all these guys are remarkable actors who are very good at being both alive and dead in the movies.

So, if you’d like to see them do all that, you can catch Wild Horse Nine in theaters now.

#3349. 25 Best Directors Of All Time, Ranked

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Ranking the best directors of all time is a formidable task. How do you weigh a director's output against their influence? Ultimately, the question is who has left the most lasting impression on film culture, and why.

Making a list like this also means confronting the industry's realities. You'll notice a dismal underrepresentation of directors of color, women, and queer filmmakers compared to the overwhelming majority of entries: white men.

Hollywood, and the filmmaking industry writ large, have historically diminished the voices of marginalized filmmakers, limiting their opportunities to create, distribute, and receive recognition for their work. When those opportunities have disproportionately gone to the same insular group, it's no surprise their work has come to dominate the cinematic canon. Hopefully, future renditions of this list will reflect a greater appreciation of historically overlooked filmmakers and the continued emergence of exciting, diverse voices pushing the medium forward.

For now, the directors on this list reflect film history's achievements and the inequities that have shaped it. Here are the 25 best directors of all time, ranked.

John Carpenter may not watch his own movies, but for the rest of us, he's left an indelible mark on genre cinema. He made "Halloween" in 1978 for a reported $325,000, scoring one of horror's most recognizable piano themes in three days and drafting a slasher blueprint: the ominous quiet of suburbia shattered by violence, all in gorgeous Scope framing. That's just one of his essential films, as "Assault on Precinct 13," "Escape From New York," and "The Thing" have helped cement his legacy.

Hollywood never quite knew what to do with Carpenter, not that he cared. "Big Trouble in Little China" flopped before becoming a respected cult object. "They Live" screamed its anti-consumerist messaging to the rafters inside a winking sci-fi B-movie, featuring one of the longest and goofiest fight scenes ever filmed. Few filmmakers have maintained such an unmistakable sensibility as Carpenter's stylish, innovative takes on horror and pulp.

Billy Wilder fled terror in Europe and arrived in Hollywood with limited English, eventually becoming one of the town's sharpest writers. As a director, he constantly hopped genres without a hitch. "Double Indemnity," co-written with Raymond Chandler, helped define film noir; "The Lost Weekend" won Best Picture and Best Director at the Academy Awards for its unflinching look at alcoholism; the Gothic Hollywood nightmare of "Sunset Boulevard" scandalized the industry and aged into one of the most essential showbiz movies ever.

"Some Like It Hot," starring Marilyn Monroe, was named the greatest American comedy by the AFI. "The Apartment" threaded office-politics farce through a funny, emotional, deeply bittersweet story of loneliness, heartbreak, and workplace exploitation, going on to take home Best Picture. Wilder's films were often cynical, funny, and deeply humane all at once. If you need a place to start, we ranked 14 of his best movies.

Christopher Nolan's legacy is already set in stone as a modern-day showman, and he's perhaps the last director who can conjure blockbuster events based on his name alone. His modest breakout "Memento" hinted at his cerebral ambitions. "The Dark Knight" elevated the gritty, tactile superhero movie into a new blockbuster standard, and "Inception" cemented his reputation as a purveyor of brainy yet crowd-pleasing big-budget spectacle. Of course, he is also the movie theater's loudest and most ardent evangelist, championing IMAX cameras, real film stock, and practical stunts.

His overwhelming ambition has never insulated him from criticism though, as detractors harp on cold characters, muddy sound mixes, and an unholy amount of exposition. But to see "Interstellar," "Dunkirk," or "The Odyssey" in a true IMAX presentation is to immerse yourself in the palpable vision of a man who knows exactly how to stage a set-piece. To watch "Oppenheimer" is to be amazed at how he can turn a three-hour biopic of men talking in rooms into something as high-octane as his thrillers. Nolan is in a league all his own, so we had a hard time ranking his movies.

Nobody captures the sensorial experience of longing quite like Wong Kar-wai. The Hong Kong auteur, often working with cinematographer Christopher Doyle, built a visual language of romantic yearning from neon smears, slow-motion blurs, and step-printing warps of time and motion. Countless filmmakers have chased the ineffable quality he summons in his films about the aches and desires of the human experience, especially his standout film "Chungking Express," anchored by Tony Leung's exquisite features. The film helped make him an international name, with a boost from Quentin Tarantino, whose short-lived Rolling Thunder Pictures label brought it to American theaters, and "Happy Together" earned him Best Director at Cannes in 1997.

But it's "In the Mood for Love" that gave him legendary status. Pairing Tony Leung with Maggie Cheung as neighbors in 1962 Hong Kong who discover their spouses are having an affair, he turns it into a romance of pure, repressed feeling. It's the epitome of the entire Wong Kar-wai project, and it's the movie that has cemented his legacy. It also landed at #5 in Sight & Sound's 2022 critics' poll.

Robert Altman wasn't one to conform to Hollywood's tidy, controlled storytelling. A former bomber pilot who cut his teeth on industrial films and television, he broke through with "M*A*S*H," a profane, anti-authoritarian war comedy that won the top prize at Cannes in 1970. He developed a signature style built on overlapping dialogue, wandering zoom lenses, and enormous ensemble casts, often capturing multiple conversations simultaneously and extracting moments of clarity from the chaos. He adapted this style across the gamut of genres: "McCabe & Mrs. Miller" envisioned the Western as a hazy character study; "The Long Goodbye" subverted the noir by turning it into a shaggy, meandering ramble; and "Nashville" makes a compelling case for being the great American movie of the 1970s.

After the troubled "Popeye" in 1980, he spent years on the margins, working in theater and low-budget stage adaptations, before roaring back with "The Player," his biting Hollywood satire, followed by "Short Cuts" and "Gosford Park." He was nominated for Best Director five times, never won, but finally received an honorary Oscar in 2006, months before his death at 81. Altman may not have spent much time analyzing his own films, but a wealth of genius remains.

Before becoming an architect of cinematic epics, David Lean worked his way up from studio cutting rooms to become one of British film's finest editors. The training shows in the precision of everything he would go on to shoot. After co-directing "In Which We Serve" with Noël Coward, he made "Brief Encounter," a beautifully felt railway-station romance of aching restraint, whose DNA is evident in beloved movies such as "Before Sunset" and "The Bridges of Madison County."

It was later that he would prove his gift for scale. "The Bridge on the River Kwai" won Best Picture and Best Director, but, of course, it's "Lawrence of Arabia" that turned his name into shorthand for grandeur — a movie with a rare perfect Metacritic score. That film alone earns him a spot here, even without his other wonderfully helmed features, which all reveal a filmmaker attuned to the most crucial tenets of storytelling.

Not just one of the most influential comedy stars in history, and one of the most famous entertainers to ever work in Hollywood, many of Charles "Charlie" Chaplin's greatest successes were helmed by the man himself. From London poverty and the music-hall stage, he began experimenting with directing at Keystone in 1914 with "Twenty Minutes of Love." "Caught in the Rain" followed, his first film with sole directing responsibility. From there, he spent his career proving how his formal prowess complemented his physical dexterity.

His silent and early sound masterpieces include "The Kid," "The Gold Rush," "City Lights," "Modern Times," and "The Great Dictator," his first full talkie, in which he lampooned Hitler while the United States was still neutral. Such boldness had consequences: While sailing for London in 1952, amid the Red Scare, the government revoked his re-entry permit, and he settled in Switzerland, later returning for an honorary Oscar in 1972.

Howard Hawks left enduring imprints across seemingly limitless genres. He helped define the violent gangster picture with "Scarface." He directed two of the best screwball comedies of all time, "Bringing Up Baby" and "His Girl Friday." He made the tough-minded adventure "Only Angels Have Wings." He paired Humphrey Bogart with Lauren Bacall twice, in "To Have and Have Not" and "The Big Sleep," creating one of the most seductive cinematic pairings ever seen on screen. "Red River" and "Rio Bravo" can both claim a place among Hollywood's most essential Westerns.

Hawks did it all. He accentuates the material with an invisible style: eye-level camerawork, unfussy staging, and a preoccupation with professionals who earn each other's respect, including strong-willed women who demand to be treated as equals. He was the kind of Hollywood workman who made masterpieces by simply showing up and understanding the job.

Federico Fellini began as a cartoonist and gag writer, then he co-wrote for Roberto Rossellini on "Rome, Open City" and "Paisan," foundational works of Italian neorealism, before broadening his scope. "La Strada" and "Nights of Cabiria," fables of the poor and discarded, announced his talent, but it was "La Dolce Vita" that cemented his international reputation and became one of the greatest Italian films ever made — it was also Roger Ebert's favorite movie of all time. The Palme d'Or winner follows Marcello Mastroianni through Rome's decadent nightlife, capturing the estranged emotional perspective of a hollow, meaningless pursuit of glamour.

From there, he turned inward. "8½" is perhaps his most famous film, the definitive movie about a director paralyzed by his own creative crisis, blending memory, fantasy, and self-doubt in a way self-reflective directors have tried to imitate in Fellini's wake. Later came the carnivalesque "Fellini Satyricon," "Roma," and the nostalgic "Amarcord," another Oscar winner. His singular vision earned him a word of his own: "Felliniesque."

In a decade, Francis Ford Coppola made a run of films that may be the greatest in history. He fought a studio that didn't want Marlon Brando or Al Pacino in what would be his seminal, culture-shattering "The Godfather." He followed that up with two masterpieces in 1974: "The Conversation," which took home the top prize at Cannes, and "The Godfather Part II," the rare sequel that exceeded its predecessor and became the first sequel to win Best Picture. "Apocalypse Now" followed, after a legendarily disastrous shoot in the Philippines so troubled it inspired its own documentary, "Hearts of Darkness."

That run alone earns Coppola his place among the greats, even if all that risk-taking nearly broke him. The expensive flop "One from the Heart" crippled his Zoetrope studio, and he spent years making movies to pay off debts. Even so, he kept swinging, from "Rumble Fish" to the operatic "Bram Stoker's Dracula," and bankrolled the truly zany "Megalopolis" himself, reportedly with money from his wine business. Whatever you make of it, few directors have been this ambitious for this long.

Spike Lee, for all his prolificacy, can be an uneven director — there's a reason we were able to list his eight best and seven worst movies — but he's responsible for some of the most important American movies ever made, particularly in his exploration of Black American life. Arriving with "She's Gotta Have It," he would soon follow with his critically acclaimed drama "Do the Right Thing," a loving yet raging cultural firestorm of fractured societal relationships that refuses to placate its audience.

His refusal to back down from his beliefs comes through in a brash, flashy style that is instantly recognizable, particularly in his signature "double dolly" shot. But he can be flexible too. "Malcolm X" showed his epic reach, "Inside Man" his mainstream chops, and "BlacKkKlansman" his insight into how yesterday's politics collide with today's. Consistency be damned, he's an essential component of American filmmaking.

Agnès Varda came to cinema as a still photographer with almost no film training, and she made her debut, "La Pointe Courte," in 1955, years before the French New Wave she's often credited with anticipating. She was one of the few women in a scene dominated by cinephile men, and she stood out by making her sensibility entirely her own: curious, playful, and warmly attentive to ordinary people. "Cléo from 5 to 7" is a luminous examination of a pop singer drifting through Paris as she awaits medical test results, while "Vagabond," which won the Golden Lion at Venice, is an unsentimental portrait of a young drifter found dead in a ditch.

Varda also slipped freely between fiction and documentary, often blending the two. "The Gleaners and I" found poetry in scavengers and discarded produce, while "Faces Places," co-directed with the artist JR, earned her a Best Documentary Feature nomination at the 90th Academy Awards in 2018, making the 89-year-old Varda the oldest Oscar nominee in Academy history at the time. She kept working until her death in 2019 and made waves with critics throughout her career, including being among the highest-rated female-directed movies on Metacritic.

Hayao Miyazaki is animation's most devoted craftsman, introducing generations of children internationally to the detailed artistry of Japanese animation while also exposing them to challenging, scary, and profound ideas that have helped prepare them for adulthood. He co-founded Studio Ghibli (whose films we've ranked) in 1985 with Isao Takahata and Toshio Suzuki, and made a run of films that treated childhood as serious business: the gentle fable "My Neighbor Totoro," the coming-of-age story of a young witch discovering her purpose in "Kiki's Delivery Service," and the ecological fantasy epic "Princess Mononoke."

Then came "Spirited Away," which won the Golden Bear in Berlin and the Oscar for Best Animated Feature, and it was Japan's highest-grossing film for nearly two decades. The free-wheeling, wafting nature of Miyazaki's films comes from his unconventional process: He storyboards without a finished script, discovering the heart of the films as he draws. After returning from retirement to make "The Boy and the Heron," which earned him another Oscar for Best Animated Feature, Miyazaki remains creatively active well into his eighties. His extraordinary animation is a legacy any filmmaker could only dream of.

Andrei Tarkovsky made only seven features, each with seismic influence across generations. He once called filmmaking "sculpting in time," and that idea shapes his often abstruse yet spiritually profound work. As Ingmar Bergman once said, he invented a new language for film. Watching a Tarkovsky movie means being enraptured by its emotional depth, hidden within its mysteries.

His major works are must-sees. These include "Solaris," which turns Stanisław Lem's novel into a fractured meditation on memory and guilt; "Mirror," which weaves Tarkovsky's own childhood, newsreel footage, and his father Arseny's poetry into a chimerical collage; and "Stalker," one of the most influential and widely imitated sci-fi films ever made. Along with works such as "Andrei Rublev" and "Ivan's Childhood," Tarkovsky left behind a slim yet crucial filmography that helped define Soviet cinema and continues to influence filmmakers worldwide.

Sidney Lumet was a child actor on stage before becoming one of television's most active directors, and the discipline of working quickly and efficiently for television remained in his DNA. He put his TV work to good use with "12 Angry Men," his iconic pressure-cooker juror drama, which now stands as one of the best film debuts ever. He favored complex characters and sharp commentary on the modern world, as seen in movies like "Serpico," "Dog Day Afternoon," "Prince of the City," and "Network."

Lumet loved actors, rehearsing them like a stage company, and many of his stars delivered some of their best performances under his direction, from Al Pacino's sweaty bank robber in "Dog Day Afternoon" to Paul Newman's washed-up lawyer in "The Verdict." He made great movies until the end of his career, releasing "Before the Devil Knows You're Dead" at age 83, before his death in 2011.

Alfred Hitchcock earned the nickname "The Master of Suspense" for a reason. After honing his craft on British silent films and thrillers like "The 39 Steps" and "The Lady Vanishes," he crossed the Atlantic to work with producer David O. Selznick and made "Rebecca," which won Best Picture. However, since Best Picture statues go to a film's producers, Hitchcock would ultimately go 0-for-5 in the Best Director category.

Hitchcock's legacy has rested less on awards than on his ability to shock audiences. He made archetypal horror and thriller masterpieces, including "Rear Window," "North by Northwest," "Psycho," and "Vertigo," which would later topple "Citizen Kane" from the top of Sight & Sound's critics' poll in 2012, ending a 50-year reign. His genius endures to this day, and his films feel just as thrilling and transgressive as ever, which is fitting for the director with the most perfect movies, according to Metacritic.

It's often said that Joel and Ethan Coen are a directing duo who share a single brain, each completely in tune with the other's dry, morbid, gleefully caustic sense of humor and irony in their portrayals of people whose downfalls are their own making. They distilled the sensibility of their entire career in their debut neo-noir "Blood Simple" and kept that same mordant sensibility across genres and decades. From the screwball kidnapping farce "Raising Arizona" to the surrealistic Hollywood allegory "Barton Fink" to the breakout Minnesota nice-crime story "Fargo," which won a screenplay Oscar and Best Actress for Frances McDormand, nearly all of the Coens' films share a harmonious blend of dark comedy and drama.

Their mid-career run was just as strong: "No Country for Old Men" is one of the best neo-Westerns ever, while movies like "A Serious Man," "True Grit," and "Inside Llewyn Davis" continued to prove the success of their strange amalgamations of tenderness, humor, and bleak perceptions of reality. The Coens also pull career-best performances from their actors, so good that we had to rank the best of them. Their decision to pursue separate projects in recent years has only accentuated the miraculous consistency of their work together — and with the brothers now expressing plans to reunite behind the camera, there may yet be another chapter in one of cinema's great creative partnerships.

Any time you need a shock to the system, remember that Paul Thomas Anderson made "Boogie Nights" when he was just 26. Most recently in the spotlight for finally winning Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Adapted Screenplay for "One Battle After Another," his freewheeling riff on Thomas Pynchon's "Vineland," Anderson has spent years as your dedicated cinephile's de facto favorite contemporary director.

With a career defined by such formal bravado, how could he not be? Nearly all his films have defenders who call them masterpieces, from the three-hour interconnected melodrama epic "Magnolia" to "Punch-Drunk Love," which proved Adam Sandler's capability as a dramatic lead. Of course, it's "There Will Be Blood," one of Daniel Day-Lewis' best films, that tops many best-of-the-century lists, but his subsequent work, "The Master," "Phantom Thread," and "Licorice Pizza," is imbued with his radiant sensibility just as well. Anderson makes movies that buzz with pure cinematic brilliance.

Nothing captures David Lynch's sensibility better than the clip of him being asked to elaborate on why "Eraserhead" is his most spiritual movie, and him curtly replying, "No, I won't." For as routine as the term "Lynchian" has become when describing movies that are any shade of strange or surreal, the true ethos of Lynch's movies is that intangible quality that's hard to explain in the first place and nearly impossible to replicate. Even still, Lynch's filmography is diverse: the tender, Oscar-nominated "The Elephant Man," the misfired blockbuster "Dune," the unsettling revelations of suburban secrets in "Blue Velvet," and the surprising warmth of his G-rated, Disney-produced road movie "The Straight Story."

His legacy will be remembered mostly for "Mulholland Drive," a project initially conceived as a spinoff of his groundbreaking television series "Twin Peaks," which later evolved into a standalone ABC pilot that Lynch reworked into a film after the network passed on it, as well as his return to "Peaks" with "The Return" in 2017, perhaps the boldest television has ever been. Lynch sadly passed away in 2025, but he leaves behind a legacy of unsettling dreams and devoted compassion toward the human experience. No other voice will ever be like his.

Martin Scorsese is cinema's most passionate student and, increasingly, its most devoted steward and custodian, through work such as his World Cinema Project, which preserves, restores, and showcases neglected and underseen films from around the world. Raised in Little Italy, he was an asthmatic kid who spent his childhood in movie theaters and nearly became a priest before NYU film school pointed him elsewhere. Sin, guilt, and the hunger for redemption would color so many of his works: the raw street poetry of "Mean Streets," the Palme d'Or-winning "Taxi Driver," the bruising "Raging Bull," and "Goodfellas," one of the defining landmarks of gangster cinema.

At 83, he's still making some of his best work. Take a look at movies like "The Wolf of Wall Street," "Silence," "The Irishman," and "Killers of the Flower Moon" to see a director who has never lost his touch, continually finding new ways to explore his perspectives on faith, morality, and humanity through his unmistakable cinematic style. There is indeed an argument that Scorsese is our greatest living filmmaker.

Stanley Kubrick's legendary attention to detail casts an imposing shadow across film history. Though he may never have won a Best Director Oscar, the skill he exhibited across a diverse slate of masterpieces is, in effect, one of the greatest influences on his contemporaries and those who followed in his wake.

His films have become synonymous with filmmaking mastery, and yet it still manages to stun that the same man made the likes of "Dr. Strangelove," "2001: A Space Odyssey," "A Clockwork Orange," "Barry Lyndon," "The Shining," "Full Metal Jacket," and "Eyes Wide Shut." That's not even counting his impressive early work, which included "The Killing," "Paths of Glory," "Spartacus," and "Lolita." He may not be the most prolific director on this list, but the caliber of his work has earned him enduring renown, plus a new tome-like brick from the Criterion Collection with 4K restorations of all his films.

No director has stared directly into the abyss quite like Ingmar Bergman. The son of a Lutheran pastor, he arrived at film after years in the theater, ruminating on guilt, faith, and dread, though he broke through with the bittersweet comedy "Smiles of a Summer Night." But his most revered works soon followed: the heavy gloom of "The Seventh Seal," the gentle "Wild Strawberries," and perhaps most notably the surreal, psychologically labyrinthine "Persona," a dreamlike investigation of identity.

Bergman built his vast filmography with trusted collaborators, including cinematographers Gunnar Fischer and Sven Nykvist and actors like Liv Ullmann, Max von Sydow, and Bibi Andersson, whose faces he observes with the same care as epic landscapes. "The Virgin Spring," "Through a Glass Darkly," and "Fanny and Alexander" each won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film, the last a warm, autobiographical epic he originally intended as his farewell to theatrical filmmaking.

John Ford made beautiful Westerns, but he also established much of the cinematic language the genre has followed ever since, all while demonstrating remarkable mastery across other genres. A veteran of the silent era, he directed more than 130 films between 1917 and 1970 and holds the record for Best Director Oscars with four — "The Informer," "The Grapes of Wrath," "How Green Was My Valley," and "The Quiet Man" — none of them Westerns. Two wartime Navy documentaries also won Oscars: "The Battle of Midway" and "December 7th." Ford personally filmed much of the former while under fire during the battle.

But the frontier was where Ford's poetry truly shines. "Stagecoach" turned John Wayne into a movie star, and Orson Welles reportedly studied it up to 40 times before making "Citizen Kane." His later Westerns interrogated the very mythologies he helped create: "The Searchers" cast a shadow of obsession and racism over Wayne's heroism, while "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance" questioned the romanticized stories America tells about its own history. He's your favorite director's favorite director, from Scorsese to Spielberg, and his influence looms large in modern cinema.

Akira Kurosawa had a career that expanded the horizons of both Japanese and Western cinema: while his own films were masterpieces, the filmmakers he inspired would become mavericks. After debuting with "Sanshiro Sugata" in 1943, he impressed audiences abroad with "Rashomon," a film about a crime recounted in four contradictory ways, which won the Golden Lion at Venice in 1951 and an honorary Oscar. In the years that followed came "Ikiru" and, perhaps most notably to film fans, "Seven Samurai," whose team-assembling structure and staggering sense of craft became a blueprint for the action genre.

Kurosawa's echoes are everywhere in the movies you grew up loving: "The Magnificent Seven" remade "Seven Samurai," Sergio Leone's "A Fistful of Dollars" borrowed "Yojimbo," and George Lucas has cited "The Hidden Fortress" as an inspiration for "Star Wars." Yet no imitator can fully capture his signature style: telephoto compositions, multiple cameras, wind and rain as powerful reflections of his characters' emotional states, and precise editing. Trace the DNA of modern cinema, and you'll find Kurosawa somewhere in its lineage.

If anyone seems truly put on this Earth to entertain, Steven Spielberg may be the man. His name is both a brand and an adjective. He is an indispensable practitioner of moviemaking who completely changed the way Hollywood approached its business when he made "Jaws" before turning 30, the shark thriller that helped establish the modern summer blockbuster. He became the highest-grossing director in box-office history, with generational favorites like "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Raiders of the Lost Ark," and "E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial."

In 1993, he released both "Jurassic Park" and "Schindler's List," the latter winning him Oscars for Best Director and Best Picture,  and "Saving Private Ryan" brought him a second directing win. Critics call him sentimental, but "Munich" and "A.I." are darker and more ambiguous than his reputation suggests, and "The Fabelmans," his portrait of his parents' breakup and his own obsession with the camera, finally turned the lens on himself in stunning fashion. Across film history, it's hard to find a director who combines formal prowess with the ability to move and compel commercial audiences more effectively. He is the director for every flavor of film fan. His name is unmatched in film culture.

#3348. Sega’s Most Influential Platformer Deserves Its Big Remake Moment Next

With The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and even Star Fox recently proving there is still an appetite for remakes done right, other game publishers are likely looking at their backlogs for inspiration. Sega, no stranger to fantastic franchises, suddenly finds itself once more in an enviable position. It has a bunch of great old games ripe for revival, and several of them seem capable of making a mark again.

One franchise that deserves to make its triumphant return celebrates its 25th anniversary this month. After its arcade launch earlier that year, Super Monkey Ball arrived as a GameCube launch game in November 2001. With proper care, that simple but effective game could thrive in 2026, even though recent entries in the series haven’t made quite the same splash.

Super Monkey Ball’s main event lets players choose one out of four monkeys. The simian is then enclosed in a ball that resembles the capsules we used to collect from toy machines at the supermarket as children. From there, they roll toward goal posts on floating platforms, collecting bananas along the way to improve their score. If they fall off the platform or run out of time before reaching their destination, they lose a life.

In the traditional sense of the term, Super Monkey Ball isn’t a platformer. There’s no sign of Mario, for instance, and jumping isn’t a central mechanic. But there are platforms and pits, so the label fits in a more general sense.

When Super Monkey Ball debuted, it reminded me immediately of an old NES favorite of mine, Marble Madness. But that pioneering older game could be completed in five minutes. There were only a few stages, all of them far too short for my liking. I wanted more of that sort of experience, which Super Monkey Ball delivered. There are dozens of stages. Most of them are smaller than the typical Marble Madness level, but they’re similarly compelling, and their quantity makes up for their brevity.

At the start of Super Monkey Ball, rolling through the goal tape is easy enough. Even by the end of that first set of courses, however, the process grows tense. Then there are 30 more courses of more difficult vintage to tackle, and an even larger and more demanding batch after that.

As they advance, players control not the monkeys themselves but the platforms they occupy. Mastery requires the player to tilt each board, which in turn allows the balls to build up enough speed to launch from small bumps in order to clear gaps, or to negotiate rougher terrain, all without moving so quickly that it becomes impossible to proceed along razor-thin beams that span wide gaps.

A full-fledged remake of that original game could add visual polish. It might also double down on the personality of the starring characters, who make irresistible mascots. AiAi even drove a cart in 2012’s Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed, besides starring in various Super Monkey Ball sequels. The included party games and competitive play, which feature attractions such as launching balls toward distant targets, could provide satisfying online play with friends or strangers, especially if they were expanded with additional content.

Sega certainly hasn’t forgotten about Super Monkey Ball. In fact, Super Monkey Ball Triple Pack, a physical-only bundle for Nintendo Switch, will be released on Nov. 10. That compilation is welcome, gathering several recent installments in the series, like Banana Rumble. It also includes Banana Mania, which remastered the stages from the original GameCube releases. But none of those modern installments have managed to have quite the impact that the original one once did, and might again if it were to receive an ambitious remake like Nintendo produced with Ocarina of Time. The main question now is whether Sega has the desire to make it happen.

Gotta go fast? Mark your calendar for Nov. 12

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Yes, Marble Madness can be completed in 5 minutes, but only once you've already mastered it.

You think Super Monkey Ball is more influential than Sonic?!

#3347. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

Emily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City.

#3346. Kristen Stewart's Family-Friendly Sci-Fi Box Office Bomb Is Worth Revisiting

While she's best known for a certain fantasy romance franchise (and has since gone on to do her best work in small indie dramas), Kristen Stewart is no stranger to genre filmmaking. In fact, she's amassed a nice little resume within the sci-fi genre, having acted in movies like "Jumper," "Crimes of the Future," and "Undersea."

Unfortunately, Stewart hasn't had much luck in the genre so far as the box office is concerned. But that doesn't mean you shouldn't seek out her various sci-fi projects. Quite the opposite: Her family-friendly 2005 bomb "Zathura: A Space Adventure" features a great cast of once and future franchise stars. It also marked an early directorial effort from the man who would eventually put Grogu and Martin Scorsese together on the big screen, and it boasts some pretty good practical effects to boot.

Yes, "Zathura" was Jon Favreau's third outing as a director and had a script credited to David Koepp and John Kramps, itself adapted from Chris Van Allsburg's book of the same name. "Zathura" is even technically part of the "Jumanji" movie franchise, as Allburg's original work takes place in the same universe as his classic fantasy adventure creation.

In "Zathura," Josh Hutcherson and Jonah Bobo play two brothers who constantly fight and are struggling with the recent divorce of their parents. Dealing with a workaholic dad and an older sister (Kristen Stewart) who couldn't care less what her siblings do, the pair find a magical board game that transports their house to outer space. From there, they're forced to survive various alien dangers and finish the game if they ever hope to get back safely home.

"Zathura," as mentioned earlier, features two then-future stars in the YA genre space, with Kristen Stewart becoming the face of the "Twilight" films and Josh Hutcherson co-leading the "Hunger Games" movies years later. The movie also co-stars Dax Shepard, Frank Oz as the voice of a defective robot, and Tim Robbins (decades out from his performance as the most underrated character on "Silo").

Admittedly, "Zathura" never really hides the fact that it really is just "Jumanji" in outer space, with a mysterious adult man chasing after the protagonists, huge special effects, and animalistic threats preying on the house where the story takes place. Yet, it mostly works, in no small part due to Stan Winston's contributions to the film's visual effects. Some of its CGI looks dated nowadays, sure, but the practical effects from Stan Winston Studios remain convincing and enhance the movie's sense of wonder. With its assorted fantastical creatures, "Zathura" helped to kickstart Jon Favreau's fascination with technology and effects as well — for better and for worse.

Sadly, Stewart doesn't have to do much in "Zathura," as her character ends up spending most of its runtime cryogenically frozen (with Stan Winston Studios having devised a life-size model of a frozen Stewart for the occasion). Of course, when she's not frozen, Stewart succeeds in giving her onscreen counterpart more than just the annoyed big sister who panics about her predicament. Her character gets some emotional moments with her brothers, too, along with some fun banter with Dax Shepard's Astronaut (who gets the film's best scene, in which we learn his true identity and tragic backstory).

"Zathura" has a 77% critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with the vast majority of the film's reviews being positive. Indeed, Roger Ebert was among those who praised the movie, writing that it works "gloriously as space opera" and commending Jon Favreau for bringing "a muscular solidity to his special effects" that infuses them with imperfections and personality (which, in turn, makes them feel more grounded and real).

Sorry to say, though, all that critical praise wasn't enough to make "Zathura" a hit. Instead, the film was overshadowed at the box office by Disney's "Chicken Little," which was the studio's first fully computer-animated movie. Making matters worse, "Zathura" was all but forgotten about a week later when "Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire" opened in theaters. In the end, the film barely matched its $65 million budget at the global box office. Still, it was nominated for several Saturn Awards, including Best Fantasy Film.

Some 14 years after its theatrical release, "Zathura" found its way back into the public consciousness when Jack Black, who was promoting "Jumanji: The Next Level" at the time, reminded audiences that "Zathura" is part of the same franchise (via Variety). Today, it remains a pleasant, family-friendly sci-fi flick that's worth your time, should you find yourself in the mood for some cosmic hijinks.

#3345. LACMA Art+Film Gala: Nicole Kidman, Timothée Chalamet honor Denis Villeneuve

“It’s a pleasure to be here. You guys are just crazy party people,”said artist Vija Celmins, as she summed up the jovial atmosphere at the 15th annual LACMA Art+Film Gala during her casual and off-the-cuff acceptance speech as one of the two honorees that night.

The annual fundraiser is a party, and unique among the many galas that hit the town this time of year. Along with raising money for the museum’s initiative to make film more central to the museum’s programming (this year they raised a record-breaking almost $7 million), it brings out an eclectic mix of A-list talent, up-and-coming filmmakers, and giants of the art world.

Honoree, Denis Villeneuve, Honoree Vija Celmins, co-chair Eva Chow and LACMA CEO Michael Govan

Just a quick scan of the packed room: Al Pacino sitting with artist Ed Ruscha and art dealer Larry Gagosian; artist Alex Israel wrapping his arm around Orlando Bloom for a photo; model Alex Consani crouching down to chat with influencer and comedian Quenlin Blackwell; and artists Jonas Wood and Mickalene Thomas chatting in one corner while Sarah Paulson and Parker Posey catch up in another.

Anya Taylor-Joy set the mood for the evening as the first arrival on the red carpet, where talent posed in front of Chris Burden’s famed public art installation, Urban Light. There in support of Dune director Denis Villeneuve, who was honored along with Clemins, the Dune: Part Two star wore a vintage 1997 Pierre Cardin Haute Couture bridal gown with a sheer silver overlay that looked both of the past and of the future.

Villeneuve's leading man, Timothée Chalamet, skipped the carpet all together, instead slipping into the crowded tent for dinner in a seat next to Villeneuve and his wife, producer Tanya Lapointe. Chalamet arrived separately from girlfriend Kylie Jenner, who did walk the carpet in a low-back Ashi Studio gown. When Jenner arrived at her table, she was seated opposite Chalamet, reaching across to grab his hand.

Seated next to Villeneuve was Nicole Kidman (in a voluminous, ballerina-inspired Chanel dress), who flew 15 hours from Australia to give Villeneuve his award. “The truth is I've never really met Denis. I've met him on some red carpets and sort of waved at him,” she said during her remarks. “Yet somehow I feel like I know the deepest parts of him because that is what extraordinary filmmakers do. They let you in. They reveal themselves to us through their work. They invite you into their imaginations, into their dreams, into their questions and into their fears.”

Monica Barbaro, Salma Hayek and Kim Kardashian

Before Villeneuve took the stage, a video capturing his film legacy of big, bold, and personal epics like Sicario, Blade Runner 2049, Arrival, and the Dune trilogy was played, featuring a slew of A-list directors singing his praises, including Steven Spielberg, Alfonso Cuaron, Alejandro G. Iñárritu, James Cameron, and Chloé Zhao. “I've always felt that cinema is seen as a pop art—the film carries the burden of being popular in the present,” said Villeneuve in his acceptance speech. “But at the end of the day, the real challenge is to make something that can enter the test of time.”

Speaking of tests (screen tests, that is) Villeneuve got a bit playful with the end of his speech, announcing to the room that he would right here, right now, announce which actor would play James Bond. The French-Canadian director is helming the next Bond film and over the past week, reports have been flying about who might be cast. Would Villeneuve put us all out of our misery and spill the beans? “The actor who will play the next James Bond is—and I will stop right now because [producer] Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack,” he said with a smile.

The gala, once again presented by Gucci, hosted a slew of this Oscar season’s most exciting young filmmakers, including Obsession filmmaker Curry Barker and Club Kid’s Jordan Firstman, along with La Bola Negra directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (known as Los Javis). The latter told me they didn’t plan to party as hard as they did at the Academy Museum Gala a few weeks ago, where they went viral for singing along to Taylor Swift's performance of "Love Story." Said Ambrossi, “I’m drinking only water tonight.”

Among the other guests, Joel Edgerton chatted with Abbott Elementary’s Quinta Brunson and Daniel Scheinert, one half of the Oscar-winning directing team Daniels (Everything Everywhere All at Once). Kim Kardashian wove her way through the crowd, pausing perfectly to look over her shoulder for a trailing photographer. And several stars made a date night out of the event: Sienna Miller brought fiancé Oli Green; Julia Garner sat with musician Charlie Walker; Viola Davis enjoyed the night with husband and producing partner Julius Tennon. Paris Hilton, who introduced Rosé onstage with her classic catchphrase “that’s hot,” wore a glittering Jenny Packham gown as she cascaded through the room with her husband Carter Reum.

Eva Chow, who had co-chaired the gala for the past 15 years with Leonardo DiCaprio, announced that she’d be stepping down from her post after this year. Dubbed the "Culture Queen of Los Angeles," she is credited with bringing together Hollywood and the art world for the event, helping grow it into the must-attend party of the season. DiCaprio couldn’t make it this year because he has a cold, but his girlfriend, model Vittoria Ceretti, was there to represent him.

But with all these big Hollywood types in the room, it was Celmins who stole the show—though she didn’t mean to. In a video that ran before her acceptance speech, the artist welcomed the video crew into her home, revealing her quick-witted humor, her ornery cat (she claims to be a dog person), and her love of Bob Dylan. Celmins is best known for her boundless work inspired by nature, including ocean waves, desert floors, starry night skies. She charmed the crowd with her boundless personality as well.

LACMA had plenty to celebrate this year, too. After a 20-year-long planning and development process, the David Geffen Galleries were completed this past year. As partygoers entered the tent for dinner, the silhouette of the formidable new building stood out in the background. “Same tent. Different buildings around it,” joked LACMA CEO Michael Govan during his opening remarks.

After his speech, Villeneuve and all the guests made their way out to LACMA’s main courtyard, where Rosé would perform under the stars. I joked with him that I thought he would make some news with that tease of a Bond casting, and then wondered if he likes being the center of attention at a gala like this. He said he values the connections he makes with other filmmakers and artists at these events. “I like talking one-on-one,” he said.

Noor Alfallah, Al Pacino, Erica Pelosini, Larry Gagosian and Ed Ruscha

While Rosé performed four songs for the black-tie-clad audience, Emily in Paris star Ashley Park and In the Heights actor Anthony Ramos swayed to her ballad, “Number One Girl.” Popcorn and cotton candy were passed out to the audience, who, naturally, sang along when Rosé ended her set with her biggest hit, “APT.” Andrew Garfield led his Artificial co-star Monica Barbaro by the hand through the crowd. Though the pair didn’t pose for photos on the carpet together, the couple (who have been romantically linked since 2025) spent the evening in close contact as they chatted with friends like Salma Hayek Pinault.

Villeneuve's speech best captured the evening’s one-of-a-kind mashup of art and film when he spoke passionately about the importance of human effort in the era of AI. “I can create something with a prompt or I can go into the desert with actors, with a crew and go on a real adventure where I learn about life and become better at my craft,” he said. “More important than the result is the process. The process is how the human experience acquires its meaning. In this moment in time, it is more important than ever that human beings keep making art together.”

Odessa A'zion in a Charles & Ron + Maison Privee coat.

My favorite Stephen King adaptation is, without a doubt, Stand by Me. Almost two years ago, we here at CinemaBlend lamented that the Rob Reiner-directed movie was leaving Netflix, but now it’s back, and I definitely plan on watching it again with my Netflix subscription. It’s actually been a lot longer than two years since I last saw Stand by Me, and I’m definitely ready for a rewatch of the movie with a now legendary cast including Wil Wheaton, River Phoenix, Jerry O'Connell, Corey Feldman, Keifer Sutherland, and John Cusack. I have a strong emotional attachment to the movie that outshines any other of King’s book-to-screen adaptations.

I was ten years old when Stand by Me was released in 1986, and I was 11 when I saw it. While the kids in the movie were a touch old, as with any 11-year-old, I thought of myself as slightly older than I actually was. That made me right in the sweet spot for the movie. Sure, I was a child of the '70s/’80s, and the characters in the movies were my parents' generation, but I felt a kinship with them. Plus, because they were my parents' generation, I had a direct connection to the 1950s, having heard all the stories about my mom and dad’s childhoods.

That also meant that I connected with the music in the movie. Director Reiner and music supervisor Celest Ray picked some bangers from the early days of rock n’ roll for the soundtrack, and I loved it. I’m sure I heard the soundtrack before I saw the movie, much like another Boomer nostalgia movie, Good Morning, Vietnam. For kids in the 1980s, the soundtracks to movies like Stand by Me were often our first exposure to them.

The ‘80s were a different time, and seeing Rated-R movies way before we ever should have meant that I had seen a couple of King adaptations before Stand by Me. Movies like Firestarter and Cujo were staples of cable TV, and I’d seen both. I’d also been terrified of both. I didn’t even know Stand by Me was based on a King novella until I saw his name during the opening credits. It blew my mind. I thought he wrote horror stories. Stand by Me definitely wasn’t that, although the dog “Chopper” scared me as much as Cujo did.

Stand by Me is the first adaptation from a King story that showed that other side of the author. The one we all know now from movies and books like this one and The Shawshank Redemption. I had no idea he wrote such heartwarming stories to go along with the ones that kept me up at night, like The Shining and Carrie. Before Stand by Me, all the movies based on his books were like those and Maximum Overdrive, which was another movie I saw around this same time and really scared me, like, a lot.

Stand by Me has no horror at all, and nothing supernatural. Just a deeply personal story about friendship that kids of any era can connect with, just like I did. It's one of the best King movies, despite not being what he's most famous for. I can’t wait to watch it again this weekend.

#3343. This Canceled 2010s Fantasy Series Deserved More Time To Flesh Out Its Ambitious Premise

The supernatural TV series "The Secret Circle" debuted on The CW in 2011, falling squarely into the network's penchant for teen dramas and YA-inflected soaps. Sadly, it only lasted for one 22-episode season, ending its run in 2012. And like other TV shows that possess as much lore, backstory, and interpersonal relationships as this one, "The Secret Circle" needed to live a lot longer to fulfill its potential.

Based on the series of novels created by L.J. Smith (best known for writing "The Vampire Diaries"), "The Secret Circle" stars Britt Robertson (who also fronted the guilty pleasure that is Netflix's "Girlboss") as Cassie, a teenager who recently lost her mother in a fire and has since moved to Chance Harbor, Washington, to live with her grandmother, Jane (Ashley Crow). Cassie doesn't initially know this, but she's secretly a witch and has eerie magical powers. However, it doesn't take long for the other teen witches at her new high school to recognize that Cassie is a witch and invite her to be part of their Secret Circle.

Cassie isn't just a witch, she learns, her matronly lineage goes all the way back to the beginning of witchcraft. Cassie's father, it's revealed, is John Blackwell (Joe Lando), a mysterious dark warlock who lurks in the show's margins. Other members of the Secret Circle include Adam (Thomas Dekker), Faye (Phoebe Tonkin), Diana (Shelley Hennig), Melissa (Jessica Parker Kennedy), and Nick (Louis Hunter).

True to the soap opera spirit of The CW, there are romantic dealings between the Circle's members. For example, Nick and Melissa are dating, and Nick eventually has to learn to respect Melissa more. That is, in addition to being killed and resurrected (!). Cassie, meanwhile, instantly falls for Adam, which upsets Diana, who has always had a thing for Adam.

In addition to the kids in the Circle, Gale Harold plays Charles, Diana's father and a former Circle member. Elsewhere, Natasha Henstridge from "Species" plays Faye's mother, another former Circle member, and the principal of the high school where the show's action takes place.

"The Secret Circle" belongs to a vast and well-populated matrix of teen supernatural dramas that were very much in vogue on television in the 2000s and early 2010s (although L.J. Smith started publishing her "Secret Circle" novels in 1992). Indeed, it's worth recalling that The CW had already scored a hit when its TV adaptation of "The Vampire Diaries" began its run in 2009, to the point that the network would go on to develop multiple spin-offs (like the since-canceled "Legacies"). Clearly, "The Secret Circle" was an attempt to bottle the same lightning. Vampires, witches, teen drama, magic: It was all boiling together on The CW.

And "The Secret Circle" certainly doesn't lack conflict. It carefully balances the magic of a witch coven with the drama of being a regular high school student. As such, it features just as many stories about school dances and friend-group inter-flirting as ones about spell books and dark witchy forces that aim to attack the Circle for nefarious purposes. Case in point: The show includes three episodes that center on school dances, and its penultimate episode takes place at Prom. On the witch side of things, several plot lines focus on magic crystals that are coveted by various magical players for a variety of reasons.

Back in 2015, writer Gavin Hetherington penned a post-mortem on "The Secret Circle" for Spoiler TV, revisiting it three years after its cancelation. Hetherington noted that "The Secret Circle" actually began quite strong in the ratings, but it fell off quickly, falling far behind "The Vampire Diaries." For Hetherington, this was a tragedy, as he declared the show's finale to be its best episode up to that point, arguing that it only showed more potential going forward. In fact, four new characters arrive in that episode, with all of them being part of Cassie's witch ancestor's lineage. Sadly, though, the show ended before audiences could learn their whole story.

When "The Secret Circle" was canceled, its many fans tried to convince The CW to keep it going via a letter-writing campaign, but it was not successful. "The Vampire Diaries" simply left a deeper impact and is generally regarded as one of the best vampire shows of all time. Due to its truncated run, "The Secret Circle" just can't compete with that series.

It probably didn't help that critics were less impressed with "The Secret Circle" than its loyal fans. Reviewing the series for Variety in 2011, Brian Lowry even described it as "'One Tree Hill,' only with witchcraft," writing that "nothing in the pilot conjures any genuine magic, TV-wise." Still, it's a vestige of what the old CW used to be in all its glory.

#3342. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Halle Berry is known for being something of an open book, as she’s shared aspects of her life and career with her fans over the years. (Of course, she’s also known to share the occasional bikini photo or two.) In more recent years, Berry really hasn’t had a problem publicly highlighting her relationship with boyfriend-turned-fiancé Van Hunt. Comments shared by the Oscar-winning actor and Hunt suggest they have a firm relationship. And, apparently, that’s carried right through her ongoing custody battle.

For weeks now, Berry and ex-husband Olivier Martinez have been engaged in a legal skirmish, with the latter having leveled accusations against the X-Men star. Berry (via her lawyer) has since vehemently denied the claims and has appeared in court a few times. By her side has been Van Hunt, who’s been photographed walking with her after the court hearings she’s attended. According to Page Six, Hunt has been a major source of support for Berry amid the legal proceedings. The outlet’s insider says this:

Van has really been Halle’s rock through all of this. He’s been by her side throughout the whole custody battle and restraining order situation.

Hunt and Berry began dating back in 2020 and, before long the singer/songwriter/music producer began making frequent appearances in Berry’s Instagram posts. Although these latest comments are from an insider, they do appear to align with what’s been said and shown of Berry and Hunt’s romance. The source went on to drop further claims about what Hunt’s presence has meant for his partner throughout this time:

It’s obviously been an incredibly difficult and stressful time for her, but he’s been such a calming presence and a huge source of strength. He’s been incredibly supportive through everything, and having someone like him to lean on has made a big difference for her.

Halle Berry Shared How She And Van Hunt Happened: 'I'm Convinced I Manifested My Now Partner'

As previously alluded to Berry and Hunt have appeared together in more than a few of the former’s social media posts over the last several years. For example, years back, Berry posted about their outing at the NY Spring/Summer 2024 fashion show, and she’s also shared sweet tribute posts to Hunt. Berry is even far past the point at which she’s comfortable sharing her and Hunt’s Christmas festivities.

It was in 2025 that Hunt proposed to Berry, though both of them confirmed around that same time that the Bruised actress had yet to formally accept it. Berry explained that after having been married three times, she wasn’t eager to jump into another marriage right away. In her estimation, she and Hunt also didn’t need to “validate” their love in any way. However, earlier this year, Berry clarified that she did accept the proposal but that she and her partner had yet to set a wedding date.

Halle Berry and Van Hunt have emerged as something of a fan-favorite couple on social media, so many take comfort in the notion of the latter comforting his lady amid these legal proceedings. And, as for when or where the pair might actually tie the knot, that remains to be seen.

#3339. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

#3338. Zelda: Ocarina of Time and WoW: Forever Are the Good Kind of Remakes

Zelda: Ocarina of Time and World of Warcraft: Forever were made for different reasons than most remakes, and you can tell

Why are there so many video game remakes these days? We think we know the answer. New ideas are hard to come by, and big games are harder, more expensive, and take longer to make than ever before. Even a new sequel in an already-popular franchise is a huge, risky undertaking. But game companies need reliable products to put on the shelves quicker than they can make new ones. Remakes answer that need, as well as keeping back catalogs relevant for an industry whose relentless technological advances swiftly render classics obsolete.

That's all accurate. But what if the game developers working on remakes had reasons of their own for revisiting the classics — reasons that weren't just learning their way around Unreal Engine 5, plugging a gap between new releases, or answering market forces? We got an emphatic answer this week, in the form of not one but two remarkable new versions of two of the greatest and most influential games ever made. Those two games, released on consecutive days, are The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and World of Warcraft: Forever.

A few months ago, I said that we need to decide what we want from remakes. This is what we want.

Nintendo’s excellent Switch 2 remake recaptures the soul of a masterpiece

Blizzard's retro MMO is about to sail into uncharted waters, but right now, it's clearly something special

These games have some similarities in their approach to remaking a classic, and some differences. Both games make smart modernizations while working hard to retain the spirit of the original. Ocarina of Time is a faithful recreation of a masterpiece that takes few liberties with its content and design, but makes a forceful departure in its lavish and technically dazzling art style.

WoW: Forever preserves the original WoW's art beneath a subtly impressive new rendering layer, and is built out from the same content. But it makes substantial additions, gets its hands dirty under the hood of the design, and, with its promise of a fixed progression cap and "horizontal" expansion, even seeks to boldly recontextualize WoW — and MMOs in general, and maybe even live-service games — in a new form.

In both cases, the developers have talked in interviews about their desire to preserve and carry forward something intrinsic about the games' design that they think has been lost in modern games.

Nintendo's top Legend of Zelda producers talk the remake, the future, and more

In a Nintendo "Ask the Developer" interview, Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma spoke about his desire to educate a new generation of Zelda developers who worked on Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom and weren't intimately familiar with the intricate mechanical mesh of classic Zelda design.

"By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake, it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development," Aonuma said. "If we could achieve that, I thought it would be incredibly valuable. That’s what led us to the conclusion that now is the right time to revisit The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time once again."

It's incredible to think that Nintendo's primary motivation in mounting this expensive production might have been bolstering institutional knowledge. But that's what makes Nintendo Nintendo.

The grassroots reimagining of classic World of Warcraft seems huge, but the team wants to stay small

Meanwhile, at Bizzard, a desire to see and play a "Classic Plus" version of WoW bubbled up naturally among the developers at the same time as it did in the WoW Classic community. This makes sense, since the WoW Classic team was mostly staffed by enthusiasts of the original game. It was the small, enterprising Classic team that experimented with the idea during the Season of Discovery event and then pitched it to leadership.

Lead Forever designer Kris Zierhut, who admits to having "drifted away" from modern WoW, explained it to me as a kind of thought experiment, a chance to imagine a different path the game might have taken. "Imagine if that team from 2004 — you know, Jeff Kaplan, and Eric Dodds, and Tom Chilton, and Scott Mercer, Pat Nagle, all those people — they've given them two more years to develop the game and add more stuff to it and perfect it," he said. "What would they have done with the time?"

What Zierhut and Aonuma are articulating is not a desire to preserve these epochal game designs for posterity. It's a desire to get inside them and explore them, find out what they can teach us, and maybe point out some things we've lost to progress — like an epic adventure game that puts craft before sheer scale, or a live-service game that's about the journey and not the destination.

Both these remakes were made with sincerity, passion, and above all, purpose. You don't have to take my word for it, or the developers'; you can tell when you play them. That's why they're so exciting, and how they honor two classics while bringing them alive for a new generation of players. Don't be too quick to dismiss remakes as cynical cash-grabs and schedule fillers. They can be beautiful acts of creation in their own right.
