#3337. Was This Short-Lived '60s Sitcom Really The Worst Show To Ever Air On TV?

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The 1960s was truly a golden era for weird little shows that melded the quotidian and the fantastical. This was the decade that gave us the great fantasy sitcoms, in which some larger than life character with supernatural abilities would be slotted into a suburban setting for laughs. "Mister Ed" was one of the first, featuring a talking horse who could only be understood by his architect owner Wilbur Post (Alan Young). The much lesser-known "The Hathaways" was sort of in that vein as well. Rather than featuring an animal with fantastical powers, however, it featured three chimpanzees whose owners treated them as if they were actual children.

You might already be able to see why this series didn't last longer than a single season. But not only was "The Hathaways" short-lived, it seemed to stoke significant ire among certain critics. In "Watching TV: Four Decades of American Television," authors Harry Castleman and Walter J. Podrazik outright described the show as "possibly the worst series ever to air on network TV."

Of course, such a claim is subjective. But there was an undeniably uncanny and slightly unsettling air to "The Hathaways," which saw Peggy Cass' Elinore Hathaway and Jack Weston's Walter Hathaway acting as "parents" to their three chimpanzees, referring to them as "the kids" and dressing them in human clothing. The suburban Los Angeles couple seemed to have completely lost the plot, yet it was all played for laughs. At least, it was for about 10 months. After that, ABC quite sensibly pulled the plug.

The sheer volume of failed shows in TV history is kind of breathtaking when you consider the amount of effort that goes into these things. Scripts are written, casts and production teams assembled, sets designed, and significant amounts of money are spent. (In the case of the swiftly-cancelled 1970s TV flop "Supertrain," we're talking major sums.) How many actors have been convinced that they were on the verge of their big break, only to become yet another footnote in TV history? It's weirdly tragic to think about. In the case of "The Hathaways," its chimpanzee stars were likely unfazed by the show's hasty cancellation, due to the fact they were in high demand elsewhere. That and they were literally animals.

Non-chimp leading man Jack Weston stars as Walter Hathaway, a real estate agent whose wife Elinore Hathaway acts as a mother to Candy, Charlie, and Enoch. These ape "kids" were part of the Marquis Chimps, a group of trained chimpanzees owned by Gene Detroy that were popular at the time. As the New York Times noted in a contemporaneous report ahead of the premiere of "The Hathaways," "The chimps got their new job through a TV guest appearance on 'The Jack Benny Show' [...] Robert Sparks, executive producer of the new series, saw them on the 'Benny' program and decided to develop a series."

That series saw Walter and Elinore taking care of their chimpanzee children while also booking them as a performing act, in which they would ride bicycles and build things. Otherwise, they would hang out at home, earning the Hathaways some strange looks from their neighbors. Other non-chimp cast members included Harvey Lembeck as talent agent Jerry Roper and Belle Montrose as neighbor Mrs. Harrison.

Was "The Hathaways" really one of the worst sitcoms of all time? Well, it was certainly strange. Perhaps, viewed in retrospect, the show feels a little too close to the unforgettable "Gordy" scene in Jordan Peele's "Nope," in which a chimpanzee mauls the entire cast and crew on the set of his sitcom. (Thankfully, nothing of the sort happened during filming on "The Hathaways.") But there's just something unsettling about the series, which seemed like a particularly cynical attempt at leveraging the chimps' popularity, even at a time when fantasy sitcoms featuring similarly unusual setups were coming to the fore. As Harry Castleman and Walter J. Podrazik write in their book, "The premise itself was utterly degrading to both the audience and the actors," adding that "The Hathaways" "stood as an embarrassing example of the depths programmers had reached in their desperate search for a chance hit in any format or premise."

Unsurprisingly, the sitcom didn't last long. "The Hathaways" debuted on ABC in October 1961 and was canceled by August 1962. A decade later, CBS tried its luck at a chimpanzee-led sitcom with "Me and the Chimp," which starred Ted Bessell as a dentist who lives with his family and a chimpanzee named Buttons. It, too, lasted one season. For some reason, NBC thought it could do better and unleashed "Mr. Smith" in 1983, a sitcom about a talking orangutan (played by the same ape who accompanied Clint Eastwood in his controversial project "Any Which Way But Loose") who becomes a political advisor after ingesting an experimental drug. Yep, one season. But "The Hathaways" remains the first and arguably the worst of these ape-led sitcoms.

#3335. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

#3334. Why Michael Stuhlbarg Left HBO's Boardwalk Empire

In "The Godfather Part II," Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) meets with the aged gangster Hyman Roth (Lee Strasberg) in his modest Florida home. Roth muses, "I've loved baseball ever since Arnold Rothstein fixed the World Series of 1919."

That reference isn't a movie embellishment. New York racketeer Arnold Rothstein really was alleged to have fixed the 1919 World Series in what's called "The Black Box Scandal," the blowback of which is explored in Season 1 of HBO's Prohibition period piece "Boardwalk Empire," featuring Michael Stuhlbarg as Rothstein. "AR," as his men often call him, remains a fixture of "Boardwalk Empire" during its first four seasons, and Stuhlbarg gives one of the show's standout performances.

Historians describe Rothstein as the one who put the "organized" in organized crime, thanks to a sharp knack for math and business. Stuhlbarg's Rothstein lives up to the history books. He's often shown playing pool or gambling and notes a great gambler never makes a bet without fixing the odds in his favor. He's extremely eloquent but only polite except in the most surface-level ways. Ice water runs in his veins.

So, it's a shame that he doesn't even get a real ending. History says that Rothstein died in 1928. "Boardwalk Empire" Season 4 ends in 1924, and then its fifth and final eight-episode season jumps ahead to 1931. That meant the show skips over lots of real history, including Rothstein's death. He simply disappears from the series, save for vague references to his demise in Season 5.

It's even more noticeable since his legacy hangs over the show's finale. "Boardwalk Empire" Season 5 includes a fictionalized account of how Rothstein's protégés "Lucky" Luciano (Vincent Piazza), Meyer Lansky (Anatol Yusef), and Benny "Bugsy" Siegel (Michael Zegen) took over the East Coast American mob.

Rothstein's death is a pretty big missing chapter in Season 5's story, but a consequence of the larger "Boardwalk Empire" production. Looking in from the outside, "Boardwalk Empire" appears to be a show that got cut short. A fifth and final season that's only two-thirds as long as the previous ones? And which leaps past several years of story? It's hard to believe that was always the intention. It really feels like a series that ran out of runway and jumped ahead to the intended ending to resolve itself as best it could. (Mind you, Season 5 still has some great episodes.)

The often repeated narrative is that "Boardwalk Empire" cost too much for HBO for too little a return, so it had to go. It was an unavoidably expensive show that came with a lot of homework for its cast (being a period piece), costing a reported $5 million per episode. The reported episode ratings do also show a consistent downward slump across seasons. From "Boardwalk Empire" Seasons 1-4, each successive season premiere and season finale was watched by fewer people than the previous one, and by Season 4, the show was slipping below even two million viewers an episode.

Nonetheless, "Boardwalk Empire" creator Terence Winter maintained back in 2014 that ending the series was a creative call. Speaking with Time and Hitflix, Winter said he and his writers felt series lead Nucky Thompson (Steve Buscemi) was already nearing his story's end by Season 4. 1931 was chosen as the most natural endpoint because it's when Al Capone (Stephen Graham) went to prison, Luciano and Lansky began the mafia's Commission, and Prohibition was winding down. The cost was skipping over major events like Rothstein's murder, which in real life remains shrouded in mystery.

Reportedly, Rothstein owed $300,000 after a poker loss and refused to pay up, earning him a bullet to the gut on November 4, 1928. But he took his killer's identity to the grave. Rothstein's real death being unsolved would give "Boardwalk Empire" dramatic license to fill in the details. I'm confident it would've pulled it off since whenever Rothstein was onscreen, "Boardwalk Empire" became a more compelling show.

The ending of "Boardwalk Empire" Season 4 even directly teases more to come from Rothstein. He enters a business alliance with Nucky's ex-wife, Margaret Thompson (a pre-"Lanterns" Kelly Macdonald), who is working as a secretary at a New York City investment firm and agrees to slip Rothstein insider information. Instead, nothing comes of that.

Stuhlbarg deserves a mountain's worth of credit. The actor studied his character, including how the real Rothstein thought of himself as a businessman and held his conduct to such a standard, and he's said the "Boardwalk Empire" writers' room was "amiable" about implementing his own research into his character. Stuhlbarg was similarly gracious about not returning for Season 5, especially considering it wasn't even his choice to leave the show, saying during a 2014 press junket that:

"They had to act fast, and they had a lot of ground to cover. It was amazing that we all got as much coverage as we did, considering how many characters they were juggling. I had so much fun doing the show, and I had no regrets. And yeah, sure it would've been fun to have shown [Rothstein's death], but I thought what they came up with was very cool, as it was. I think if they could have, they would've shown it, but they didn't have the time."

Video game adaptations have a way of making everybody angry. However, I can understand why Zach Cregger expected a different conversation around his Resident Evil movie. The director behind Barbarian and Weapons has opened up about the one part of releasing his 2026 movie calendar horror hit that genuinely "frustrated" him, and I get where he's coming from.

During an appearance on The Town with Matthew Belloni, Cregger was asked whether he'd consider tackling another established franchise after Resident Evil. His answer led to a candid discussion about the reaction to his film, which follows Austin Abrams' medical courier Bryan through a nightmare in Raccoon City. Cregger felt people cared more about what he changed from Capcom's games than about the movie itself. He explained:

I think I was frustrated at the conversation around Resident Evil and how much of the conversation really didn't have anything to do with the movie. It had everything to do with whether the movie was living up to the different standards that different fans of the games had, whether it was using the characters or not, or what did I get wrong in the lore, or why is it? It was just a lot about why isn't this like the source material or why is it good that it's not like the [source material].

I can understand why that would be exhausting. After spending years making a new horror movie, you release it into the world, and suddenly everyone argues about why Leon Kennedy isn't included. However, I also empathize with fans who have waited a long time to see their favorite characters properly adapted.

Cregger chose to tell an original story within the Resident Evil universe instead of recreating one of the games, and the movie's biggest strength has nothing to do with lore or Easter eggs. His movie swaps familiar protagonists for Bryan and leans into the sensation of playing survival horror: limited resources, increasingly awful encounters and the knowledge that the next room might be your last. Before release, some fans objected to the missing characters and changes to Raccoon City.

What's interesting is that the movie did incredibly well. Resident Evil has earned more than $400 million worldwide, according to Box Office Mojo, while Rotten Tomatoes lists a 96% critics' score. Early reviews praised RE for its relentless pacing and the way Cregger captured the experience of playing the games.

Still, success didn't erase Cregger's disappointment with the discussion surrounding it. He continued:

All the conversation just felt like it was about not the movie. And I'm proud of the movie. I really love the movie. I should have known better going into it. I should have understood that that was going to be the case, but for some reason I was a little shocked.

That last admission is what stuck with me. Cregger is a fan himself, and he previously acknowledged that players hoping for Leon's story had a fair reason to feel disappointed. But he also wanted people to judge the actual movie he made. Surely there's room for both opinions.

Zach Cregger's not necessarily finished with Raccoon City, either. He told Belloni he'd like some creative input if the series continues, even if somebody else directs the next installment. Personally, I hope he gets that chance. Given how well this one turned out, I'd much rather see what else he dreams up than spend another round arguing about which character didn't show up.

Resident Evil arrived on digital video-on-demand (VOD) platforms to rent or buy on November 3, 2026, so check your favorite streamer for details.

Ryan graduated from Missouri State University with a BA in English/Creative Writing. An expert in all things horror, Ryan enjoys covering a wide variety of topics. He's also a lifelong comic book fan and an avid watcher of Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon.

#3332. Sebastián Lelio, Chilean Director of Oscar-Winning ‘A Fantastic Woman,’ Dead at 52

Sebastián Lelio, the humanistic Chilean filmmaker whose trans drama “A Fantastic Woman” won the Best International Feature Film Oscar in 2018, has died at age 52.

The Chilean publication Emol first revealed the news that he was found dead in his home in Santiago on Friday, November 6, amid an undisclosed health issue. His body was discovered by his partner, the actress/director Amalia Kassai, who starred in his final film, the protest musical “The Wave” from Cannes 2025. Kassai also posted a statement in Spanish on her Instagram account.

Lelio was reportedly mid-production on the feature “Chilean Poet,” adapted from Alejandro Zambra’s Viking-published 2022 novel. Along with “A Fantastic Woman,” he also directed the Hasidic lesbian romance “Disobedience” in the same year, 2017; it starred Rachel McAdams and Rachel Weisz, and helped bring the filmmaker to international prominence. In 2013, he directed Paulina García to a Berlinale Silver Bear Best Actress win with “Gloria,” a late-in-life romantic comedy about a 58-year-old divorcee starting over again. He remade his own film in 2018 in English as “Gloria Bell,” released by A24 and starring Julianne Moore in the role García originated, opposite John Turturro.

Lelio regularly collaborated with the Chilean brothers Pablo Larraín and Juan de Dios Larraín, who served as producers on nearly all of his films. They were also collaborating with Lelio on his ongoing, now-final feature. Born in Argentina, he emigrated to Chile at age two with his mother and later graduated from Chilean Film School, after which he launched his career with short films and music videos. His debut narrative feature, “The Sacred Family,” premiered at the San Sebastián International Film Festival in Spain before his follow-up, “Navidad,” premiered at Cannes in 2009. The post-Chilean-earthquake drama “The Year of the Tiger,” starring beloved Chilean actor Luis Dubó, debuted at Locarno in 2011.

His fourth feature, “Gloria,” shot digitally and with a script and dialogue developed in part with his actors, including García, received U.S. distribution from Roadside Attractions and was widely regarded as one of the best films of 2013.

Lelio directed the first Best International Feature Oscar entry to win the Academy Award with 2017’s Golden Bear-nominated “A Fantastic Woman,” an exuberantly styled drama that put trans actress Daniela Vega on the international map. As Vega consulted on the script, it’s widely seen as a groundbreaker of trans portrayals onscreen in the 21st century. And it helped reform the perception and attitudes toward transness in Lelio and Vega’s home of Chile — and inevitably, within the Academy.

Lelio’s favorite films on the 2022 Sight & Sound poll included “La Dolce Vita,” “Playtime,” “The 400 Blows,” and “Singin’ in the Rain,” and you can feel their impact across his often irreverent, at times burstingly colorful, playful body of work.

His 2017 TIFF premiere “Disobedience” received U.S. distribution from Bleecker Street, and told the story of a forbidden, transgressive romance between two Orthodox Jewish women (McAdams and Weisz) in North London. The tender, taboo drama performed well in North America, grossing nearly $3.5 million domestic during a spring-through-summer 2018 run.

Lelio, that year, deftly remade “Gloria” as “Gloria Bell” with Julianne Moore as the free-spirited divorcee being wooed by John Turturro, and weighing choices in her next chapter living as a yoga instructor in Los Angeles. Returning to filming after the pandemic, Lelio broadened his collaborative scope to adapt “Room” author Emma Donoghue’s “The Wonder,” with Donoghue and Alice Birch co-writing the script with him. Florence Pugh starred as a British nurse sent to Ireland to observe a miraculous “fasting girl,” in a film that played Telluride and streamed on Netflix to strong reviews.

His last film, “The Wave,” took a minute to get off the ground after playing out of competition in Cannes 2025. The story of an introverted music student whose passion for protest is awakened amid a growing feminist movement on campus, “The Wave” received a small release from Wolfe Video earlier this year and received positive response throughout its festival run.

The status of Lelio’s final film isn’t known right now, but we can imagine that Lelio’s sensitive approach to character — and unstable identities finding their footing, their purest expression — will carry into the new work. The Larraín brothers were also producing the film, with Lelio’s regular cinematographer Benjamín Echazarreta on board as DP.

#3331. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.

#3330. This X-Men-Esque '80s Sci-Fi Series Launched Courteney Cox's Career

The premise of James D. Parriott's 1985 superhero/comedy series "Misfits of Science," which featured a young Courteney Cox, will sound very familiar to fans of Marvel Comics' X-Men titles.

The series follows a human scientist named Dr. Billy Hayes (Dean Paul Martin), who has taken an interest in what he called "human anomalies," which are people who have been born with a variety of unpredictable superpowers. In the show's pilot episode, he assembles the main cast of powerful castoffs with the intention of studying them, but also helping them come to terms with their supernatural abilities.

The team was small but mighty. It included Dr. Hayes' lab partner, Dr. Lincoln (Kevin Peter Hall), who can shrink for a limited period. Additionally, Mark Thomas Miller plays "Johnny B" Bukowski, a rocker who can suck up electricity and who wears shades to cover his glowing eyes. He can throw lightning bolts.

Most strikingly, Courteney Cox, future star of "Friends" and "Scream," plays Gloria, a troubled teen with "Carrie"-like telekinetic powers. "Misfits of Science" wasn't Cox's first credit: She had appeared in an episode of "As the World Turns" back in 1975, when she was still a kid, and famously danced with Bruce Springsteen in the "Dancing in the Dark" music video in 1984. "Misfits of Science," though, was the first time Cox starred in a TV series.

"Misfits of Science" is not currently available to stream, but resourceful media hunters will be able to find episodes online easily enough. It's a whimsical, lighthearted show that prodded at the conventions of superheroes as much as it vaunted them. It's definitely worth a glance.

"Misfits of Science," it should be noted, only lasted for a single 16-episode season, so it's okay if you don't remember it.

The series does have something of a superhero legacy, as R. Timothy Kring, a.k.a. Tim Kring, wrote an episode of "Misfits of Science," and he would go on to create the hit series "Heroes," the first season of which remains a must-watch (the later seasons, though, less so). Kring's "Misfits" episode, called "Twin Engines," is about a young man (Joel Polis) who is plagued with uncontrollable visions. It's eventually revealed that he was sharing the visions of his long-lost twin brother.

Indeed, the entire show was based on a long series of super-powered shenanigans and investigations. Mostly, the protagonists get involved in run-of-the-mill spy plots. The main characters aren't costumed vigilantes, but they do seem to operate as freelance spies. Famed drummer Mikey Jones appears in the show's pilot as a character with freezing powers named Ice Man. According to Giant Freakin' Robot, that character was abandoned after Marvel Comics "raised objections" over its own Ice Man character. And speaking of Marvel, Courteney Cox's character was very similar to the X-Men's Jean Gray.

Some fun trivia: Shortly after the time "Misfits of Science" was being made, Dr. Lincoln actor Kevin Peter Hall (who played the original Predator in John McTiernan's sci-fi action classic) was in contention to play either Data or Geordi La Forge on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." /Film has previously talked about all the finalists for the roles, and Hall eventually lost the roles to Brent Spiner and LeVar Burton, respectively.

As mentioned, "Misfits of Science" was not successful. Thanks to low ratings, the series was canceled before all of its episodes could even air, leaving one of them unaired in the United States.

Courteney Cox continued to work undeterred, of course. In 1987, she appeared in the low-budget, high-profile Cannon adaptation of "Masters of the Universe," a movie so goofy, it has been subjected to a "How Did This Get Made" oral history. That same year, she began playing the recurring role of Lauren Miller on the hit sitcom "Family Ties." By 1994, she was appearing in the comedy "Ace Ventura: Pet Detective" and began playing one of the six lead roles on "Friends." "Misfits of Science" was her first starring role, but it certainly wasn't her last.

#3329. Mike Flanagan’s 10-Episode Netflix Thriller Masterpiece Is Everything ‘Carrie’ Should Have Been

Carrie is missing something this show has in spades

Mike Flanagan knows how to make horror. He also knows how to make serialized TV. His most recent show is a mix of most of the things we’ve come to love about him: his bond with Stephen King, his skills as an adapter, his great eye for casting, and his ability to deliver pathos. But one key thing is missing: fear.

Carrie came out in October of this year, sparking much conversation, with many praising how it brought King’s ‘70s novel to 2026. One of its major criticisms, though, is that it’s not scary, especially for Flanagan, a guy who’s known for making some truly spooky stuff. Case in point: The Haunting of Hill House.

Released on Netflix in 2018, The Haunting of Hill House was Flanagan’s first TV show. Based on Shirley Jackson’s landmark novel of the same name, Flanagan takes her characters and reimagines them, at times scrapping their identities completely. While Jackson collected a group of strangers in a haunted house to explore their deepest traumas, Flanagan turned them into siblings, transforming Hill House into a story about their childhood home.

It’s an adaptational choice that many hardcore Jackson fans don’t forgive. Still, if Flanagan does one thing, it’s commit fully to the haunted house concept, taking the psychological fear that permeates the novel and literalizing it. Hill House is a true house of horrors.

Rather than leaning on jump scares, Hill House runs on dread, the type that has your eyes scanning through every inch of the screen so you’re not caught off guard by something that looks out of place. “If you go back and watch the series again, in every episode there’s probably somewhere between eight and 10 ghosts that are just hidden in plain sight that we called no attention to but they’re there,” Flanagan told Bloody Disgusting.

Flanagan also revealed that the ghosts had personal origins. The tall man with the bowler hat was added because one of the writers is afraid of tall people. “People on stilts freak her out,” he said. “It’s one of the most specific and weird phobias I’ve heard. We all thought it was so funny that we decided to make the tall man.”

And while Hill House delivers plenty of scary ghosts for texture and disquiet, some pull double duty, driving the story too. Flanagan splits Jackson’s Eleanor in two characters, giving her instability to the Crain siblings’ mother, Olivia (Carla Gugino), and her frailty and imagination to Nell (Victoria Pedretti). He turns the latter into the perfect example of a house cannibalizing its weakest. The series’ standout episode, “The Bent-Neck Lady,” relies on the twist that (spoiler alert) the ghost that has haunted Nell her entire life is herself, driven mad and killed by the house. Hill House’s biggest twist makes the horror intimate. Carrie’s twist does the opposite, removing the horror from her completely.

Warning: Spoilers follow for Carrie’s final episodes.

While Flanagan’s Carrie sticks closer to the book, keeping its mythology, sequence of events, and its characters' identities, it veers off in the one place it shouldn’t: the prom. We spend an entire season building up to one of the most famous moments in horror history, only for the series to unnecessarily complicate it. Instead of making the prom the place where Carrie breaks and enacts her revenge, it’s Emaline (Thalia Dudek), Carrie’s friend, who bears the majority of the blame, taking over Carrie’s body for most of the massacre.

In an interview with Polygon, Flanagan discussed the prom scene at length, clarifying what had happened. He shared that he and the writers wanted Carrie to be "100% solely responsible for" the deaths of key characters, innocent and guilty alike, including Tommy Ross (Joel Oulette), Billy Nolan (Arthur Conti) and Chris Hargensen (Alison Thornton).

They drew the line at the prom massacre. "None of us believed the Carrie White we created would consciously choose to kill Principal Grayle (Matthew Lillard), would choose to kill Ms. D (Amber Midthunder), and would choose to ignite innocent people around her,” he said.

Carrie has always been more than a story about a girl setting her prom on fire. It’s about the cruelty of high schoolers who use their weaker peers to feel better about themselves. That comes through in Flanagan’s show; as with Hill House, he has the ability to make us care deeply about his characters. But the prom is the moment where all that cruelty infects Carrie, where she transcends the page and becomes a horror icon. It’s there the show flinches. There’s no Bent-Neck Lady moment, just a massacre with no one clearly to blame. Is the show called Emaline?

The Haunting of Hill House is streaming on Netflix.

It’s no secret that Heated Rivalry is one of the biggest book-to-screen adaptations of recent years. The smutty, queer hockey romance stole the hearts of fans everywhere when it was released in late 2025, and its popularity hasn’t wavered at all. Fans are only going to get more intense now that news has dropped that Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie will be suiting up for a third season as well. However, I'm concerned about one detail.

Fans of Heated Rivalry have already known about Season 2 kicking off production, as photos from the set have been leaked despite the show’s creator, Jacob Tierney, kindly asking fans to give them space while filming. The news about a third season has been highly speculated, and now, that has been confirmed as well. Both seasons are reportedly being filmed back-to-back. This theoretically means that there shouldn’t be a huge wait between seasons, and maybe fans could get all twelve episodes sometime next year.

In addition to two more seasons with Shane and Ilya, Deadline reports that Tierney is working on a standalone theatrical release that the trade believes will be a “Christmas special” or “holiday-themed episode” centered around Season 1, Episode 3 couple Scott (François Arnaud) and Kip (Robbie G.K.). It’s not the Heated Rivalry-centric bonus episode fans have been hoping for, but the holiday special could be inspired by the short holiday story author Rachel Reid penned for the couple and earlier this year took down from her official website.

As a fan of the sports drama series, I’m overjoyed at the news, but I do have one concern heading into these news seasons when it comes to what it might mean for Shane and Ilya’s relationship.

Unlike the other couples in Reid’s Game Changers book universe, Shane and Ilya’s relationship unfolds over several books. When the series was released (and subsequently renewed for a second and a secret third season), the couple’s second book, The Long Game, was the final installment in their relationship. But then Reid announced she was writing a third book, Unrivaled, centered on the fan-favorite couple.

Had Reid not made the announcement that she was writing Unrivaled, I would have confidently said that Tierney and the creative team behind Heated Rivalry planned to split The Long Game into two seasons. This would allow the show to really dig deep into Shane and Ilya’s relationship challenges and give fans a faithful adaptation like the first season did. It would also provide space for the show to explore some of the other couples in the Game Changes universe, which seems to be happening based on casting announcements for Season 2.

Splitting The Long Game into two seasons might still be the case, which is great news for fans of the novel; however, it does raise concerns about the potential for an adaptation of Unrivaled. After all, if Seasons 2 and 3 are centered on the second novel, then the show would need to be renewed for a fourth season in order to see the third book and the presumed conclusion of Shane and Ilya’s love story on screen.

Given the show’s popularity, a hypothetical fourth season seems like a no-brainer, but one also has to consider the schedules of the cast and crew. With Storrie and Williams both cast in new shows and movies, it might be hard to get them on board for another season beyond these next two. Still, I’d like to believe that the talented actors would be eager to see Ilya and Shane's storyline through to the end.

All of this is purely speculation, as we don't know much about Season 2 of Heated Rivalry other than it's expected to drop in Spring 2027. When that happens, we'll know what to expect from Season 3. Until then, I’ll be streaming, or as fans have dubbed it “reheating,” Season 1 of Heated Rivalry with my HBO Max subscription. Fans can also catch the episodes playing for a limited time in theaters in the US and Canada.

#3327. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

#3326. Could ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Re-Ignite Quentin Tarantino’s Bruce Lee Controversy?

It does not take long for the new trailer for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” to invoke the most discourse-inducing scene from “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” In fact, the very first words we hear are “You heard the story about Bruce Lee getting his ass kicked by a stuntman?” Another reference to the Bruce Lee scene follows soon after, long before we hear any mention of Rick Dalton or any of the more consequential events of the first film..

The Netflix pseudo-sequel, directed by David Fincher and written by Quentin Tarantino, sees Brad Pitt reprising his Oscar-winning role as Cliff Booth. It’s billed as a separate adventure that happens to feature one of the film’s main characters — Leonardo DiCaprio is either completely absent or an incredibly well-kept secret, and Tarantino has said the film shares more DNA with Elmore Leonard’s paperback crime novels than the hangout movie style that defined the first film. But the marketing had to remind audiences who Cliff Booth is, and it’s curious that the second trailer’s primary reference point is a scene that is more memorable for the controversies it sparked than its role in the film’s plot. No mention is made, for instance, of the part Cliff played in dispatching several members of the Manson Family. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

A brief recap for those lucky enough to have been offline during the original saga. “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” features a scene in which Cliff is left to hang around a TV set while DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton shoots an episode. While killing time, he ends up in a fight with Bruce Lee (played by Mike Moh). Neither man is particularly polite to the other, with Cliff appearing more interested in Lee’s sidekick role on “The Green Hornet” than his higher profile movie roles, and Lee quickly challenges him to a fight. Each man wins one round of the fight before it’s broken up, ensuring there’s no clear winner — but the mere fact that Cliff was able to throw a martial arts legend into the side of a car is a feather in his cap.

Following the film’s release, Bruce Lee’s daughter Shannon publicly objected to the way the film portrayed her father.

“It’s unfortunate because it has started this narrative in some places where some people are saying, ‘Oh, Bruce Lee was an asshole,’” Shannon Lee said in 2020. “Look, everybody can be an asshole sometimes. I can be arrogant and angry in my life — is that something I would say I am like generally? No, my father was not generally like that. He was extremely passionate and driven.”

She continued, “He could have a temper sometimes, but he did not go around challenging people to fights. Certainly not after he was a teenager. Anyway, he didn’t behave or boast in that way…My father worked extremely hard and directly toward the idea of authentic representation in Hollywood for an Asian man, so I don’t think he would’ve gone around beating up stunt people and that kind of stuff as a way of furthering his cause.”

Tarantino frequently defended the scene, saying that he based his fictional portrayal on real anecdotes about Lee from people who knew the actor.

“Bruce Lee was kind of an arrogant guy,” Tarantino said in a 2019 press conference. “The way he was talking, I didn’t just make a lot of that up. I heard him say things like that to that effect. If people are saying, ‘Well he never said he could beat up Mohammad Ali,’ well yeah he did. Alright? Not only did he say that but his wife, Linda Lee, said that in her first biography I ever read. She absolutely said that.”

The controversy still rears its head sporadically. During a 2021 appearance on “The Joe Rogan Experience,” Tarantino told critics of the scene to “suck a dick,” with the caveat that he understood why a daughter would object to any negative portrayal of her father.

By the time “The Futher Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” hits select theaters this month (and expands to Netflix in December), more than seven years will have passed since “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” premiered. Perhaps all parties have said everything there is to say about the Bruce Lee scene. But given how much the trailer leans into the matter, we could be in for another round of arguments about the portrayal.

#3325. This Chilling Japanese Folk Horror Series Is One Of Hulu's Best Hidden Gems

If you're in the mood for a discrete dose of folk horror, Hulu recently added Adam Scott's terrifying horror "Hokum." But if you'd like to extend your trauma over, say two seasons of sheer terror, then "Gannibal" is for you. The show stars Yuya Yagira as a police officer who leaves the city to start over in a remote village. Here, he quickly discovers things aren't quite as idyllic as they seem.

"Gannibal" premiered in December 2022 but has failed to make much of an impact outside of Japan, despite arguably being one of the best horror series of the 2020s. Thus far, two seasons of "Gannibal" have been released, and had they hit Netflix in the United States, the show may well have become a big hit stateside. As it stands, this is one of Japan's best kept secrets and it's waiting to be discovered on Hulu.

Masaaki Ninomiya's "Gannibal" manga was originally serialized across thirteen volumes from October 2018 to November 2021. In October of that year, it was announced that "Gannibal" would be adapted as a TV series, with Shinzo Katayama directing from teleplays by Takamasa Oe.Thankfully, it turned out to be a worthy adaptation.

One of the best foreign horror shows streaming right now, "Gannibal" shares much in common with the South Korean horror movie with a 99% Rotten Tomatoes score "The Wailing." Both are set in remote villages and follow a police officer who becomes increasingly menaced by some terrifying ancient evil. But "Gannibal" departs from the movie with its tale of a cannibal conspiracy.

Yuya Yagira plays police officer Daigo Agawa, who after an unfortunate ordeal in Tokyo moves to the small mountain village of Kuge with his wife Yuki Agawa (Riho Yoshioka) and daughter Mashiro Agawa (Kokone Shimizu). At first, this secluded hamlet seems like the ideal refuge from the city and Agawa's fraught past. But things get off to an eerie start as Kuge's previous police officer has mysteriously vanished.

As Agawa and his family become more acquainted with the village and its people they discover the Goto family essentially run the town, and they don't seem like the most charming bunch. Meanwhile, a woman's body is found on the mountain, and while the Gotos claim she was killed by a bear, Agawa notices a human bite mark. Soon, his family's escape starts to turn into a nightmare. As such, this is not a horror TV show you can watch with the whole family. But it definitely deserves your attention regardless.

While you may never have heard of "Gannibal," the series has become a sensation in its native Japan. In April 2025, The Hollywood Reporter reported that "Gannibal" had become the most-viewed title in the country on Disney+ since its second season debuted in March of that year. The show also set new records for the streamer, solidifying its status as a bonafide mega-hit in Japan. In the United States, however, "Gannibal" mostly flew under the radar.

There are no "top critic" reviews for the series on Rotten Tomatoes, and it hasn't shown up on any "best horror series" lists since its 2022 debut. But it has managed to generate a small amount of buzz among non-Japanese viewers. One Redditor described the series as "grim folk horror" and was evidently left "completely wrecked" by it. Elsewhere on Reddit, another user described the series as "like 'Midsommar' meets 'Resident Evil 7'" and praised the "amazing actors, great cinematography, chilling and memorable soundtrack, and an absurdly dark story."

Letterboxd users are similarly impressed. "I just love it," writes one, who goes on to commend the series for its "sharp plot," "creepy characters," and "unsettling vibes," as well as the "splendid cinematography." Another also highlighted how the show is "beautifully shot and incredibly well-acted." Unfortunately, it seems unlikely there will be more to come. "Gannibal" Season 2 was released on March 19, 2025 and that wrapped up the story told in Masaaki Ninomiya's manga. Thankfully, if you are able to binge your way through both seasons of the series, there are plenty of great folk horror movies to tide you over.

#3324. 10 Hacks Every iCloud User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you accidentally delete or overwrite a file or contact that's synced to iCloud, you can restore it from the Recovery portal on iCloud.com. This feature works across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Photos, Notes, and Reminders, as well as Drive, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. When you restore an old version of your data, the current version is archived so you can revert back if you change your mind. Deleted files can be recovered within 30 days.

One benefit of an iCloud+ subscription is Apple's Hide My Email, which allows you to create unique, random aliases to keep your real email address private. These addresses forward to your primary inbox, and replies appear to come from the alias rather than your personal email. There's no limit on how many Hide My Email addresses you can generate, so you can use them for newsletter sign-ups, online shopping, and any other credential you may want to deactivate if you start getting spammed. Hide My Email is compatible with Safari, Mail, Apple Pay, and some third-party apps.

Apple supports legacy contacts for Apple Accounts, meaning you can designate someone to receive access to your data—including photos, files, messages, and backups—after your death. This allows you to use iCloud as a digital vault for storing documents and other important information that can be securely passed down. (Note that legacy contacts will not receive iCloud Keychain data like passwords and passkeys, so you'll need another way to share this information if desired.) To designate a legacy contact, go to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact and follow the prompts. That person will need the access key you generate and your death certificate to take over your accounts.

Apple's Family Sharing allows up to six users to share a single iCloud+ subscription while maintaining separate Apple Accounts. This means that each user has their own private vault for photos, documents, and backups while gaining access to premium features and a lot more storage overall. iCloud+ offers plans from 50 GB to 12 TB of storage. Family Sharing likely makes the most sense if you can fill most or all of the seats and/or already pay for or plan to use close to the limit of one of the higher-cost plans (compared to each individual paying for their own subscription).

Sorting through photos and adding them to a shared album after a vacation can feel like a huge project—but iCloud can do this work for you in real time if your friends and family have iPhones with Bluetooth enabled and are logged into their Apple Accounts. Set up an iCloud Shared Photo Library in the Photos app under Collections > [Your account] > Shared Library and add up to five participants. Then, from Shared Library, tap Sharing from Camera > Share Automatically. If you take photos when other album participants are nearby, they will be uploaded to the shared album.

If you want to text a large photo or video to someone who doesn't have an Apple Account and access to iCloud photos without compressing the file, you can create a temporary link that gives them access to view and download the file for 30 days. This also allows you to share multiple files with a single link rather than sending them individually, and you can revoke access whenever you'd like. To create an iCloud link, open an image, tap Share, and select Copy iCloud Link.

Note that as of iOS 27 and macOS 27, Apple now supports adding Windows and Android users to iCloud Shared Albums. However, temporary links are still a good solution if you don't want to share whole albums.

iCloud's backup feature will automatically back up your iPhone periodically so you can restore your data if your device is lost or stolen. This includes information that isn't regularly synced to iCloud storage, like settings and app organization. You can disable cellular backups to restrict backups to wifi only—or you can turn on low data mode, which will allow for backing up over your cellular connection except when speeds are low, or your data is capped. Low data mode could also save battery by not straining a slow connection. You can enable low data mode for cellular via Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Data Mode.

If your Apple device is backing up to iCloud, you could regularly bump up against your storage limit, especially if you aren't paying for a large amount of space. One way to mitigate this is to cut down what gets backed up, which you can do at the app level. If you have apps you don't use regularly or don't need data from, you can disable them from your iCloud backups. Go to your Apple account in the Settings app and tap iCloud > Storage > Backups > [This iPhone] to manage app backups.

If you sync tons of photos and files to iCloud along with device backups, you may find yourself hitting the storage cap. But you don't necessarily have to buy more storage space, nor are you stuck manually deleting items one by one. Instead, go to Settings > [Your Account] > iCloud > Recommended For You to find suggestions for freeing up storage space. This may include deleting inactive backups or reviewing your files or photos and videos, which are categorized by duplicates, screenshots, and videos (the content you're most likely to be able to offload). If you don't see these options under Recommended For You, go back to iCloud > Storage and select the app you want to clean up. Finally, check what's included in your device backups, and disable any apps you don't need under iCloud > Storage > Backups.

India’s most expensive movie ever is Ramayana, which is one of the latest 2026 movie releases to hit theaters. The movie was a massive undertaking, and that's evident just by watching the trailer. All in all, the film is firmly steeped in the culture its representing. But, even though the flick was made thousands of miles from Hollywood, a producer was very much inspired by one of our greatest filmmakers, Christopher Nolan, as CinemaBlend recently learned.

Did you know that Ramayana is co-composed by Hans Zimmer? The German musician has become one of the most beloved and prolific composers of modern cinema, and that’s exactly why the movie's producer, Namit Malhotra, asked for him to come aboard the filmmaking team. Here’s how he told us the story during CB’s exclusive Ramayana interview:

I grew up in India completely fanboying on A.R. Rahman, who I absolutely love and his music has sort of formed a big part of my growing up and childhood and youth. And then, I moved to L.A. in 2010, the year Inception came out. I started to fall in love with Chris Nolan and Han Zimmer's music that was done for The Dark Knight and all the films that came subsequent to that. And, it was one of those moments when we decided to make Ramayana. I said literally as a fanboy, ‘What if I could take Han Zimmer and A.R. Rahman together and they would create a new sound, a new feeling, a new energy that the world has not heard before?’ And everybody is like, ‘Yeah, why not?’

Malhotra called himself a self-described “fanboy” of Nolan movies who's been in awe of his movies for a while. So, when he went on to make his own epic, he thought he'd take the long-shot move to try to get Zimmer on board for Ramayana alongside his favorite composer from India, A.R. Rahman. (Did you know Zimmer actually helped convince Nolan to make Interstellar, by the way? A greatly overlooked detail is just how important musicians like him are pivotal to the filmmaking process.) As Malhotra added:

One thing I learned in America, there's no harm in asking because the worst you'll be told is ‘No’. That's not how we grew up in India. Like you normally don't ask the question if you think the answer is no.

Even though Namit Malhotra had never met Zimmer and didn't know would react to the request, the producer took “a cue from [his] American friends” and reached out to the Interstellar composer. This is what happened next:

I made a pitch and a presentation to him. I couldn't have been more surprised by his intellect, his intuitive judgment because he was like, ‘Namit, you don't have to sell me on Ramayana. If something has existed in the world for over 5,000 years and generation after generation, more people are excited to consume it, learn from it, and it's still not lost its relevance, there must be more than what you and I can understand. So we should just figure out how we do this and not worry about whether we should do it.’

Ramayana Is Making A Huge Global Push. I Still Can't Tell From Reviews What I'm Getting Into

The idea really does sell itself, doesn’t it? Ramayana is a Hindu epic poem that’s very central to India’s culture. It has inspired the celebrations of Diwali and Dussehra, and the story also serves as a moral cornerstone as well. It focuses on two characters: Rama and Ravana. Prince Rama is the seventh incarnation / avatar of Lord Vishnu, who becomes responsible for taking down King Ravana from having uncontrollable power over people. It's India's own classic good vs. evil story, and it has really stood the test of time.

I'm no sure how aware Zimmer was of the legend of Ramayana before it was pitched to him, yet he was apparently sold quite quickly. He got the importance of it being told for the big screen. Malhotra told us that Zimmer’s reaction to his pitch even “revalidated” his own reasons to make it and “reinvigorated [his] own confidence” since he respects the composer so much.

Hans Zimmer is a busy musical savant, who’s recently worked on the Dune movies and the upcoming Harry Potter TV series, so he could have easily passed, but he clearly didn’t want to. And, as a result of his participation, one of Hollywood's best got to put his mark on a historical Indian film. You can hear Zimmer’s original music for Ramayana, which is playing in theaters around the world right now.

#3322. ‘Soul Patrol’ Review: The Vietnam War’s First Black Special Ops Team Shares Their Stories in An Enlightening Documentary

Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. “Soul Patrol” opens in select theaters from Kino Lorber starting Friday, November 6.

The Vietnam War ended over a half-century ago, but the 20-year war remains a conflict that American artists keep going back to, finding new avenues and perspectives to tackle the many stories of the generation of men who had their lives irrevocably shaped by the conflict. Recent takes have centered the (often-neglected) perspective of the Vietnamese, or — like Spike Lee’s underrated late-career great “Da 5 Bloods” — explored the relatively under-examined service of Black men who served in the war. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“Soul Patrol,” a new documentary from director J.M. Harper, looks at the Black soldiers of the war through the perspective of Ed Emanuel, a writer who served as a 17-year-old. In his 2003 memoir of the same title, Emanuel described tracking down and reuniting with the men he served with in the first Black special operations Long-Range Reconnaissance Patrol team, during his short 1968 to 1969 tour.

“Soul Patrol” finds the men in 2024, in what will be the last reunion they hold. Gathering together, the men — Emanuel, Lawton Mackey, Thad Givens, Emerson Branch, Jesse Lewis, Willie T. Brown, Willie Merkerson, and Norman Reid — sit in the conference room of a Florida hotel to discuss the memories of their service that has stuck with them over the decades, in the hope that their discussion can help them move on.

The opening, and Emmanuel’s narration, help bring context to the small stretch of the war that the film explores. In 1968, as the young men went to serve their country, America itself proved more turbulent than ever; Emanuel was on the plane to Vietnam as Robert F. Kennedy’s assassination was first reported. Protests against the war were growing, and the Civil Rights movement opposed the war as well; a speech from Martin Luther King Jr. becomes a crucial emotional turning point for Emanuel later, as he begins to wonder whether the trauma he experienced serving in the war was worth it.

Through the film, Emanuel and the footage of the reunion between the men guide the audience through their experiences, from the trauma they endured to the discrimination and tokenization they faced as Black soldiers fighting for America. One scene peels back at the men’s conflicting feelings around the nickname for their unit, a racialized moniker that’s simultaneously endearing and patronizing. Others focus on formative experiences Emanuel experiences throughout the war, including a hazy night in Bangkok that’s proves formative both sexually and emotionally.

Harper — whose debut feature “As We Speak” also played at Sundance — has a loud, uncompromisingly blunt style, and the film missteps most clearly when his directorial choices verge on heavy-handed. The film makes clumsy use of actor-led reenactments that are a little too slick and generic to slot seamlessly into the Super 8 footage and actor interviews that make up the bulk of the story. This particularly applies to an opening visual metaphor, in which an old veteran is haunted by a vision of his past, which proves more excessive and obvious than enlightening. Other formal choices feel designed to provoke emotional reactions the material can easily do on its own, particularly a loud, string-heavy score that feels overly generic for the material.

It’s when the film mostly gets out of its own way and lets the men’s experiences do the work that “Soul Patrol” really shines. The Super 8 footage collected from their tour in Vietnam, most of which was shot by the men themselves, is visually arresting and intimate, and Harper frequently employs quick cuts and montages of that on-the-ground film and b-roll of newscasts and ads of the time to flesh out the world they once inhabited. The reunion scenes are simply but artfully shot in black and white, including a revealing conversation among the men’s wives and partners about living with them that gently broadens the perspectives in the film’s portrait.

“Soul Patrol” admirably never tries to sum up the full experience of what Vietnam was, rather just trying to sum up what it was for these men. In the film’s closing stretch, it turns its attention to the men’s difficult experiences returning home from the war, with a candor and a vulnerability that’s hard not to tear up from. As one member of Soul Patrol reflects eloquently towards the end of the film, “We need to tell the stories to look at where we were at, where we come from, and where we headed. You need to know your beginning before you can figure out your ending.”

“Soul Patrol” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Kino Lorber opens the film in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

#3320. Patrick Stewart's '90s Fantasy Movie With Neve Campbell Is Streaming For Free

An adaptation of Oscar Wilde's 1887 short story, Sydney Macartney's "The Canterville Ghost" aired on ABC on January 27, 1996, and, perhaps surprisingly, featured notable central roles for both the late legend Sir Patrick Stewart and Neve Campbell. Indeed, 1996 was a banner year for both actors, with Stewart appearing in the film "Star Trek: First Contact" and Campbell headlining two of the best teen movies of the 1990s over the same 12-month period (namely, "The Craft" and "Scream"). Stewart, of course, was already riding high professionally by that point. But for Campbell, this was the final vault before proper stardom following her breakout role on the hit series "Party of Five."

It should be noted that Wilde's original story is a light tale about a haunted mansion, and Macartney's TV movie — which is currently streaming for free on platforms like Tubi and Prime Video — affects a similarly lighthearted tone. Wilde's source material concerns the Otises, a family of two parents and three children who move into Canterville Castle, despite warnings that it is haunted. Sure enough, its ghost tries to frighten them off, but the Otises react with mere annoyance. For example, when Mrs. Otis spots a bloodstain on the carpet, she dryly states, "I don't at all care for blood-stains in a sitting-room."

Macartney's adaptation transposes the action to the modern day. In the movie, the Otises inevitably have to deal with the specter of Sir Simon de Canterville, played by Stewart. Campbell, meanwhile, plays the young Virginia Otis, and the story is told largely from her perspective. As for Sir Simon, he eventually reveals the trauma that left him in his ghostly state, which has to do with his beloved dead wife, Eleanor.

The TV movie version of "The Canterville Ghost" adds a few fun flourishes to the story. The Otis family patriarch, Hiram, is played by Edward Wiley, and there comes a scene where Virginia and the Ghost, having begun communicating, have to convince Hiram that ghosts are real. In a nod to Sir Patrick Stewart's past with the Royal Shakespeare Company, Virginia and the Ghost get Hiram's attention by staging a scene from "Hamlet" wherein Sir Simon plays the Ghost of Hamlet's Father. Fittingly enough, Stewart would later portray both the Ghost of Hamlet's Father and Claudius in a celebrated 2008 BBC production of the play opposite David Tennant.

Initially, as mentioned, Sir Simon is determined to scare away the Otis family to remain in his sad, ghostly state. Soon after moving in, however, Virginia finds a secret passageway inside the Canterville Castle leading to a chamber where Sir Simon hangs out during the daylight hours. Soon, she and her brothers befriend Sir Simon, and we learn that, despite his intense demeanor, he isn't so terrible or scary. (Virginia's brothers even startle Sir Simon with a fake ghost puppet they construct themselves.) At the same time, Virginia develops a crush on Francis, the Duke of Cheshire (Daniel Betts), a local nobleman who plays a larger role here than he does in Oscar Wilde's original story.

The central drama arises when Hiram believes Virginia is responsible for Sir Simon's shenanigans and threatens to send her back home to the U.S., where she won't be able to flirt with Francis anymore. This is basically her motivation for proving the ghost is real because, again, "The Canterville Ghost" is a fairly fanciful yarn.

There aren't a lot of professional reviews of the "Canterville Ghost" TV movie readily available. One can find a write-up on Common Sense Media by Brian Costello, who gave the film a high rating (which indicates that it's perfectly okay for younger kids). Costello also praised Patrick Stewart, writing that he brings a Shakespearean relish to his character. "[H]is performance," the review reads, "more than makes up for the dated special effects."

David Saunderson, writing for the British/Irish horror website Spooky Isles, had some mild complaints about how the TV movie strays from Oscar Wilde's original story. With weary resignation, he observed that Otises had to be made American for American audiences, despite being British in Wilde's source material. He added that the movie isn't as good as the 1944 film adaptation starring Charles Laughton in the title role and that he found the modern contrivances to be a little tiresome, despite Stewart's solid work. As he put it:

"Patrick Stewart is a fine actor, and fine actors make fine Canterville Ghosts — he's very dramatic, a bit scary, and works well with Neve Campbell [...] who plays the Otis daughter who hates that she has been brought to England but soon befriends the ghost and learns from the experience — blah, blah, blah — usual teenage angst in TV movie!"

Notably, 1996's "The Canterville Ghost" won an Emmy for Outstanding Individual Achievement in Music Composition for a Miniseries or Special, which is no small feat. Stream it now, and see what you make of it.
