#3261. Forget John Wick, HBO Max's 96-Minute Action Thriller Is Still Undefeated

If you asked someone what their favorite action movie is, John Wick would probably top the list. Chad Stahelski and David Leitch turned years of stunt experience into a bloody, gripping action movie that helped reinvigorate Keanu Reeves' career. John Wick is also notable for its deep themes of grief, as its protagonist mourns the loss of a dog meant to help him cope with the loss of his late wife. Long before John Wick hit theaters, another action thriller about a normal man trying to escape his violent past gripped audiences, and it's now streaming on HBO Max.

That movie is A History of Violence. Based on the DC Comics/Vertigo graphic novel by John Wagner and Vince Locke, A History of Violence is a pitch-perfect take on its source material, thanks to director David Cronenberg and lead Viggo Mortensen. Mortensen plays Tom Spall, a mild-mannered man who runs a local diner with his wife Edie (Maria Bello) and his two children. When two criminals attempt to hold up the diner, Tom kills them with ice-cold precision. This makes him a local hero, and reveals secrets from his past that he's tried hard to bury. What follows is a gripping thriller that will hook viewers from beginning to end.

To say that A History of Violence is . . .well, violent, is an understatement. The scene where Tom takes out the two robbers in the diner is a key example, as he slams a coffee pot into one's face and blows the other's brains out when he gets stabbed. What makes it so surprising is that the movie was a departure for its director and leading man. Cronenberg was best known for truly disturbing horror movies like Scanners and Videodrome, while Mortensen was coming off of the massive success of the Lord of the Rings trilogy. No one was expecting them to make a gritty crime thriller, and yet that's part of the draw of A History of Violence. Mortensen's mild-mannered demeanor as Tom makes the violence hit all the harder, while Cronenberg uses his horror experience to ramp up the tension leading to firefights.

A History of Violence also takes the time to explore what living a life full of violence does to a man, as it's slowly revealed that Tom was once a mob enforcer named Joey Cusack. Not only does his brother Richie (William Hurt) want him back in the "family buisness", but the revelation puts a strain on his marriage and arguments with his son about getting into fights. Cronenberg would even talk about how he wanted to explore the consequences of violence, and how he wanted his audience to think about those consequences:

"In this movie, we've got an audience that's definitely going to applaud these acts of violence, and they do because it's set up that these acts are justifiable and almost heroic at times. But I'm saying, "Okay, if you can applaud that, can you applaud this?" because this is the result of that gunshot in the head. It's not nice. And even if the violence is justifiable, the consequences of the violence are the same."

A History of Violence is still held in high esteem, to the point where it's considered to be one of the best movies released in the 21st century. It wouldn't be the last time that Viggo Mortensen and David Cronenberg worked together, as the duo reunited for two more movies. Eastern Promises stars Mortensen as a Russian enforcer forced to confront the evil his employers take part in, mirroring the conflict Tom finds himself in during A History of Violence. A Dangerous Method took a different approach, as Mortensen portrayed Sigmund Freud while exploring more of the famed psychologist's personal life.

Most crime thrillers thrive on a buffet of blood and violence, but A History of Violence is the opposite. It stays with its audience long after the credits roll, thanks to a stellar performance from Viggo Mortensen and David Cronenberg's taut, thoughtful approach to the material.

#3259. Stephen King’s Supernatural Sci-Fi Series Is Officially Back, And It’s The Perfect Carrie Follow-Up

Mike Flanagan's Carrie became the biggest Stephen King hit of the year, and it is all set to be followed up with season 2. However, it will be a while before Carrie season 2 sees the light of day. While waiting for its release, horror fans can now watch another ongoing TV adaptation of a Stephen King book, which has officially returned in 2026.

The show in question, The Institute, has a lot in common with Carrie, and these parallels between the two Stephen King stories will now be even more evident.

Carrie marked Stephen King's literary debut. The Institute, in contrast, ranks among the King of Horror's more recent books as it was published in 2019. Its first TV adaptation of the same name landed on MGM+ and garnered a more mixed reception compared to recent shows like It: Welcome to Derry and Carrie. Still, MGM+'s The Institute performed well enough to be renewed for another season.

Interestingly, The Institute season 1 exhausted the story from the original Stephen King novel. Owing to this, its second season is now expanding the source material's lore. After season 1's developments and season 2's opening arcs, The Institute is already starting to look like the perfect follow-up to Stephen King's Carrie. The two Stephen King stories also share some hidden connections.

Carrie was the first breakout horror novel in which Stephen King used telekinesis as a narrative device to highlight the impact of abuse on a young adult. The Institute not only riffs on the same themes but also significantly raises the stakes. Instead of featuring only one character with the "Shine," it shows how multiple children are gifted with telekinesis (TK), telepathy (TP), and precognition.

The characters in The Institute, however, are subjected to explicit institutional abuse after being abducted from their homes and subjected to immoral experimentation. It almost feels like a sequel to Carrie where the White Commission has realized that more children like Carrie White exist. Now, they have started an "institute" to exploit their powers.

The Institute season 2's episode 1 further leans into these overlaps. It shows how entire systems have been built to exploit children with superpowers. The episode introduces older test subjects who use their abilities to help an organization serve a perceived greater good. This introduction of older subjects suggests that humans with TK and TP have been around for a very long time.

Its origins can probably be traced back to Carrie White.

Season 2's episode 1 also reveals how the overarching corporate-backed project is trying to develop an AI that could replace humans with precognition, TK, and TP. However, AI is just not as effective as humans. Mike Flanagan's Carrie also ends with the titular character surviving, paving the way for season 2.

It is hard not to see how her story will be similar to the young characters from The Institute who are struggling to escape the clutches of a powerful shadow organization.

Stephen King never draws any explicit connections between The Dark Tower, Carrie, and The Institute. However, it is hard not to notice many clear overlaps between all three. For instance, in The Dark Tower universe, all psychic abilities are manifestations of a single cosmic force called the "Shine."

In The Dark Tower book series, specifically in Wolves of the Calla and The Dark Tower, characters with psychic powers are called are held captive by the Crimson King and referred to as Breakers. The Breakers are collectively expected to use their powers and chip away at the Beams of reality. Even the characters in The Institute are expected to do the same through quantum manipulation.

Put simply, in the grand scheme of Stephen King's larger horror universe, Carrie tells the foundational story of young adults with superpowers. The Institute and Firestarter step things up by featuring organizations that exploit these powers. Finally, The Dark Tower walks through the cosmic purpose of these powers, revealing why those with the "Shine" are so sought after in every Stephen King story.

Carrie serves as the first step for Mike Flanagan to establish a larger Stephen King universe on the small screen. He will double down on these connections and overlaps in Carrie season 2 and his highly-anticipated Dark Tower adaptation.

The Institute, released in 2025, follows 14-year-old genius Luke Ellis, who is kidnapped and wakes up at a mysterious facility filled with children possessing unusual abilities. Meanwhile, Tim Jamieson, a former police officer, seeks a fresh start in a nearby town, inevitably intertwining his fate with Luke's.

#3256. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

We are still digging into the beta, but here’s a taste of what new things you can get Siri AI to do:

You can now use Siri AI with the Calendar app to create events featuring invitees, location, video call links and more. And in Reminders, you can now create urgent reminders for the first time with Siri.

In Safari, you can now use Siri to create tap groups from a list of URLs, sort your tabs, clear your history, delete reading list items and more.

Journal support with Siri AI is new for the first time. You can create entries with text transcription, or record audio entries.

There’s also wide support for file and folder management with Siri AI Files integration. You can get file content, create files and folders, send files to the trash, organize by type, rename files, and more, using just your voice.

We are also seeing new Siri features for Weather, Maps, Preview and Shortcuts, and will keep testing to find new integrations. Apple is also opening up this support to third-party developers.

#3253. Developers can now create advanced ‘app skills’ for Siri AI

Apple today announced a major new Siri AI initiative for third-party developers, allowing any app to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. The first versions of Siri AI were limited to a much smaller set of supported schemas.

The new ‘app skills’ also let apps teach Siri how to coordinate complicated multi-step actions. These features are testable in the iOS 27.3 betas.

The app skills sound very similar to what other LLM-driven AI models offer, enabling richer understanding of complicated tasks.

For example, a flight tracking app skill will be able to cleanly map what app intents Siri should use to service a particular kind of user request; something that the first version of Siri AI was simply incapable of doing.

Of course, Apple itself has also taken advantage of the new Siri AI foundational features, with a significant rollout of new capabilities across Apple’s apps.

Here’s an example of what Siri will be able to do, from the developer documentation:

Siri can find custom content from one app, transfer it to a specified app, and perform an action. For example, somebody might request “Hey Siri, send my favorite sneakers to my partner in name of a messaging app.” Siri finds sneakers that the person added to their favorites, understands who the partner is, finds them in Contacts, then sends the sneaker information to them using the messaging app.

It’s also going to be a lot easier to initiate Siri actions for third-party apps. With the Siri AI Developer Preview, users don’t have to explicitly mention the app’s name in many circumstances. For instance, if a Live Activity for a ride-sharing app is active, Siri will automatically understand that a request to “change the ride address” corresponds to the app driving the Live activity.

This gives you a sense of the kinds of things Siri will be able to do in the future, coordinating more complicated actions across Apple and third-party apps.

The new OS releases are in developer beta right now, but Apple says the app skills support is only an early developer preview and is scheduled to officially roll out in the spring.

#3252. 34 Years Ago, Marvel's Best Creators Rebelled Like Never Before

Back in 1992, a crew of Marvel Comics' best artists dramatically left to start their own venture; that decision would end up having a colossal impact on the comics industry of today. Image Comics is nowadays known as a powerhouse unto itself, historically publishing major works like Spawn, The Walking Dead, and Savage Dragon. Meanwhile, Robert Kirkman's Invincible has been adapted into what's arguably the 21st Century's best animated superhero series so far.

Despite a slew of top-tier material, what makes Image Comics a particular standout in the history of comics is the publisher's fraught origins. Nestled within its founding and the early years when Image defined '90s comics is a story of independent comics, creators' rights, and more that connects back to creators' disillusionment with Marvel for decades. Image Comics just happened to have the right combination of things to make a true creators' rebellion work.

Image Comics was born from what was effectively an exodus of Marvel's hottest talents of the time: Todd McFarlane (Spider-Man), Rob Liefeld (X-Force), and Jim Lee (X-Men), all of whom had broken sales records—Lee's X-Men #1 remains the best-selling comic of all time. This wasn't something that Marvel rewarded. For Marvel, brand identity was the most important thing—over and above the personalities working on the comics, themselves. Comics were effectively written freelance as work-for-hire, meaning that creators themselves were—and often still are—disposable.

This had two effective consequences for breakout stars working under the Big Two. The first, for some creators like Liefeld, was the feeling that their stardom made them disposable; creators with star power presented a risk to the brand-centric paradigm. The second, for other creators, was a feeling of being undervalued: because they worked as freelancers, they had no actual rights to things like royalties for merchandise based on their work.

While Invincible enjoys its well-deserved place in the spotlight today, it’s worth remembering the groundbreaking work done 24 years earlier.

All of this should also be understood in the context of a tide-shift in the industry, generally. More and more independent and creator-owned publishers were cropping up, with varying levels of success. Creator's rights had always been a major concern in the industry: milestones included the 1978 formation of the Comics Creators Guild (featuring huge names like Neal Adams, Frank Miller, Chris Claremont, and more). Todd McFarlane had made efforts to unionize creators at Marvel prior to Image Comics being established.

For the Image Comics exodus in particular, the minutiae were well documented in Michael Dean's four-part series "The Image Story" for The Comics Journal, charting the history of Image Comics up to its publication in 2000. What the deep-dive shows isn't an organized group of rebels but disgruntled artists with variable motivations and wavering commitments simply seeking to own the works they create if they were going to stay in the comics industry.

Image Comics was the end result of a long process through which Liefeld found other options—it was Liefeld who would bring Marvel's top artists together, and it was Liefeld who went to Malibu Comics and probed into whether they would publish black-and-white lines from Marvel's biggest names. Liefeld would go on to recruit McFarlane, Lee, Erik Larsen, Jim Valentino, Marc Silvestri, and Whilce Portacio as a united front to bargain with Marvel for creative control.

The triumphant Image Comics rebellion doesn't start with an exodus, but with an ultimatum given to Marvel Comics' president by Liefeld, Lee, and McFarlane in December 1991: that they would continue working at Marvel on their own creator-owned lines, or they would leave to publish elsewhere. The outcome was perhaps predictable, and the artists left with intentions to defect completely.

In 1992, Image Comics was officially established. The underlying principle of creators owning their own works wasn't new, but Image's managerial structure was relatively novel; Image would act as infrastructure for the studios and partners working under its umbrella, and no partner could interfere with another partner's work. Malibu Comics played a critical role in realizing those principles, willing to take on the Marvel talent at face value and provide essential early support with marketing, publication, and distribution.

Through a combination of luck, timing, and star power, Image would become a massive hit, even briefly overtaking DC's market share with record-breaking titles like Liefeld's Youngblood, McFarlane's Spawn, and Larsen's The Savage Dragon. To this day, many of Image Comics' best titles can be traced to the company's first year. By 1993, Image was successful enough to leave Malibu entirely and become independent.

The Youngblood franchise returns and expands this summer and ScreenRant is proud to offer an exclusive first look at two exciting variant covers.

The following year, more non-partners would start publishing under Image with titles like Alan Moore, Steve Bissette, and Rick Veitch's 1963 and Larry Stroman's Tribe (which would become the best-selling African American comic from an African American creator of all time).

To an extent, Image's structure would also become its undoing for a while. The surrounding hype combined with its creators' failures to deliver books on time would arguably play a considerable role in comics' speculative bubble bursting in 1993. The same varied motivations that birthed Image Comics would pave the way for intense disagreements, tension, and poaching between founders—Liefeld would officially resign in 1996, right before a meeting where he would have been fired.

Despite everything, though, Image Comics eventually righted the ship, steadily expanding their line of comics and eventually bringing on a new partner, Robert Kirkman. Today, Image stands as an emblem of independent comics publishing in general: independent studios can not only survive and thrive in an ecosystem dominated by the Big Two, but they can become enough of a force to compete with them.

This is despite unglamorous origins in an often understated history of creator's rights in comics that, ironically, found a major watershed at Marvel itself when the foundational figure Jack Kirby, co-creator of many of the brand's biggest characters, started to publicly criticize Stan Lee and the company over rights, royalties, and the work-for-hire model in the '70s and '80s.

The MCU Slump is still at the front of fans' minds, and 1 Marvel creator says the dip is happening on comics for the same reason.

In other words, the stardom that would propel Image to success was latent in Marvel's own machinery. Image stands as a spiritual win for creator's rights in comics. But its huge success also meant it could provide a truly commercially viable platform for independent creator-owned works that could stand up against the Big Two—the lack of which creators had been circling for years before.

The history of Image Comics is fascinating precisely because it's rocky. There was no golden origin, and the reality is that the bedrock was there for something like Image Comics to emerge eventually—the industry had been setting up for a creator-focused behemoth that could actually contest the Big Two for decades. But Image Comics is what emerged, and through the rebellion of seven disgruntled Marvel artists, the company now stands as a beacon for the stories mainstream publishers might not want to tell.

#3251. 6 Romance Books That Are a Masterclass in Yearning

No matter what tropes you prefer, there will be a number of romance books out there that meet the criteria of what you're looking for. From older romance books to modern ones, there are so many excellent romance books across subgenres. The best romance books have strong characters that readers can get attached to. Both of the lead characters are well-written and have their own lives and wants outside each other, but their scenes together are the heart of the book.

One thing that most romance readers tend to look for is an element of yearning. It is especially exciting to see one or both leads pine after the other for a long time, even when – and especially when – they don't know they're doing it. Romance books with excellent yearning might see the characters fighting to be together despite impossibly high stakes, or secretly harbor feelings for each other for years. These are amazing romance books that are a masterclass in yearning.

Before it was a hit Netflix rom-com, People We Meet on Vacation was an amazing romance novel by Emily Henry. The book follows Poppy Wright and Alex Nilsen, two polar opposites who have been best friends ever since they roadtripped back to their shared hometown together for a college break. Ever since, Poppy and Alex have gotten together once a year for a week-long summer vacation, where they visit a different place together every time. The book moves back and forth through time to tell this story. In the present day, Poppy and Alex haven't spoken in two years after a mysterious falling out. As a professional travel writer, Poppy goes on vacation for work now, and she decides to invite Alex with her this time to try to start their old tradition back up. She'll also be going with Alex as his date to his brother's wedding that same summer.

In the past, People We Meet on Vacation follows Poppy and Alex's other trips together, showing how their feelings for each other have been building up since the very beginning of their friendship. Every time their friendship starts to become something more, an obstacle gets in the way, from work to other people. The past timeline builds up to their final trip where their friendship ended, while they avoid talking about their falling out and just try to rebuild their friendship on their present-day trip. People We Meet on Vacation has amazing yearning from both Poppy and Alex, especially because Poppy doesn't fully understand what she's feeling for most of the book. Over the course of their past vacations, Poppy and Alex's feelings build for each other while they both try to ignore them and prioritize the friendship. In the present, there's an even deeper aspect to the yearning, as the two long for their old friendship while still harboring hopes of something more.

Atmosphere by Taylor Jenkins Reid is a historical fiction romance novel set in the 1980s. The book starts with a flash-forward to December 1984, where astronaut Joan Goodwin is working from the ground to navigate a malfunctioning NASA space shuttle back to safety. Three of the astronauts on the shuttle have already died, one is unconscious, and only astronaut Vanessa Ford is left to work with Joan to get the shuttle home. The story then rewinds all the way back to 1980, where Joan joins NASA's Space Shuttle program and meets the rest of her class, shortly after the program started to include women. Joan's class is made up of the astronauts who will later be on that shuttle four years later, including Vanessa, with whom she strikes an instant connection.

Joan has never been in love before, but about a year into the program, she realizes that that's what she feels for Vanessa. The two would lose their jobs if anyone found out that they were lesbians, though, so they have to keep their relationship a secret from everyone in their lives. Atmosphere features a different depiction of yearning, because Joan and Vanessa are together for most of the book. All the while, they long to be able to be together publicly, and to get to experience everything that the straight couple in their class gets to. In the present day, Joan is stuck on the ground trying to get the woman she loves to safety, all while the two have to hide their love for each other during their monitored communication. Atmosphere is a beautiful, heartbreaking novel that sees Joan and Vanessa risk everything to be together, all while trying to still find a way for both of them to continue to pursue their dreams of going to space.

Red, White & Royal Blue, the extremely popular romance novel that was adapted into a hit rom-com for Prime Video, is one of the best depictions of yearning of any romance book. The book follows Alex Claremont-Diaz, the college-age son of the first female President of the United States, Ellen Claremont. Ellen is nearing the end of her first term, and tensions are high as she runs for re-election. Alex has a passion for politics and wants to help, especially because he's now in his final year of college. At a wedding thrown by the British royal family, though, Alex makes his mother look bad when he gets into a public altercation with his longtime rival, Prince Henry.

For the sakes of both their families and countries, Alex and Henry then have to do damage control by pretending to be friends. They start meeting up over the course of the following months for staged hangouts where they know they will be photographed. Along the way, though, Alex and Henry start to really get to know each other, and they realize they were wrong about each other. They start talking to and messaging each other all the time, and they soon become best friends, which turns romantic at a New Year's Eve party. Alex and Henry cannot actually be together, though, because of their respective titles. As such, they try to compartmentalize their feelings for each other, but they ultimately can't help but fall in love with each other. Red, White & Royal Blue is full of intense yearning throughout the book, and Alex and Henry also just have phenomenal chemistry and banter. It's easy to root for them no matter the odds stacked against them, and their pining for each other jumps off the page through every one of their conversations and emails.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

I've Got Your Number by Sophie Kinsella follows an unlikely romance that develops between two polar opposites who get temporarily stuck with each other for the sake of convenience. Poppy Wyatt is happily engaged to be married, but she finds herself in a messy situation when she loses both her cellphone and her engagement ring on the same day. Luckily, Poppy finds a discarded cellphone in the trash, so she gives out the number in case anyone finds the ring. The only problem is, the phone is actually the work cell of Sam Roxton, a no-nonsense business executive who is frustrated by this inconvenience.

Still, Sam agrees to share the phone with Poppy until she finds her ring. Through sharing the cellphone, Poppy and Sam get daily glimpses into each other's lives. They also start to become friends by talking to each other all the time in order to coordinate their shared usage of the phone. Poppy and Sam start to get used to their arrangement and even depend on each other, but it's just temporary. Eventually, Poppy will find her ring and get married to her fiancé, Magnus, and Sam will get his phone back to himself. While Poppy spends most of the novel in denial of her growing feelings for Sam, Sam's yearning for her is apparent from early on. Each of their interactions is charged, as the two long to be more than what they are, relegated mostly to virtual interactions while still becoming involved in nearly every aspect of each other's lives.

The Flatshare by Beth O'Leary, which was adapted into the romance miniseries of the same name, follows the growing romance of two people who have never met. After a bad breakup, Tiffy Moore is in a rush to find a new place to live that she can afford, so she winds up in an unconventional arrangement. Leon Twomey is a hospice nurse who works nights and sleeps during the day, so he rents the apartment to Tiffy half the time. They share the space and its single bed, but their hours never overlap, so they become roommates who have never met each other.

Tiffy and Leon use post-it notes to communicate with one another, starting out with practical back-and-forth about their living arrangement and slowly getting to know each other through these notes. Over the course of The Flatshare, Tiffy and Leon fall in love through their post-it notes, while still working vastly different hours and never meeting in person. The yearning between them is beautiful as they both become more reliant on their post-it note system over time, while trying to determine whether what they have is worth risking by finally meeting each other.

Before it was a massively popular TV show, Heated Rivalry was the second book in Rachel Reid's Game Changers series. The romance novel tells the love story of rival NHL players Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov over the course of about a decade. The novel starts with a flash-forward that shows Shane and Ilya carrying on a secret fling, before then going back in time to show them meeting in their rookie year. For years, the two regularly hook up in secret, compartmentalizing their feelings for each other because they know that they could never actually be together.

Shane and Ilya's careers are everything to them, and they would likely lose it all if anyone every found out about them, due to both rampant homophobia in the NHL and their status as professional rivals. Still, they can't fight their growing feelings for each other. No matter how many times either one of them tries to end things, they just keep finding their way back to one another. Both Shane and Ilya's yearning for one another is very clear throughout the book, even as neither of them knows just how deep their own feelings run, until they ultimately have to face these feelings and decide what to do about them.

Heated Rivalry centers on two hockey stars whose fierce competition transforms into a complex relationship as they navigate conflicting feelings and the sport’s demands. As they attempt to balance personal emotions with professional ambitions, their unexpected bond challenges traditional expectations in the world of competitive hockey.

#3246. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with a surprisingly extensive set of new features and improvements across the system. One of them is the expansion of the iPhone Duo’s redesigned StandBy experience to other iPhone models. Here are the details.

When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, one of its exclusive new features was a redesigned StandBy experience with new clock faces and expanded customization options.

StandBy mode was introduced with iOS 17, and it essentially turns the iPhone into a smart display when placed horizontally while charging.

Until now, users of other iPhone models were limited to the original StandBy experience, which offered clock, widget, and photo views, but lacked the additional faces and more extensive customization options introduced with the iPhone Duo.

#3244. Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars Officially Arrives November 12

Project Hail Mary was one of the best movies of the year, and whether you're a fan of the film or the book by Andy Weir, you'll have something new to look forward to this November. Billed as an untold chapter, Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars sees Ryland Grace and Rocky return for one more adventure. A new trailer debuted at the end of October, ahead of Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars' official release date on November 12, 2026.

Story details on Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars are pretty scarce. Thankfully, the latest trailer briefly shows off Rocky, so we know the beloved Eridian is back. The upcoming VR game is available to preorder now from Meta, and also offers up three exclusive preorder bonuses. You can view the trailer below.

"Work together in the face of disaster to keep the Hail Mary intact and bring their world-saving cargo to Eridani — Rocky’s home planet, and Grace’s new home," reads the official description for the game. As Ryland Grace, players will get to manage the ship and its cargo, diagnose failing systems, and improvise scientific solutions while abord the Hail Mary. Perhaps most importantly of all, you'll be able to interact with Rocky on the journey to Eridani. And, yes, this is a brand-new story not featured in the movie or book.

Honestly, just getting to hang out with Rocky sounds like enough of a selling point.

Even if it offers up nothing groundbreakingly new, it'll at least be nice to return to the Hail Mary again. For all the fans of Project Hail Mary out there, be sure to mark your calendars for November 12.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir (The Martian), Project Hail Mary is an action-adventure sci-fi film that stars Ryan Gosling as an astronaut who must save Earth from an oncoming ice age by heading to a faraway galaxy.

#3243. Netflix's Unhinged Alan Ritchson Thriller 'War Machine' Is Officially Best of the Year

The breakout movies and TV shows of 2026 are putting certain actors in the spotlight. Tom Holland became summer's biggest star thanks to the one-two punch of Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey. Inde Navarrette's breakout role in Obsession led to her snagging the role of Rogue in Marvel Studios' upcoming X-Men reboot. It's Alan Ritchson, though, who's had the biggest surprise. While Ritchson's best known for playing the title role in Reacher, he also starred in a gritty sci-fi/action thriller that quickly became one of Netflix's biggest movies.

That movie is War Machine, which is directed and co-written by Patrick Hughes (The Hitman's Bodyguard.) War Machine centers on a unnamed soldier (Ritchson) who is currently training to join the Army Rangers. The soldier, given the designation "81", is about to complete the test known as the "Death March" where he and other soldiers destroy a prototype aircraft. It turns out that the aircraft they're meant to destroy is a highly advanced alien machine that starts picking off soldiers left and right. What follows is a blood-soaked, adrenaline-fueled story that's been described as "The Terminator meets The Hurt Locker," and it wouldn't work without Alan Ritchson.

War Machine takes its time building up to the reveal that its protagonist is fighting an alien machine, which makes the carnage hit that much harder once it begins. The real meat of the movie's story lies in exploring 81's emotional state. At the opening of the movie, he loses his brother (Jai Courtney) during a firefight; the lingering guilt and grief lead him to take greater risks and have his superiors questioning him. It isn't until the machine attacks that 81 is forced to rely on his fellow soldiers, even taking the leadership position he kept denying.

Ritchson helps give War Machine an emotional core through his performance. Over time, he showcases a slowly defrosting exterior, going from a tortured soldier to a bona fide leader. It doesn't hurt that he has a great supporting cast to bounce off, whether it's Stephan James as fellow Ranger trainee 7 or Dennis Quaid and Esai Morales as his superior officers. Unlike Reacher, which has settled into a predictable but reliable formula, or Motor City, which prioritized its no-dialogue gimmick over an actual story, War Machine develops its characters while still delivering the action you'd expect from Army men taking on alien machinery.

While War Machine drew mixed reviews, it was a hit for Netflix and still holds a spot on the streamer's Top 10 list of most popular movies. That puts it among other Netflix breakouts, like KPop Demon Hunters and Ryan Reynolds' time travel epic The Adam Project. Ironically, War Machine wasn't developed as a Netflix movie. Patrick Hughes originally meant to release the movie theatrically until Netflix partnered with Lionsgate. Hughes also told Decider that War Machine was part of a larger story he wanted to tell if given the chance.

“I know exactly where I want to take it, and what that broader story is...We absolutely love the character of 81. For me, I wanted to tell a film that started with the micro, and ended with the macro. And I thought that was a really unique take on the genre that we were working in. Let’s see what happens.”

Hughes is about to get his chance as Netflix greenlit a sequel to War Machine, appropriately titled War Machines. Details are scarce, but the sequel is more than likely following up on the end of War Machine where it's revealed that more alien machines have touched down on Earth — and 81 is the sole man who knows their weakness. Alan Ritchson is also continuing his working relationship with Netflix, as he's set to star in the upcoming action thriller Malestrom. The smash success of War Machine proves Ritchson has a future outside of Reacher, and that sci-fi remains Netflix's most successful genre for original projects.

#3242. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3241. Xcode 27.3 adds GitHub Copilot to its built-in coding assistant

Apple released Xcode 27.3 beta 1 today with multiple new features, chief among them an expansion of its built-in coding assistant to support GitHub Copilot. Here are the details.

Since Xcode 26.3, developers have been able to integrate AI coding agents directly into Xcode, to help with tasks ranging from writing boilerplate code to updating entire projects based on their documentation, file structure, and more.

Apple initially introduced ChatGPT integration in Xcode 26, followed by Anthropic’s Claude. Then, in Xcode 26.3, the company expanded both integrations with agentic coding capabilities through OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Agent.

With Xcode 27, Apple added support for Google Gemini, alongside a redesigned interface, interactive planning, and multi-turn conversations.

Now, with Xcode 27.3, Apple is expanding the list of supported AI coding tools once again, this time adding GitHub Copilot.

The Xcode 27.3 beta 1 release notes include the following under the Coding Intelligence section:

As with the other agentic integrations, this is particularly good news for developers whose companies have standardized on GitHub Copilot, as they can now use their company’s preferred AI coding tool directly within Xcode.

Here are the full release notes for Xcode 27.3 beta 1:

Xcode 27.3 beta includes Swift 6.4 and SDKs for iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, tvOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3. Xcode 27.3 beta supports on-device debugging in iOS 17 and later, tvOS 17 and later, watchOS 10 and later, and visionOS. Xcode 27.3 beta requires a Mac running macOS Tahoe 26.6 or later.

See Xcode Support to learn more about compatible platforms and deployment targets.

Xcode 27.3 is expected to be released in December, alongside macOS 27.3 and its counterparts.

Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited is a PS5 pad for pro players

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve spent thousands of hours with my PS5 since launch. But in all that time, every single one of the best PS5 games I’ve enjoyed has been played on a stock DualSense controller. I’ve never used a so-called “pro” controller.

That was until this week, when I got my hands on Nacon’s new Revolution 5 Unlimited controller, designed for use with Sony’s current generation console (and PC). It’s opened my eyes to a whole new way of experiencing competitive gaming. It's made returning to my regular old DualSense a challenge (sadly, the Revolution 5 Unlimited sometimes needs to charge).

This $230 / £179 pad most definitely qualifies as a pro controller, offering a vast array of features and upgrades: Magnetic TMR joysticks, dual-mode actuation triggers, and seven (yes, seven) fully programmable shortcuts. And that’s just the start; there’s one upgrade that stands out most of all, and it turns this third-party controller into a genuine game-changer.

Designed for the PS5 and with competitive online gaming in mind, the Nacon R5U is a proper pro controller. Its biggest upgrade is the built-in display, which lets you customize any of its seven shortcuts on the fly, and it also sports TMR joysticks, dual-mode actuation triggers, and a docking station for easy charging. It's also compatible with PC.

You can’t fail to notice the biggest thing that sets the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited apart from a stock PS5 DualSense. It’s not the offset sticks, redesigned d-pad, or all those extra buttons on the back of the controller. No, the eye-catcher is the (roughly) 1.8-inch display on the controller face.

Replacing the DualSense’s largely useless touchpad (on the R5U the touchpad is reassigned to a button between the d-pad and right analog stick), Nacon calls it the “command screen,” and it’s a very fitting name.

The display gives you instant access to the controller’s “mapping” features, letting you select inputs for the four back buttons, two buttons on the top of the controller, and even reassign the “touchpad” button. I recommend keeping the latter set to the default input, as most games require it.

There’s no need to mess around in the PS5’s settings menus or use a companion mobile/desktop app; you can assign each additional button directly on the controller’s display. While I haven't used a controller that requires an app, I can't imagine not having a built-in display now. Assigning shortcuts on the fly is unbelievably convenient and makes experimenting with different input combinations straightforward.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The controller also offers up to eight individual profiles, which you can swap between directly on the R5U at the touch of a button. This allowed me to create input combinations tailored to the various games I’m playing right now, and leap between them instantly. It’s a breeze!

Sadly, it’s not all upgrades. While this new Nacon controller is officially licensed, it doesn’t include some DualSense-exclusive features, namely haptic feedback and adaptive triggers. And it can’t be used to turn on your PS5 console, which is a small inconvenience in the grand scheme. Plus, to connect it wirelessly, you’ll need to use the supplied USB dongle.

There isn’t really a scientific way to judge whether I play better on the DualSense or the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited, but I’d say I feel more in control when playing with the R5U.

Well, I do now, at least; that was most certainly not the case initially. A pro controller like this is designed for competitive online play, and what better way to test it out than on the recently released Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, the latest installment in the annual shooter series.

Turns out that trying to unlearn more than 30 years of muscle memory playing on a standard controller is kind of hard, and out of the gate, my fingers were confused, caught behind using the back buttons to shoot and the regular triggers. But this adaptation period didn’t hold me back for too long, and eventually I was able to start developing new muscle memory.

I’m a pretty average CoD player in general (my K/D averages out to an unspectacular 1.0), and while using the R5U hasn’t seen my performance suddenly leap up into e-sports pro territory, in a game like CoD where micro-seconds count, I feel like I’m getting the drop on enemy players where previously I might not. But this could be a placebo effect, of course.

Another game I’ve been using to test out the R5U this week is Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and this is one where I can say the R5U has made a difference. Assigning my speeder’s boost and drift to back buttons (X and Square on a DualSense) means I never have to take my fingers off either stick. My racing lines have never been cleaner, and my lap times better.

Nevertheless, if you’re more of a single-player gamer, I don’t think there’s much of a case for a controller like the R5U. But if you enjoy competitive online play, it offers additional control options, and because it’s so customizable, you can find the setup that enhances your skills.

We’ll have a full review of the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited on Tom’s Guide soon, but as far as initial impressions go, it’s quickly become my preferred PS5 controller. As somebody who’s loved the standard PS5 DualSense since day one, that is a very big compliment.

#3238. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

#3236. Shark AquaReach Pro review: The cordless mop for hard floors that can reach everywhere — but there’s one catch

The Shark AquaReach Pro is a decent option for homes with hard floors. Its cordless design offers mobility, smaller attachments reach tight spaces, and it effectively lifts grime. However, the non-retractable extendable hose looks clunky in storage, dock self-cleaning is very loud, and the one-hour battery life limits longer cleaning sessions.

Roller mop is good at scrubbing the floor

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Vacuuming alone won’t keep the hard floors in your home clean. And a quick mop isn’t always enough to lift all the grime from everyday activities. One of the best vacuum mops, like the Shark AquaReach Pro, is a great addition to any home.

There’s a great deal to like about the Shark, including how it effortlessly gets into tight spaces and can be moved anywhere thanks to the cordless design. It effectively lifts grime, and the roller mop is fast.

But it’s not all roses. The extendable hose is clunky in storage, and the self-cleaning process on the dock is extremely loud. The one hour of battery life may also put off some users. To find out more, read on for my full Shark AquaReach Pro review.

The Shark AquaReach Pro is available to purchase from Amazon U.S. for $529. In the U.K., you can buy the cleaner directly from the SharkNinja website for £499.

It’s a little cheaper than the Roborock F25 ACE Pro, which costs $599, but this model effortlessly glides along the floor, and means you’re not always manually pushing the mop. That said, if you want the convenience that comes with smaller attachments to get into small spaces, then the Shark is the better option for you.

I’ve also tested the Dreame H15 Pro Heat, which costs $899. This wet/dry vacuum is a better option if you tend to find more stubborn stains in your home, as the water can be heated. But keep in mind that the heated water means the battery life will diminish a lot faster. So if you just want a basic clean, the Shark is a good option.

The Shark AquaReach Pro is a good-looking home device. Its rose gold and blue accents make it look like a well-thought-out home design piece. When not in use, the Shark sits on a docking station. This is where the device self-cleans, and it has a tray on the side to store smaller attachments for the nozzle.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The docking station plugs into a power outlet and charges the Aqua Reach Pro, and the 5.9-foot power cord means you'll need to keep it near a power outlet. The extendable wand lets you reach surfaces the roller mop can't, and the two extra included attachments get into smaller gaps.

Although this extendable hose helps you get into those hard-to-reach places, It’s probably my least favorite feature of the device from a design perspective. The hose is simply far too long, and when storing the device, it doesn’t retract, as I’m used to with other vacuums and mops. Instead, it clips to the body of the AquaReach Pro and springs back out. I’d love for this to have a more slinky design, so it isn’t fully extended at all times. However, since it has a cordless design, there aren’t any wires to carry around with you, which I appreciate.

There’s a clean water tank on the front of the Shark, and this easily clips on and off. The dirty water tank is on the side, and this has a max fill line so I knew when it needed to be emptied.

For simple floor cleaning, I prefer the design of the Roborock F25 Ace Pro. It looks a lot more basic, but I found it a lot more convenient to use.

The control buttons at the top of the device light up when each mode is in use. After reading the included instructions for the first few uses, I got to grips with each function quickly.

The Shark AquaReach Pro did a great job of making the floors in my kitchen and bathroom incredibly shiny. I filled the clean water tank with water and topped it up with the included cleaning solution as per the guidance on the tank.

The device works by letting out water and then sucking it back up with a vacuum. If a tougher stain requires a bit more help, you can use the trigger on the handle to squirt out more cleaning solution.

This device is designed to be used on hard surfaces, so firstly, I carried out my usual lab testing. I splashed some mayonnaise, soy sauce and ketchup on the floor and allowed them to dry down. The process wasn’t as quick as when I tested the Dreame H15 Pro Heat, but since that’s a heated floor cleaner, I also had to use less elbow grease than with this Shark vacuum mop to lift stains.

The Shark AquaReach Pro brought up all of the mess with relative ease though. Initially, the condiments were moved around the floors but in just six passes, all of the grime had been lifted.

I then took the AquaReach around the house to clean windowsills and in small spaces such as the toilets where the roller mop can’t quite reach. This was very useful, and it left everything feeling fresh. The smaller attachments are very useful; I still wish the hose design was more compact though.

Follow Tom's Guide on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our up-to-date news, analysis, and reviews in your feeds.

The Shark AquaReach Pro needs to be stored on its docking station. This means that it will have a permanent home near a power outlet wherever you set it up. It measures 4.53 x 11.61 x 11.02 inches, which is about the same size as a vacuum cleaner, so it’s not a home appliance that can be hidden.

It’s self-cleaning; however, this operation is very loud. When I measured the process using the Decibel X app, I got readings between 60db and 75db. This is what I expect when I’m testing a blender. The self-cleaning on the Dreame H15 Pro Heat is much quieter.

The battery life of the Shark AquaReach Pro lasts for around an hour, which is around the same as the Dreame H15 Pro Heat, which has 72 minutes of cleaning time. And this would be good if I were only cleaning the hard floors in my home.

But that’s not all the AquaReach Pro is for. Since I can use it on all hard surfaces in my home because of the extendable arm and attachments, I needed more than an hour when using it for cleaning.

It also takes three hours to fully charge, and I felt like I was waiting around forever when I just wanted to get on with cleaning.

The Shark AquaReach Pro is a decent option if you have hard floors throughout your home. It has a cordless design, so you’re not limited by power outlets when cleaning, and it can reach into tight spaces with its smaller attachments. It effectively lifts grime, and the roller mop does a great job of agitating the stains on the floor to completely lift them.

However, there are awesome things I don’t love. The extendable hose looks clunky when in storage as it doesn’t retract, and the self-cleaning on the dock is very loud. The hour of battery life may also put you off when you can use it for so many jobs around your home that will certainly take longer than an hour to complete.

I’d recommend it for basic cleaning of floors and baseboards, but if you want something more heavy-duty for other areas of your home like the bathroom, I’d opt for something with a longer battery life.

The software experience is less impressive, with advertisements and recommendations dominating the home screen, leaving relatively little room for your actual apps. There's also no support for Apple AirPlay or Google Cast, so sharing content directly from your phone isn't particularly convenient. Still, if you're comfortable with Amazon's interface and don't need the missing Dolby formats, the Fire TV Stick 4K delivers responsive streaming and a useful remote for just $25.

#3234. Apple now explicitly bans employees from using confidential information in prediction markets

Apple has updated its insider trading policy to explicitly prohibit employees from using confidential information to bet on prediction markets. Here are the details.

Following yesterday’s fiscal Q4 2026 earnings report, Apple today published its fiscal 2026 Form 10-K, which is a mandatory annual filing with the SEC that provides a detailed look at the company’s finances, business, and risks.

Among the documents included in the filing is an updated version of Apple’s insider trading policy.

Until last year, Apple’s insider trading policy, filed with the SEC as Exhibit 19.1, included the following prohibitions:

However, the updated policy includes a new prohibition:

No Trading in Prediction Markets Based on Confidential Information. Do not participate in “prediction markets” or similar platforms to wager, bet, trade, buy or sell contracts based on the outcome of future events, or otherwise enter into event contracts, when such activity involves the use of Apple Confidential Information (as defined in Apple’s Business Conduct Policy) about Apple or any other company (including Apple suppliers, manufacturers, vendors or customers, such as cellular network carriers or other business partners) obtained in connection with your work at Apple. You must also not tip Apple Confidential Information to others who may participate in such markets. Apple Confidential Information includes, but is not limited to, material nonpublic information. This prohibition applies whether or not the activity constitutes insider trading or securities trading under applicable laws.

While much of this may seem obvious, how insider trading rules apply to prediction markets has been something of a gray area, to put it mildly. And while major prediciton markets explicitly ban the practice in their terms of service, enforcement remains a challenge.

In Apple’s case, the new language explicitly extends restrictions beyond traditional securities trading, making it clear that employees cannot use confidential information to place bets on prediction markets, even when those transactions don’t qualify as insider trading under applicable laws.

You can read Apple’s full 2026 Form 10-K on its Investor Relations page.
