#3233. 7 Perfect Sci-Fi Movies That Hooked Me From the First 10 Minutes

The brilliance of science fiction lies in its ability to blend thrilling, out-of-this-world spectacle with explorations of human fears, ethics, and big ideas rooted in science. Through wonder and escapism, these films transport us to strange new worlds, futuristic cities, or deep space, giving our brains a moment of reprieve. Whether robots, clones, aliens, or artificial intelligence, these stories often mirror our mortality, isolation, and capacity to be human.

A good flick will sustain and entertain, but a brilliant sci-fi film will hook you immediately. Though incredible sci-fi movies exist throughout cinema history, these seven hook you within the first ten minutes. From a thrilling chase to a scrolling exposition that establishes an entire galaxy, these movies capture you instantaneously, leaving an impression that lasts far beyond the final credits.

Based on Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel, Blade Runner is a cyberpunk neo-noir science fiction thriller set in a dystopian Los Angeles in 2019. Retired police officer Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford) is forced back into service as a blade runner to "retire" bioengineered synthetic humans known as replicants. The film uses its narrative to question the boundary between human and machine.

Through visual overload, the film opens on a sweeping industrial city landscape, seemingly foreign to our modern eye, where fire-belching smokestacks, flying cars, and neon lights dominate the skyline. The camera then cuts to an extreme close-up of a human eye reflecting the cityscape, establishing the core themes of vision, surveillance, and the blurred line between what's natural and what is manufactured. From there, the audience is plunged into Dave Holden's (Morgan Paull) high-stakes Voight-Kampff interrogation of Leon (Brion James), a Nexus-6 replicant. With the world established, our hero, Deckard, is introduced, sitting on a rainy, grimy street as his mission is about to begin.

In Alfonso Cuarón's dystopian action thriller Children of Men, the planet is experiencing global infertility as humans have mysteriously lost the ability to procreate. As civilization crumbles, plagued by suicide, despair, and terrorism, the United Kingdom stands as one of the last functioning governments, turning into an authoritarian regime that rounds up, detains, and deports "fugees." Theo Farron (Clive Owen) is tasked with transporting Kee (Clare-Hope Ashitey), a miraculously pregnant refugee, to the Human Project.

The film's opening scene masterfully hooks you through abrupt worldbuilding, sensory shock, and a complete subversion of the genre. In total darkness, a bleak news broadcast drops key information about the dystopian stakes. When the visuals kick in, the camera tracks Theo as he pushes through a grieving crowd watching the news. The action kicks in when the coffee shop he just left explodes violently. The audio drops, mirroring the ringing tinnitus and capturing our protagonist's temporary deafness as a striking image of a bleeding woman holding her severed arm is seen. The sudden, visceral violence shatters all sense of safety as Cuarón's continuous, unbroken shot forces you to experience the event in real time.

In Doug Liman's military sci-fi action film Edge of Tomorrow, Major William Cage (Tom Cruise), a military public relations officer with no combat experience, is thrust into a time loop during a desperate human war against an alien race known as mimics. As the war rages on, Cage wakes up the next morning before the battle, only to find the loop resets to the same day every time he dies. He teams up with Rita Vrataski (Emily Blunt) as they train, die, and investigate the mysterious alien hivemind.

Within the first ten minutes, the film becomes a masterclass in efficient, high-stakes storytelling. Through an aggressive montage of real-world and fictional news footage, you're caught up on years of lore before meeting Cage, a smarmy PR slickster who desperately avoids the battlefield. The tension spikes when he is unexpectedly dropped on the front lines of a suicide mission beach invasion. Liman captures claustrophobic dread as Cage, strapped into a massive, lethal, weaponized suit, has no idea how to maneuver. Edge of Tomorrow establishes a terrifying world where death seems imminent.

All it took was a scroll to change the galaxy. In Star Wars: Episode IV—A New Hope, the first film in George Lucas' long-running franchise, a classic hero's journey unfolds during a galactic civil war against the tyrannical Galactic Empire. The Rebel Alliance steals the architectural plans for the planet-destroying superweapon, the Death Star. Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill) joins Obi-Wan Kenobi (Alec Guinness) and hired smuggler Han Solo (Harrison Ford) to rescue Princess Leia (Carrie Fisher) from Darth Vader's (James Earl Jones) clutches.

Star Wars hooks you immediately with John Williams' fanfare and the epic yellow text crawl that sets up the entire story. Without lecturing or boring the audience, the rolling text throws you into the fray at warp speed. From there, an endless Imperial Star Destroyer roars overhead as C-3PO and R2-D2 bicker through the chaos, giving you characters to latch onto instantly. As the smoke clears, the greatest sci-fi villain emerges, and terror is born without a lengthy introductory monologue. The iconic opening became a franchise staple, exciting fans for generations.

The scores below reveal how the Force sees you. Your highest number is your true alignment. Read on to understand what that means — and what it will cost you.

Disciplined, compassionate, and deeply attuned to the living Force, you have walked the path long enough to understand its demands — and accept them. You lead not through authority alone, but through example. You have felt the pull of the dark side and chosen otherwise, every time. That is not certainty. That is courage.

You are earnest, powerful, and brimming with potential — and you know it, which is both your greatest asset and your most dangerous flaw. You act before you think, trust your gut over your training, and sometimes confuse impatience for bravery. The Masters see something in you, though. The question isn't whether you have what it takes — it's whether you'll be patient enough to find out.

You are not simply dangerous — you are certain, and that is worse. You have decided what the galaxy needs, and you have decided you are the one to deliver it. Your power is genuine and formidable, earned through sacrifice that would have broken lesser beings. But examine your victories carefully. Every Sith believed their cause was righteous. The dark side's cruelest trick is that it agrees with you.

You were forged in fire and reshaped by those who found you at your lowest. You serve, because service gave you structure when you had none. Your allegiance is not to an ideology — it is to survival and to the master who gave you purpose. But there is something buried beneath the conditioning. The Jedi you hunt? You recognize them. Because you remember what it felt like before the choice was taken from you.

You have looked at the Jedi Code and the Sith Code and found both of them incomplete. You walk the line not out of indecision but out of conviction — you genuinely believe both extremes miss something essential. The Jedi don't fully trust you. The Sith think you're wasting your potential. They're both partially right. But so are you.

Written and directed by the Wachowskis, The Matrix follows computer hacker Neo (Keanu Reeves), who discovers that human reality is a complex computer simulation known as The Matrix. Rebel leader Morpheus (Laurence Fishburne) and his partner Trinity (Carrie-Anne Moss) contact him and see him as "The One" with the power to bend and manipulate the Matrix's physical laws and fightthe computer programs that police the simulation.

A high-octane philosophical wonder, The Matrix establishes mystery and breaks the laws of physics as it introduces an immediate, high-stakes threat. The film opens with glowing green computer code shifting across a black screen, establishing the cyberpunk atmosphere, with the only explanation being the voice of a woman discussing the mysterious "Neo." Espionage and curiosity arrive as Trinity is cornered by a police squad, and bang! The infamous bullet time is revealed. The groundbreaking effect comes as a cinematic, mind-bending shock.

A brilliant product of its time, James Cameron's The Terminator set the tone for sci-fi action films in the decades that followed. The first film in the franchise follows a T-8000 cyborg assassin (Arnold Schwarzenegger) sent back in time from a post-apocalyptic 2029 to 1984 Los Angeles to kill Sarah Connor (Linda Hamilton). The human resistance fights back as lone soldier Kyle Reese (Michael Biehn) is sent to protect her.

Within the opening minutes, Cameron grabs your attention with a bleak, post-apocalyptic Los Angeles that shows giant machines crushing human skulls. When the story transitions to 1984, a different type of fear is introduced when two completely naked men emerge from a violent, crackling electrical storm. Both search for clothes in different ways: The Terminator's innate brutality arrives as an unstoppable, silent force of nature, killing a group of punks, including ripping through one's torso. Meanwhile, Reese is set up as the desperate underdog, without that same strength.

A truly delightful sci-fi story, WALL-E helped young viewers fall in love with the genre like never before. The story follows WALL-E, a lonely trash-compacting robot on a ruined, abandoned Earth who follows a sleek probe droid named EVE across the galaxy to help humanity rediscover its home. A beautifully filmed, philosophically tinged wonder, WALL-E remains one of Pixar's best.

Within the first 10 minutes, the film uses pure visual and auditory storytelling to build instant empathy for a rusty old robot on a ruined planet, without a single word of dialogue. The wasteland is strikingly juxtaposed with the upbeat, toe-tapping vintage sounds of "Put On Your Sunday Clothes" from Hello, Dolly! As the titular character is introduced, WALL-E becomes instantly endearing as he embarks on his daily routines, hoarding treasures and artifacts like a lighter, a Rubik's Cube, and the film's VHS. His childlike curiosity mirrors our own, letting our wonder join him on his extraordinary journey.

#3230. macOS 27.3 adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look

Starting with macOS 27.3, users can preview Markdown files with proper formatting directly in Quick Look. Here are the details.

Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and new tools for third-party developers.

Among the smaller changes coming to the Mac is a welcome improvement to Quick Look. As of macOS 27.3 beta 1, .md files are rendered with proper formatting directly in Quick Look, rather than displaying their raw Markdown syntax.

Apple has been expanding Markdown support across its platforms, including the ability to import and export Markdown files in Notes. Markdown has also become increasingly important with the rise of AI agents, which use .md files to store instructions, context, and other information.

In fact, as Federico Viticci noted today on X, Apple’s new Siri AI app skills feature also uses Markdown-based SKILL.md files, allowing developers to provide instructions that help Siri perform complex tasks within their apps.

What a journey for Markdown, @gruber The new Siri AI developer framework now officially uses skills, with specific Markdown guidance for SKILL .md agent files https://t.co/koi8K541le pic.twitter.com/TF72JJZRXc

For the uninitiated, Markdown is a simple text formatting syntax created by John Gruber in 2004, and has since become widely used for writing documentation, publishing content online (including this very post), and, more recently, providing instructions to AI agents.

Markdown is a text-to-HTML conversion tool for web writers. Markdown allows you to write using an easy-to-read, easy-to-write plain text format, then convert it to structurally valid HTML.

In practice, this means you can create headings, bold text, lists, and links using just a few simple characters. And, starting with macOS 27.3, you’ll be able to preview the results directly in Quick Look, without having to open the file in a separate app.

To learn more about Markdown, follow this link.

#3229. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

Microsoft’s flagship development tool, Visual Studio Professional 2026, reduces much of the friction that used to come with large projects, and it’s on sale for just $29.97 on StackSocial right now, which is far less than what most developers expect to pay for a professional-grade IDE.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. And CodeLens adds useful context right inside the editor—who last edited a method, which tests cover it, and whether recent changes broke anything—without forcing you to dig through menus or version history. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. It saves time on repetitive work, but you’ll still want to read what it writes.

Collaboration is another area where this version earns its keep. Live Share allows teammates to jump into a debugging or editing session without cloning the repo or matching environments. That’s useful for code reviews or troubleshooting, but it depends heavily on a stable internet connection. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a full-featured, 64-bit IDE for Windows designed for developers working on complex, multi-project codebases, and it's on sale right now for a one-time price of $29.97 on StackSocial.

#3223. 10 Most Perfect Thriller Movies of All Time

One simply can't get enough of thriller movies. Fast-paced, heart-pounding, and packed with twists and surprises, the genre feeds off the reactions of audiences as they are pulled to the edge of their seats. A good thriller delivers suspense, but an excellent one reinvents classic thriller elements, all while staying relevant to the anxieties of the era it was released in.

Whether it's the effects of corporate culture, a rookie police officer taking on 30 levels of criminals, or a chef who's sick and tired of serving uppity patrons, these movies show that there's more than one way to deliver the adrenaline. That said, here are 10 intense thriller movies that are perfect from start to finish.

What happens when a revolutionary loses his spark? One Battle After Another introduces us to Bob Ferguson (Leonardo DiCaprio), a former demolition expert for a militant group who, 16 years later, has become a jaded single father to the teenage Willa (Chase Infiniti). But when a secret is revealed about Willa’s true origins, she goes off the grid, prompting the washed-up Bob to reignite the fire he once had.

One Battle After Another has the makings of a classic thriller. However, there is a refreshing comedic edge to him. Considering that he’s not as energetic and physically limber as he used to be, he falls and stumbles as he evades the cops. Bob can barely run without losing his breath, but with his daughter kidnapped, he’s not catching a break anytime soon.

Sinners refuses to be boxed into conventional thriller norms. When twin brothers Smoke and Stack (Michael B. Jordan) open a massive juke joint on the outskirts of town, the last thing they expect is for a group of vampires to crash the party. As the night wears on, these undead intruders begin turning the brothers’ human guests one by one.

Historical, breathtaking, and full of movement, Ryan Coogler has a knack for using horror to bring up broader themes like racial identity and systemic oppression. In Sinners, blues music serves as the voice of the marginalized, giving power to those who play it. Coogler goes one step further by portraying blues as a near-magical force that can literally open portals to the supernatural.

No other thriller has tested an audience’s perception of reality more than Oldboy. For reasons unknown, a drunken Oh Dae-su (Choi Min-sik) is abducted and imprisoned in a sealed room with no communication to the outside world. 15 years have passed, and the now disoriented Dae-su is suddenly returned to society — this time framed for the murder of his wife.

It’s mystery after mystery in Oldboy, but it all boils down to a hyper-specific revenge ploy. Sometimes, death is too swift and merciful a solution — although the movie does boast graphic scenes like the violent hallway fight. Instead, the most effective kind of revenge is one that twists a person’s cognition, leading them to make immoral decisions by their own doing.

Corporate gets cold-blooded in American Psycho. Although modern movies like The Wolf of Wall Street show the high-adrenaline rush from working in investment, Christian Bale’s performance as banker Patrick Bateman is much more polished and restrained — but even more deadly. A swanky apartment and a ridiculous salary aren’t enough to fill his empty void, prompting him to find alternative sources of pleasure.

Thus begins the true thesis of American Psycho — the rich aren’t devoid of feeling because they lack material wealth; it’s because they can’t appreciate what they have. Capitalism emphasizes the idea of having more. Unfortunately, the more Bateman tries to gain — whether status, money, or women — the less satisfaction he finds, until he finds something that cannot be bought: the ability to control whether someone lives or dies.

The only thing that’s separating a 20-man SWAT team and one crime lord in The Raid is a 30-story rundown apartment. But like Dante’s nine circles of hell, each level in the building is infested with all sorts of criminals. From drug dealers to machete-wielding killers, rookie officer Rama must conquer the threats on each floor before getting his hands on the feared underworld kingpin, Tama Riyadi.

There is a non-stop, relentless pace that drives The Raid from start to finish. The not-so-fun part about raiding a high-rise building is that there is practically no way of escaping. The hallways are tight and narrow, meaning that any criminal could just jump on Rama from whichever direction, amplifying the anxiety from being only literally one step away from being stabbed by a knife.

There's no knowing where a Quentin Tarantino thriller might go, and the in-your-face Inglourious Basterds is as unpredictable as they come. Lt. Aldo Raine (Brad Pitt) is responsible for his "Basterds," a crew of Jewish-American soldiers whose job is to infiltrate Nazi spaces and kill them. Somewhere in the French countryside, Shosanna Dreyfus (Mélanie Laurent) has a personal vendetta against the infamous "Jew Hunter," Hans Landa (Christoph Waltz).

Inglourious Basterds doesn’t skimp on the anxiety of being hunted like helpless prey, and much of that tension comes from Walt's performance as Landa. Widely regarded as one of cinema’s greatest villains, Waltz plays him as chillingly polite one moment and completely ruthless the next, especially when he suspects he has found a Jew in his presence.

In Parasite, the resourceful Ki-taek (Song Kang-ho) does everything he can to pull his Kim family out of their scrappy, cramped basement apartment. His luck changes when his son, Ki-woo (Choi Woo-shik), secures a tutoring position with the affluent Park family. With no proper qualifications, he sweet-talks his way into the job, gradually bringing the rest of his family into the Parks’ lives.

Parasite challenges the audience’s pre-existing notions about the rich versus the poor. While it may seem unethical for the Kim family to manipulate the Parks, they are simply doing what they can to achieve upward mobility. The Parks, on the other hand, appear kind because they have the resources to afford generosity. The film suggests that privilege itself enables the ability to be “nice.”

A weekend out of the city goes sideways in Get Out. Black photographer Chris Washington (Daniel Kaluuya) accepts an invitation from his white girlfriend, Rose Armitage (Allison Williams), to a family gathering at her home in the countryside. Unbeknownst to him, her parents have a horrifying pastime of hypnotizing and lobotomizing Black individuals as a vessel for immortality.

Get Out reimagines how modern-day slavery would take place. The scariest part is that, unlike in the past, with recorded accounts of white masters being viciously cruel, Rose’s family initially welcomes Chris with open arms. This sense of niceness — almost too nice — strikes a nerve, considering that Chris is the only Black person in the countryside with no outside communication.

Unlike Marco Pierre White and Gordon Ramsay, Chef Julian Slowik (Ralph Fiennes) is cool as a cucumber — the perfect facade to hide his taste for revenge in The Menu. Obnoxious food snob Tyler (Nicholas Hoult) takes his less-than-enthusiastic date Margot (Anya Taylor-Joy) to a group fine dining experience at Chef Julian's secluded island restaurant, only for the night to get bloody.

Despite the terror they face from the disillusioned Chef Julian, there’s something darkly funny about paying $1,250 per person only to end up getting killed. Then again, The Menu is about a service industry man’s attempt to get revenge on the entitled guests who have caused him to lose his passion for the simple joy of cooking. The wealthy will pay anything for an “experience,” and that is exactly what they’re going to get.

Nobody can trust anyone in The Handmaiden. Set in Japanese-occupied Korea in the 1930s, Sook-hee (Kim Tae-ri) is appointed as the loyal handmaiden to the Japanese heiress, Lady Hideko. Unlike the tales of cruel masters, Lady Hideko (Kim Min-hee) shows nothing but compassion to Sook-hee. Unbeknownst to them, the male powers shadowing over them plan to use them as pawns for material and colonial gains.

The Handmaiden is as much of a period piece and a forbidden romance as it is a thriller. Considering the context of the time, the two leading women, despite their class differences, are no less put into precarious positions. For all its sickening plot twists, the bond between Sook-he and Lady Hideko gives the thriller a strong sense of heart. After all, the two are only trying to escape from their oppression, even if that route requires manipulation.

#3217. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3216. How to get access to Sonos AI features, as company aims to avoid another app disaster

When Sonos tried a major app update two years ago, things did not go well. Much-loved features disappeared, older speakers experienced connection problems, and accessibility features were broken. That debacle saw the company’s CEO fired.

The company is taking a much more cautious approach as it moves into the AI era with a Sonos 27voice update, enabling natural-language voice control via Hey Sonos requests …

The whole mess started when Sonos launched the company’s first headphones, the Ace, intended to compete with AirPods Max. The app needed to be updated to support these, and the company decided to use it as an opportunity for a ground-up rebuild, launching a completely new app just ahead of the launch.

Customers responded angrily to the loss of key functionality, compatibility issues with older speakers, and accessibility problems. Sonos initially downplayed the complaints, but CEO Patrick Spence subsequently emailed customers to apologize, and provide a timeline for fixes, subsequently making seven promises. However, customers weren’t impressed, and called for Spence to be fired – later getting their wish.

This time around, Sonos started out with a modest update in the form of the Sonos 27 app, leaving the more substantial changes to a subsequent Sonos 27voice version. This will replace the more limited voice control available today, much like the update from old Siri to Siri AI.

Rather than pushing it out to all customers, Sonos is adopting a very cautious approach. First, you’ll have to request early access to the beta and be approved. Second, the company is testing the feature with a relatively small group of users. Third, it’s seeking detailed feedback from beta testers before a planned launch next year.

The new features work in much the same way as Siri on HomePods.

You can use Sonos 27voice at any time by saying the wake word, “Hey Sonos.” While Sonos is listening, the white status light on your Sonos product will glow brighter and the volume will lower if any audio is playing. A confirmation tone will play after Sonos understands your request.

The company says you can then use natural language for both music-related commands and information searches. The company gives the following music examples:

#3212. 10 2026 Movies That Are Officially Oscar Contenders

This year, the record-breaking MCU movie Spider-Man: Brand New Day and Christopher Nolan's historical epic The Odyssey headlined the biggest summer of cinema since the COVID-19 pandemic. But the late summer nights are turning to cold winter evenings, and the attention of cinephiles has turned to the biggest event in the film calendar: the Academy Awards.

The glitz and glamor of Oscars night is coming into view, as the 99th ceremony readies to celebrate the best of the past twelve months of film. Scheduled to take place March 14, 2027, at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, next year's Academy Awards will feature all the brightest stars in Hollywood today, with ambitious blockbusters, indie darlings, and even a documentary hoping to earn a coveted Best Picture nomination. But who are the current favorites? Here's a look at 10 2026 movies that are officially Oscar contenders.

The film on everyone's lips, A24's You Can See Everything, might finally make history as the first documentary to earn a Best Picture nomination in 100 years of Academy history. The documentary, co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, explores the days leading up to the incarceration of the infamous Theranos founder, Elizabeth Holmes.

"The year's most original movie will make you question reality," wrote Collider's Samuel R. Murrian in one of countless glowing reviews for this mind-bending documentary. With its viral success helping rocket the film up the box office charts, and with the world stunned by the life-altering contents of this three-hour masterpiece, it's possible that You Can See Everything ​​​​​​won't just earn a Best Picture nomination; it could win the trophy.

One of the defining films of 2026, it would be difficult to find someone who hasn't yet seen Project Hail Mary. This epic Phil Lord and Christopher Miller-directed space story follows Ryan Gosling's Ryland Grace as he leads a one-man mission into the stars to try and save the universe. However, he isn't alone in the dense emptiness of space, as he is joined on his mission by an alien he names Rocky.

A favorite to earn plenty of nominations in technical categories, with lead puppeteer and voice actor James Ortiz potentially in the race for Best Supporting Actor, Project Hail Mary will most definitely make its mark on next year's Oscars. As one of the most critically and commercially successful films of 2026, come March 14, 2027, the world could watch Grace Rocky save Oscars.

Another of the most popular films of the year, Focus Features' Obsession will hope to follow in the footsteps of The Substance and Weapons by becoming this year's horror darling at the Academy Awards. Star Inde Navarrette seems most likely to take home Oscars gold, as she currently ranks as one of the favorites in the Best Actress category for a performance that Collider's Hannah Hunt called "one of the year's best" in her review.

A box office record-breaker, becoming the highest-grossing original horror movie of this century among many more titles, Obsession shocked the world as it overcame the latest Star Wars movie through sheer viral appeal. Curry Barker's breakout is nothing short of a horror masterpiece, as one of the most important visionaries in Hollywood's next era gets off to a flying start.

Although some titles lead the charge during the Oscars race, others perform better under the radar, lurking beneath the competition before surprising cinephiles with several nominations. Right now, it seems like one of the best outside contenders for Academy recognition is Olivia Wilde's The Invite, a remake of the Spanish-language comedy The People Upstairs.

Unfolding like a great play, The Invite takes a simple premise, a single location, and four actors at the top of their game and transforms them into an utterly unmissable comedy. But this comedy isn't without its dramatic flair, with every twist and turn playing out like a hilariously realized thriller. Starring Seth Rogen, Edward Norton, and Penélope Cruz alongside Wilde, The Invite feels destined to earn recognition in writing and acting categories.

If, for the aforementioned Penélope Cruz, Oscar night doesn't equal gold for Wilde's The Invite, rest assured she stands a second chance as part of the ensemble of one of the bookies' favorites. Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi's La Bola Negra is a 155-minute drama inspired by the unfinished work of the same name that explores the connections between three gay men and the pain they endure.

Themes of love and loss in the queer community, as well as the erasure of queer identity, become ever more relevant each passing year, with these topics better represented at the Academy Awards in the process. La Bola Negra is the latest LGBTQIA+ story to receive the Oscars spotlight, as it is deemed a favorite to not just earn a Best Picture nomination, but to win the prize.

When forecasting the Oscars nominees for 2027, it's wise to look back at the historical voting of the often predictable Academy. Both 2021's Dune and 2022's Dune: Part Two received nominations in the Best Picture category, having combined to win eight trophies so far. So, with that in mind, the final installment in Denis Villeneuve's acclaimed trilogy seems destined to pick up a handful of nominations once again.

The ambitious attempt to turn the once-thought "unfilmable" Frank Herbert story into cinematic magic has already been the subject of endless praise from critics. But in his last installment, perhaps it's time for Villeneuve to win in the biggest categories? That's what many sci-fi fans will think, and as December 18 and the consequences of Paul Atreides' (Timothée Chalamet) power inch closer, whispers of a Dune: Part Three Best Picture bid grow.

Andrew Scott has quietly proven to be one of the most consistent actors working today, submitting a fine selection of truly terrific performances over the past few years. Come Oscars night next year, it seems the Sherlock star will finally receive recognition as one of the favorites to take home the Best Actor prize as Ian Charleson in the stunning drama, Elsinore.

Directed by Simon Stone and written by Stephen Beresford, Elsinore looks likely to be the second Hamlet-related film in two years to take home an acting prize at the Oscars, following Jessie Buckley's deserved win for Hamnet. Also like Hamnet, Elsinore looks to be this year's biggest tearjerker, with Collider's Therese Lacson writing, "For god's sake, bring more than just one pack of tissues to the theater," in her review.

In 2023, The Banshees of Inisherin was one of the year's biggest nominees, having earned nods in eight categories. Sadly, it won zero prizes, a fate that Irish filmmaker Martin McDonagh will be hoping to avoid with his latest Academy Award play, Wild Horse Nine. The film follows two CIA agents on a mission from Santiago to Easter Island in 1973, and is packed with all of McDonagh's typical dark, comedic wit.

As usual, a McDonagh movie looks set to take home nominations in writing categories, with star John Malkovich heavily tipped to take on the aforementioned Scott for Best Actor. Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi, Parker Posey, and the rest of the supporting cast deserve just as much credit for this uniquely encapsulating effort from an unstoppable filmmaker.

It's rare that any given year's Palme d'Or winner doesn't make an impact at the Academy Awards. In recent years, the likes of Bong Joon Ho's Parasite and Sean Baker's Anora have won both Cannes' biggest prize and the Best Picture trophy, so it's fair to assume that Cristian Mungiu's Fjord will also make its presence known come Oscar nominations day.

Mungiu's second Palme d'Or winner is arguably his most controversial film, touching on deeply nuanced topics and never offering an easy moral way out. But it is in this nuance that Fjord thrives, with Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve delivering perfectly detailed performances that capture both the best and worst of these troubled characters and their terrifying situation.

The front-runner to take home the Academy's biggest prize is Christopher Nolan's historical epic The Odyssey, dubbed an "unrivaled cinematic spectacle" in Joe Schmidt's review for Collider. This famous tale's star-studded retelling hasn't been without its detractors, but those with a say have made it clear their love for The Odyssey, placing it firmly at the #1 spot in many people's predictions.

In fact, The Odyssey could very well overtake Ryan Coogler's Sinners as the most nominated film of all time, considering its sure impact in both the major and craft categories. Nolan delivers his typically ambitious scale and scope to one of history's grandest stories, culminating in a final thirty minutes that are, without doubt, some of the most encapsulating cinema of the decade so far. Could The Odyssey sail to a record-breaking Oscars night? All will be revealed in a few months.

#3211. Apple still charging 300% of costs on iPhone storage upgrades, says WSJ

Opting for more RAM or storage when buying Apple devices has always been an expensive business, with the company famously charging huge markups.

Apple said in its most recent earnings report that even after the price increases, its margins are being squeezed by higher component costs. But an analysis suggests that the company is still charging three times its own costs for higher storage tiers on the iPhone 18 Pro …

To be fair to Apple, some of the criticism about the premiums charged on configuring a device with more memory or flash storage hasn’t been comparing, well, apples with apples. The SSDs used in Macs, for example, are very much faster than the lower-spec third-party storage cards people typically cite as evidence for the company’s greed.

why are people defending Apple? They are bending everybody over double to keep their profit margins. They buy a billion memory chips or SSD's at a time so they are getting them much lower in price even if the price has gone up.

All the same, there’s no denying that the iPhone maker has always applied extremely high markups to its own direct costs. With the iPhone 17 Pro, for example, upgrading from 256GB to 1TB cost a buyer $400. A Wall Street Journal analysis cited by Macworld says that Apple’s cost at the time was $42, almost a 1,000% markup.

Apple this week warned that memory costs will reduce its holiday quarter profit margins.

When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs. Parekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon.

However, the WSJ’s number-crunching suggests that we probably don’t need to get out the violins just yet. The paper compared the same upgrade on the iPhone 18 Pro, where Apple has increased the price difference to $600. Although the Cupertino company is paying dramatically more, with an estimated direct cost of $192, that still amounts to customers being charged more than three times the price paid by Apple.

Mini PC or all-in-one? Here’s how Apple’s M6 desktops stack up

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’re looking for a new computer and want a Mac, your first instinct might be to pick up one of the best MacBooks. However, opting for Apple’s premium laptops or even the much more affordable MacBook Neo has its drawbacks — especially if you're paying a portability premium for a machine that will rarely leave your desk.

Sure, the new MacBook Pro OLED looks fantastic with that illuminated Apple logo on the lid, and it is the first Mac with a touchscreen. For the majority of people, though, it’s total overkill. Unless you plan on editing 8K video or running demanding local AI models on the go, you’re buying far more computer than you need.

If you just want a reliable, fast Mac to use at home, Apple’s desktops are a much better bet. The powerhouse Mac Studio will be overkill for most, too. That’s why, if you’re setting up a dedicated home office or just need a shared family machine for the living room, the new Mac mini and iMac with Apple’s M6 chips make a whole lot more sense.

While you can configure either with beefier specs, I’ll be focusing on the entry-level models for this comparison: the base Mac mini with M6 and the base iMac with M6. The latest Mac mini landed in September of 2026, followed shortly by the new iMac in November. Since both sport the latest Apple Silicon, either will easily last you for years to come.

Having reviewed both the Mac mini M6 and the iMac M6, the question is: which one actually deserves a spot on your desk and is worth your hard-earned cash? Here’s a full breakdown of their real-world performance, design, ergonomics, and value to help you decide between one of the best mini PCs and one of the best all-in-one computers you can buy right now.

2 x USB-C, 3.5mm headphone jack (front), 3 x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, 1 x HDMI, 1 x 2.5 gigabit Ethernet (back)

2 x Thunderbolt 4, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack

Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, Gigabit Ethernet

Even though the Mac mini with M6 and iMac with M6 are new Apple desktops, they share one very important thing in common: neither sports a radical redesign. Instead, they feature almost identical designs to their predecessors.

The Mac mini was completely redesigned back in 2024 with the Mac mini M4. Like that machine, this new model is much more compact at 5 x 5 x 2 inches and retains those front ports — specifically two USB-C ports and a 3.5mm headphone jack. Besides charging, you can use those front ports to quickly connect your iPhone to transfer data, and having a headphone jack on the front means you can use wired headphones without having to plug them in at the back.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Then around back on the Mac mini M6, you get three Thunderbolt 4 ports, an HDMI port, a Gigabit Ethernet port, and a power port. Those Thunderbolt ports are great if you want to use one of Apple’s first-party monitors like the Studio Display or Studio Display XDR, but they also work with most portable monitors. Meanwhile, the Mac mini M6’s HDMI port is ideal for traditional monitors without a USB-C port.

The iMac with M6’s design is even older, though, as Apple first introduced it back in 2021 with the iMac M1. Though it has a much larger footprint than the Mac mini, the iMac M6 is still quite compact for an all-in-one at 21.5 x 18.1 x 5.8 inches.

Given the iMac M6 is an all-in-one, you don’t get nearly as many ports as you do on the Mac mini since you don’t need to hook it up to a separate monitor. While my review unit has four ports, on the base model, you just get two Thunderbolt 4 ports.

Then on the left edge of the device, there’s a 3.5mm headphone jack and that’s it. You can get an Ethernet port on its power adapter, but you’ll have to pay extra for it. The iMac M6 also features a six-speaker system and a built-in 12MP Center Stage camera for video calls.

Overall, you can’t go wrong with either the Mac mini or the iMac when it comes to their respective designs. Both desktops look sleek, but if you want a computer with the smallest footprint and the most ports, the Mac mini is the better choice. You will have to bring your own display, webcam, and other accessories, though.

Although the latest Mac mini and iMac both sport Apple’s new M6 chips, there is a slight difference between them when it comes to the base models.

While the Mac mini has an M6 chip with 12 CPU and 12 GPU cores, the M6 chip in the iMac only has 10 of each. In my testing, both machines feel quite snappy for everyday tasks like opening apps and browsing the web thanks to the improved efficiency that comes with the 2nm process Apple used with its M6 chips. It’s with more demanding tasks where you’ll notice a difference.

For instance, if you’re editing a lot of photos, rendering video, or are a power user with dozens of browser tabs open simultaneously, then the more powerful M6 chip in the Mac mini will certainly make a difference. If you just want a Mac for watching videos, writing emails, and basic daily tasks, the difference between these two M6 chips will be negligible.

One other area where you will definitely see an impact though is with gaming. While neither of these Macs can serve as a replacement for one of the best gaming PCs, they’re surprisingly capable when it comes to gaming and this is especially true with older titles. Here, the two extra GPU cores in the Mac mini help keep frame rates smoother.

For those who plan on pushing their new Apple desktop to the limit or playing games on it, then the more powerful M6 chip in the Mac mini is the better choice. However, if you just need a reliable machine for day-to-day use, the 10-core M6 in the base iMac has plenty of power to get the job done.

If you opt for a Mac mini over an iMac, you’re obviously going to need to get a monitor to go along with it — or you could use one you already have, just like with your mouse and keyboard, to bring your total overall cost down. However, if you want an excellent display with a high pixel count without having to do a ton of research first, there’s no screen quite like the one on the iMac.

The iMac features a 24-inch, 4.5K display with a resolution of 4480 x 2520. Since this panel is manufactured specifically for Apple, you won’t find another standalone monitor on the market with that exact screen size, resolution, and pixel density.

Most monitors that deliver around 218 pixels per inch like the iMac cost as much or more than a Mac mini M6 on their own. Samsung’s 27-inch ViewFinity S9 runs around $800 to $1,000, while LG’s 27-inch UltraFine 5K costs around $1,000 to $1,200. Granted, those panels are slightly larger than 24 inches, but they demand a hefty premium.

If you want something larger and more affordable, 27-inch 4K panels like the Dell UltraSharp or Asus ProArt can be had for around $400 to $500. However, because they aren’t native Apple displays, you do miss out on native features — like using the brightness keys on a Magic Keyboard to dim the screen without third-party software.

Even though 24 inches might sound modest, the high pixel density of the iMac gives you plenty of usable canvas. In my testing with the iMac M6, I was able to comfortably work with two browser windows side by side without feeling cramped.

There is one big catch with the iMac, though: ergonomics. Unlike the Studio Display or Pro Display XDR, there is no height-adjustable stand option. The built-in stand only tilts about 5 degrees forward or 25 degrees back.

To get your iMac to a proper ergonomic height — where your eyes naturally align just below the top third of the panel — you’ll likely need to set it on a monitor riser or desk shelf. Alternatively, you can ditch the stand altogether at checkout and order the factory VESA mount version, though you'll need to budget for one of the best monitor arms alongside your new all-in-one.

If you want a massive display, dual or even triple-monitor flexibility, or full control over your desk layout, the Mac mini is the obvious choice. But if you want a compact, incredibly sharp screen built right into the machine, the iMac’s display is tough to beat.

As the Mac mini doesn’t give you that computer-in-a-box experience that the iMac does, there’s a whole host of optional 3rd-party accessories available for it. From stands and hubs that sit underneath to enclosures that rest on top to add extra ports and even M.2 SSD slots for expanded storage, you can really accessorize Apple’s smallest Mac to your heart’s desire.

You’ll find a few USB hubs and add-ons for the iMac, but nowhere near as many as you will for the Mac mini. One new accessory I’m looking forward to testing with the iMac M6 is BenQ’s iScreenBar, a monitor light bar designed specifically to match the color and aluminum aesthetic of Apple’s all-in-one.

Likewise, Satechi makes a slim dock that sits directly over the iMac’s base to add front-facing ports and an SSD slot — similar to its popular stand and hub for the Mac mini. It’s a clean setup, but overall, the 3rd-party accessory ecosystem for the iMac remains much smaller, and for obvious reasons: there's just less to add to an all-in-one.

When it comes to first-party upgrades from Apple, you can configure both machines with extra unified memory and internal storage. Keep in mind that because everything is soldered down, these upgrades have to be chosen at checkout when ordering through Apple’s website — you can't crack either machine open to upgrade them later.

The most unique upgrade for the iMac M6 is Apple’s nano-texture glass. Just like on high-end MacBooks, instead of standard glossy glass that catches reflections, you can pay an extra $200 at checkout to add a matte finish. The catch? Apple doesn't offer nano-texture on the base 10-core iMac. You have to step up to the higher-tier model first before tacking on that $200 display upgrade, which widens the price gap between it and the Mac mini considerably. Still, there’s no other all-in-one on the market that offers a matte display quite like it.

If you want a vast ecosystem of desk mounts, docks, and external drives to completely personalize your workstation, the Mac mini is the obvious choice. But if you work in a sunlit room with nearby windows and glare constantly drives you crazy, stepping up to an iMac with nano-texture glass might be worth the extra investment.

Although the Mac mini M4 could be had for $599 at launch, thanks to RAMaggedon and the ongoing component crunch, Apple bumped up the starting price of the new Mac mini M6 to $899. As a result, when you factor in the cost of a display, keyboard, mouse, webcam, and speakers, the Mac mini is suddenly playing in the exact same price bracket as the iMac.

The iMac M6 saw a price increase of its own. While the iMac M4 started at $1,299, the new M6-powered version climbs to $1,499. The Mac mini used to be an unbeatable bargain compared to the rest of Apple’s lineup, but if you don’t already have a desk full of peripherals at home, you could easily spend $1,350 to $1,450 just to get a setup comparable to the iMac.

The real value proposition between the two comes down to your existing hardware. If you already have a spare monitor, keyboard, and mouse sitting on your desk, the Mac mini M6 delivers better raw performance for significantly less cash. But if you’re starting completely from scratch, the iMac’s $1,499 sticker price includes a built-in 4.5K display, crisp speakers, a 12MP Center Stage camera, and a color-matched Magic Keyboard and Magic Mouse right in the box.

If this is your first dedicated desktop, the iMac is the easier, better-value buy — unless you prefer an à la carte approach where you handpick every screen, dock, and keyboard yourself. If total customization is the goal, or you already have the accessories to make it work, go with the Mac mini instead.

While you can’t go wrong with either the Mac mini M6 or the iMac M6, the choice between the two ultimately comes down to how complicated you want your desk setup to be.

Let’s say you just moved and need to get to work right away in a new apartment where space is at a premium. One trip to the Apple Store later, you have a complete desktop in a box that you can set up in less than 30 minutes. If you want to heavily personalize your workspace, however — or if you prefer a much larger display or even multiple screens — then the Mac mini makes far more sense.

Regardless of which entry-level Apple desktop you choose, make sure you know what you’ll be using it for and how demanding your workflow will be before hitting checkout. When it comes to their internal components, neither the Mac mini M6 nor the iMac M6 can be upgraded after the fact. It’s essential that you configure the right chip, memory, and storage the first time around.

Although I review mini PCs for a living and have always been a big fan of the Mac mini, setting up and testing the iMac gave me a whole new appreciation for its simplicity. Sometimes, there is undeniable value in not having to overthink your monitor, cables, and peripherals.
